Publication Year: 2015 Publication Country: United States Title: Kaularahasya
Many folios are missing from this manuscript.
Note that the conjunct letter *ṛ* is frequently added by the scribe above a word without apparent justification.
Folios 1–8 not found. "Wine, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union— O Goddess, with these five things beginning with the letter 'ma,' the Kaula should worship in the womb."
The worship of drink from the left hand is proclaimed as the "leftward" (vāmī) sequence;
it proceeds from the right hand for the offering of drink and speech, and from the satisfaction of the left hand.
Indeed, one is called a *kaula* because of worship with the right hand;
one is designated as *dakṣiṇa* simply because of worshipping with the right hand alone.
Worship is said to be of three kinds: with desire, without desire, and free from both.
That which possesses desire is the seed of liberation and the ground; that which is with desire is the source of worldly existence.
The right path is considered superior, while the left is held to be even more excellent;
he who truly knows the left is indeed the supreme Guru.
I know the full extent of the foot [of the Veda], as do Sanaka and the others; Pipala, Śiṣṭha, and the rest know half of it; and others know it according to their respective measure.
9a) Here, millions perish and are born into the wombs of worms.
Those who seek that path know it; they are liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed taught the left-hand path (vāmamārga) to Phalguna.
While I was reflecting, I perceived that impermanence is characterized by the outcaste,
the Turk, the slayer of a Brahmin, or even the wandering mendicant.
Whether he be a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) or a follower of the Left Path (*vāmamārgī*), he is a fit vessel for both enjoyment and liberation;
for the paths of the Left and the Right are traditionally held to be the procedure for Kālī and Tārā respectively.
In the Chinnā-vidhi, Vāmamārga is associated with Vagalā on the left;
while Sundarī and Vāmadivyā are established upon the right-hand path.
Vālāvidyā, Dakṣavidyā, Mātaṅgī, Vāmā,
Dakṣiṇā, Kevalā, Bhuvanā, Lakṣmā, and Dhūmā are those who travel by the right-hand path.
Sumukhī is on the left and is not satisfied; Vaṭuka is both left and right.
In the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), the Right and Left [are established]; in the Southern [Tradition], the Divine and the Left.
Kaula and Dakṣa are in the west, while Kaula and Vāma are likewise in the north.
O Maheśānī, those in the celestial realms above and likewise those in the netherworlds of the left are all the Yakṣiṇīs and other sciences, as well as Kāminī, the mistress of yoga.
They attain accomplishment through the left-hand path, and not otherwise is there any bestower of success;
by the union of the left and right, they are devoted to the practice of both.
In the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, and likewise the Svāyambhuva [Tantras],
as well as in the Cāndra, Cīna, Pāñcarātra, Vaiṣṇava, and even the Vaidika [traditions].
In the Kali age, the twice-born will become perverse;
likewise, even on the path of vision, if one does not act rightly.
O Goddess of the gods, his success does not come to pass; he is proclaimed as my enemy.
In the Kula tradition, the Vāma path is said to be superior to all others.
Even there, O Maheśānī, Kālikā Tārā is remembered as most beloved in ritual; in the Kāpālika tradition, O Goddess, the Vāmamārga is the underlying cause.
10a) By means of the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), all things are accomplished; not otherwise.
O Goddess, without the left-hand path, the deities are certainly not accomplished.
The goddesses proclaimed in the Uttarāmnāya are pleased by the five [offerings];
however, if even one essential element is lacking, they curse the practitioner.
Regarding the drinking of wine by the deities of the Western Tradition, they maintain that it may be done or not done;
yet, they declare that without the four *m's*, [the practice] is cursed.
The performance or non-performance of the rites for the deities mentioned in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya),
as well as their essential threefold mantra-practice— without these, those [deities] pronounce a curse.
The goddesses mentioned in the Ūrdhvāmnāya, as well as my Fish-forms— both manifest and unmanifest—
and my two essential forms, they curse those who exist without them.
The fourfold assembly of the deities of the Southern Tradition (Dakṣiṇāmnāya) is prohibited;
for even they will curse the practitioner if he is without Menakā.
The ritual action of one performing Kaula rites is not designated as Vedic;
the ritual action of one performing Vedic rites is not designated as Kaula.
When both are lost due to conflict, one should therefore proceed with care;
when the left path enters the right, that indeed occurs through the gods.
He is obstructed and even afflicted, and does not attain success;
O gods, when one following the right path enters the left, then [this occurs].
They cause the left-handed practitioner to fall from both worlds and swallow him up;
therefore, having understood the path of one's own family, one should perform worship.
If one hears a tantra by chance, or even through deception or force,
or if a verse spoken by another should cause harm, one should then rebuke it.
One should never speak after merely looking at a treatise; one should never act [upon it] anywhere;
one should not look [at it], nor teach it, nor perform it, nor indeed accomplish it.
For those who recite mantras after looking at them written in a book,
their sin is proclaimed to be equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Therefore, one should always perform the Tantric initiation with great effort.
Thus ends the second chapter in the venerable *Kaularahasya*. 2.11a)
Now, regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), first there are the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*):
birth, life-giving, awakening, piercing, as well as sprinkling,
purification, and nourishment.
Satiating, kindling, and satisfaction—these ten are the purificatory rites of mantra;
therefore, I shall first explain initiation (dīkṣā) in detail.
Knowledge is bestowed and the destructions of sins are diminished;
therefore, when this is received from the mouth of a true guru, it is called *dīkṣā*.
O practitioners, listen to the fault of mortals who have not received initiation:
their food is equal to excrement and their sacred thread is like urine.
Having accepted the śrāddha performed by one who is uninitiated, or [the śrāddha] for one who is uninitiated,
their ancestors fall into a most dreadful hell.
There is no doubt that [the sins] fall away indeed, even for as long as fourteen Indras endure,
provided that one recites [the mantra] with devotion and a thousandfold offerings.
Likewise, the gods do not accept his offering;
because his state of being a "listener" (karṇākhittva) is in vain, he who is uninitiated is a mere beast (paśu).
Therefore, upon seeing one who is uninitiated, one should not accomplish any rite whatsoever.
At the time of receiving initiation, however, the heap of sins flees;
intent upon that, he goes forth toward union with the state of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, one becomes oneself worthy of being served by the gods and the ancestors;
otherwise, the performed action is like an oblation poured into ashes.
In every stage of life, the necessity of initiation is proclaimed;
for one who lacks the mantra, there is no protector among the people on earth.
Likewise, for one who is devoid of initiation, there is no mastery here or in the hereafter,
neither through austerities, nor through sacrifices, nor through various types of oblations, nor even through other means of accomplishment.
But even ritual action never succeeds for one who lacks initiation,
just as the study of their own sacred duties and so forth does not succeed for twice-born men who have not undergone the initiatory rite.
Just as there is no entitlement here for those who have not undergone the initiatory rites such as *upanayana*,
so too there is no entitlement for those who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*) regarding mantras, deities, and the like.
Since one will be subjected to verbal abuse from this person, one should make oneself consecrated by the mantra.
The entire world has initiation as its root, O scorcher of foes;
having taken recourse to initiation, one may dwell in any stage of life (āśrama) while performing silent recitation (japa).
And due to death without initiation, one would go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, it is called "initiation" (dīkṣā) by the teachers who know the Tantras.
As long as initiation— which bestows the fruits of human endeavor,
which grants all accomplishments, and which bestows all prosperity— is not obtained.
They possess radiant complexions, abundant beauty, and great wealth;
they are capable of enchanting, paralyzing, attracting, killing, and driving away.
You possess mastery over the destruction of wicked poetry and intellect, as well as thousands of forms of retention;
you have the power to cross the ocean and attain victory over fire in battle.
In the forest, she indeed grants fearlessness as well as the removal of grief and suffering;
she bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—of this there is no doubt.
12b) From among many tens of millions of mantras, as well as from the vidyās themselves,
that which is obtained from the mouth of a single guru is the instigator of all accomplishments.
Having received from the teacher's instruction the recitation, ritual placement, worship, and so forth,
he should subsequently accomplish all of that, being then permeated by that state of being.
In reflection, he is called a teacher; in instruction, the teacher is a great teacher. Regarding the state of being higher or lower, in worship it is the Parameṣṭhin in practice.
There is no object equal to the Guru; there is no god like Śaṅkara;
there is no sacrifice superior to Kaurā; and there is no knowledge equal to Kālikā.
From the letter *ga* comes the perfection of knowledge; it is the illuminator of that [knowledge]. From the letter *u*, one bestows identity with Śiva; thus is the Guru remembered.
The bound soul (paśu) is said to be one whose fetters increase; the Great Lord (maheśvara) is one liberated from fetters.
Therefore, he who removes the fetters here is called the Guru, and no other.
For the mantra of the Father (Pitṛ) is devoid of potency within the Śaiva and Śākta traditions;
however, on the path of Dakṣa, the mantras of both the Father and the Grandmother (Mātāmaha) are devoid of potency.
13a) For a brother who is a householder, [the guru] who is powerful on the left path [should initiate];
a husband shall not initiate his wife, nor shall a father initiate his daughter.
One should not initiate a son, nor should one initiate a brother;
however, the initiation of women is declared auspicious, and that of a mother is said to possess eightfold merit.
She was indeed accomplished, of virtuous conduct, having conquered her senses through devotion to her guru;
she knew the true meaning of all mantras, possessed good character, and delighted in worship.
That indeed would be the fitness for a Guru, or it may be devoid of the prescribed rules;
initiation with the *mātrā* must certainly be granted, O Śāmbhavī, even if it be the truth regarding women.
Initiation obtained through the lineage of goddesses is considered auspicious for women;
now listen with reverence to the specific distinction regarding the lineage of goddesses.

The Goddess has reached the supreme state ordained by the Supreme; having attained the highest initiation for women through the lineage of successive transmission, that auspicious initiation of the Goddess is considered the ultimate.
From him, a lineage of initiated men has arisen;
hear now, O Great Goddess, that for women there is no such restriction.
13b) The restriction is to be understood as applying to the male, and not to women under any circumstances.
O Dear One, how could there be initiation for one who possesses conceptual constructions regarding the Śākta [power]?
If she is to be given by the preceptor, then she is considered his sister;
if she is indeed to be given by oneself, then she is proclaimed to be a maiden.
If one strays from the path of consciousness brought forth by another, then it becomes [lost];
for in the mantra-śāstra, many kinds of paths have been proclaimed by the Goddess herself.
For that purpose, the mind hesitates; O Śaṅkara, tell me what should be done?
It is best to offer [the fee] oneself, but the initiation is to be received from him.
O Great Goddess, that which has been declared auspicious is indeed so; now listen with respect to what occurs in its absence:
on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, conjoined with Monday.
Having inscribed [the mantra] upon a palm leaf, one should perform the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
On that day, having prepared milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
and having offered the milk-rice and other oblations, one should then worship Śaṅkara with *vilva* fruits.
Having thus performed the recitation one thousand and eight times,
O Goddess, one should offer oblations while muttering the respective mantras according to the prescribed method.
If there is no capacity for recitation, then what is prescribed?
It should be recited through the son; or rather, the preceptor himself should recite it while accompanied by his son.
O beloved, for one who has thus received the mantra, success indeed occurs.
Now, listen to the initiation by means of another crow.
At an auspicious moment and on a favorable day, having first requested the formal transmission (saṃpradāya) at a river flowing toward the ocean, one should draw the mandala of Śrī Sūrya.
Having worshipped the Sun together with his limbs and retinue, O beloved of my life,
one should write the mantra beginning with the *tāra* (om) and ending with *phaṭ*, and have it recited in the presence of that [deity].
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the movement of the breath is to the left;
there, having worshipped the Sun and Jupiter, one becomes a master of all accomplishments.
This, O beloved, is declared to be intended for the *paśus*, and not for the *vīras*;
however, the master should perform the initiation for the *vīra* *kaulikas*.
In granting initiation to her husband, there is no fault according to Kālikā;
for previously, through Śiva, Gaurī’s initiation with darbha grass brought auspiciousness. 14b)
And she is either a son or a wife; likewise here too, O Pārvatī, she is not called a daughter, but is proclaimed to be the wife of a hero.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Kaula-rahasya. || 3 ||
The Śrī Devī said:
O God, a mantra given by an unaccomplished guru to a disciple, or a guru himself,
may be accomplished through another mantra, yet neither the mantra nor the guru will ever be accomplished [otherwise].
O Lord of Gods, tell me: what kind of accomplishment (siddhi) does a female servant belonging to one lineage obtain when she serves a deity belonging to a different lineage?
Īśvara said:
The Guru, however, belongs to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya and is initiated in all the Āmnāyas;
likewise, he belongs to the Ūrdhvāmnāya among others, and to the Pūrvāmnāya among yet others.
Of these two, however, one who follows the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya) is superior, while the one of the Northern Tradition (uttara) is inferior.
One of the Inferior Tradition (adhara) can never be a guru for anyone regarding matters pertaining to the next world.

15a) A devoted lay follower who dies at the proper time attains union (sāyujya) with the deity; likewise, the former attains similarity of form (sārūpya), while the latter attains proximity (sāmīpya).
Proximity to the higher world and the fruit of contentment through the abandonment of greed indeed bring benefit, even on the downward path, by producing a favorable future result.
When a guru who is fully accomplished in another mantra imparts that mantra [to a disciple],
the disciple's success arises from following his instructions exactly as they were taught.
When the Guru, out of compassion, bestows a perfected mantra,
then success resides in one's hand, even without recitation and without worship.
In that regard, a solar eclipse is auspicious, but a lunar eclipse is never so;
during a lunar eclipse there is poverty, whereas during a solar eclipse all prosperities abound.
The solar eclipse is declared to be Śiva, and the lunar eclipse is indeed Śakti.
During a solar eclipse, one should receive the initiation of Śakti; one should not perform the initiation of a bound soul (paśu).
15b) Here,
let the matter not continue;
it has been fully proclaimed.
Kālī, who proclaims the secret of the partless, is celebrated through her divisions;
she alone becomes the one called Madhyā, whose form is sovereignty.
Candrāgnivedapañcārṇā, then Nīlā in sequence,
Haṃsatārā, Mahānīlā, and at the end of that, Vīṇāśāmbhavī.
Madhā alone constitutes the twofold rite of accomplishment;
when combined with the three, it is proclaimed as my initiation into divine sovereignty.
She who has the form of a god, the divine form, the supreme one;
she who is all forms, who was before all, she who is indeed the great empire itself.
The multiplicity of divisions has been described according to the sequence of *siddhi* and *ṛddhi*;
the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the King of Vidyās and the ritual procedure for Chinnamastā are thus remembered.
Candravahnirasa, Raktaśyāmā, and Ṣoḍaśī; likewise Paraṣoḍhā is the seventeenth, and that which is born from her is Parā.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, Malinī, Kullā, and Vighnādi bestow the kingdom in due order;
through Vagalā, O Sovereign Lady, supreme sovereignty is attained.
The difference between Śiva [and the Moon] is diminished by the Moon, the Vedas, Sumeru, and the Mantras.
The Heart-mantra, the Śatārṇā, the five weapons, and likewise the Kullukā;
through the application of the Gāyatrī in its proper sequence, one attains sovereignty and holds the supreme status.
One who possesses this union of the five and maintains the wisdom of universal sovereignty shall attain the Śrīdivya-sarvasāmrājya initiation, which is supreme above all.
Even beyond that, O Goddess of Gods, there is no initiation within the sphere of the universe;
yet the tenfold divisions of the Vidyās and the Great Vidyā have been born from me.
The various types of Siddhividyās, as well as the great mantras, O Goddess of Gods, and their auxiliary mantras— Śāvara and Daśaśāvara.
O Goddess, there is Kālaśāvaraka and likewise Siddhaśāvara;
the mantra for the threefold vision and the oral tradition (āmnāya) shall likewise arise from the sequence (krama).
The *kādi* and *hādi* [syllables] are the two heads of this [mantra], while *kahartva* is its heart-joined-palms (*añjali*).
With palms joined in reverence, they held aloft swords, spears, and vessels.
Having gazed intently at Brahmā, they remained facing his mouth; while staying each in their own respective positions, this is declared to be the common [form].
Praise of Dreams.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull:
please explain the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] for one who has slept in a dream.
At the end of the night, one sees a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious:
"Oṃ! To Viṣṇu, the all-powerful lord of all the worlds, who resides in the heart."
Salutation to the one of universal forms, the lord of dreams!
Salutation to the born one, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the great-souled! Salutation to the left-handed one, the universal-formed, the lord of dreams!
In the first watch of the night, a dream yields its fruit within a year;
in the second watch, within six months; and in the third watch, within three months.
Then, at the time of dawn, after exactly four months have passed, one should quickly perform the pacification of bad dreams.
Having remained impure for three nights, the domestic priest, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya),
should offer one hundred fuel-sticks that are smeared with ghee and accompanied by milk.
A Śūdra, having eaten food fit for sacrifice while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra over his bonds,
should offer a lamp in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, in the temple of Viṣṇu, or in a shrine of Śiva.
Having seen such an auspicious dream, one should accept it with approval;
once accepted, one should either remain as is or reflect upon another Vedic text.
Now, the instruction on the Kaula tradition.
Having performed the array of mudrās (*nyāsajāla*) and the placement of the conch-vessel and other implements, one should worship the Goddess with the syllable *A* prolated by the five [vowels].
That cause is first in the mouth, and afterwards one should unite it with the mantra-vidyā;
this, O Maheśānī, is declared to be the Kaulika instruction.
Whoever gives wealth through unjust means, or whoever receives it through unjust means—
for both the giver and the receiver, there shall be a curse upon their lineage.
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, fail to examine one another and either receive or give instruction that is contrary to the scriptures;
Both of them shall suffer in twenty-one terrible hells;
for that person of deluded intellect who imparts instruction without performing the purificatory rites is like one sowing seeds of rice in sand.
The knowledge of mantras never remains with one who is unworthy;
therefore, it must be imparted to everyone [worthy], otherwise it would be fruitless.
This knowledge is taught to a true disciple who is devoted;
the practitioner constantly attains it, just as ghee is obtained from cow's milk.
If one should initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, greed, or similar motives, he incurs the curse of the deity; what was performed becomes as if unperformed.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Śrī Kaularahasya. || 4 ||
Now, regarding the initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā): the initiation of the full consecration should take place when the moon and sun are eclipsed.
18a) Sundarī, Tālinī, and Kālī proceed through the three stages of initiation;
O Great Goddess, when the Krama is complete, one shall attain the state of Śiva through the Krama.
O Goddess, [the sequence is] Candra, Agni, Pakṣa, Ṣoḍhā, Aṣya, Parā, Nirvāṇa, and Tatparā; then the six Sāmbhavas through the piercing of the cakras.
One's own wheel is the consciousness of the body; its entry into another's body is wisdom born of knowledge. This initiation has been described by me to you.
O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, listen first to this which has been declared:
the Moon, Fire, the sixteenth vowel (rasa), and the Queen (rājñī), followed by the Great Queen (mahārājñī).
O Śivā, Mahākāmākalākālī is followed by Guhyakālī;
Guhyakālī is said to be twofold, namely Sakalā and Niṣkalā, in sequence.
The ten-faced one is said to be the Sakala-kalā, or else she is the Sṛṣṭi-kalā;
she is also threefold: fierce, gentle, and extremely cruel.
One should not perform the initiation of Viṣṇu during a lunar eclipse according to the Pañcarātra tradition;
however, an initiation performed during an eclipse of either the moon or the sun is [considered] a complete initiation...
[and] an initiation of Śakti during a lunar eclipse is the most excellent of all initiations.

There is no requirement for days of the week, lunar dates, or constellations; likewise, there is no restriction regarding the month. One need not observe astrological conjunctions (yoga), lunar phases (karana), nor perform any deliberation.
O Goddess, from the first day (pratipad) until the ninth lunar day (navamī),
initiation has been performed by the wise, which bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
In the case of awakening Durgā, one need not examine whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious;
it is the eighth day known as Aśoka and likewise the ninth day known as Rāmā.
Or, when a Guru is seen or heard of at a most auspicious *siddhikṣetra*, the arrival of the Guru and the deities, and the initiation that follows, shall then take place.
Whenever there is a desire, then initiation [should be performed] according to the command of the Guru;
there is no need for a specific lunar day, no vow, no fire-offering, no ritual bathing, and no recitation of mantras.
However, the cause for initiation is one's own desire once a true Guru has been found;
if, out of compassion, the Guru summons the disciples and bestows it [the initiation].
At that time, one should never consider anything such as the ascendant or other astrological factors.
Thus, O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, the examination of the ground has been described to you as part of the time for initiation.
By smelling the scent of earth, one discerns the auspicious and the inauspicious;
by the scent of saliva, there is great sorrow; and by the scent of flesh, one becomes a lord of wealth.
If it has the smell of a pungent root, one will become ill; if it smells of excrement, it is fruitless;
if it smells like a lotus, one will be free from disease; and if it is foul-smelling, it portends fear.
Success does not arise from a foul odor; a pure smell leads to trade. A pungent smell likewise brings destruction, while the smell of a bridegroom conveys inauspiciousness.
Now, the meditation on the site.
One should remember the deity with hands folded and face upward when performing worship;
however, in the case of entering a new house or similar occasions, one should remember the deity with the face turned downward.
The knees [should be placed] toward Śakti, the elbows toward the directions of Vāta and Hutāśa;
the feet and calves toward Pitṛ, and the speech toward Guru and Vipra.
Attachment should be abandoned with one's whole being; one should dwell in seclusion apart from the Guru.
Association with the virtuous and discernment are the two eyes that lead one safely.
How can one who is blind to that [reality] obtain happiness from the contrary? To one who is attached to worldly pleasures and who merely says, "I am Brahman," [happiness is impossible].
O outcaste, one should likewise abandon this karma that is parched by fear of Brahmā;
as well as liquor, meat, the drinking of surā, fish, and the husbands of those who have strayed.
Where many [beings] are born, there the left [channel] bestows movement;
yet, remaining on the right path, one secretly enjoys meat and other such things.
He goes to a terrible hell and becomes a worm in excrement;
he who eats meat without offering a portion to the gods, or drinks liquor without performing worship.
If a messenger goes to a sacrifice without [proper authorization], she becomes a woman who leads men astray;
if, through lack of understanding, she practices the conduct of the *samaya* and uses the substances of the *kula*, [she falls].
Both that guru and his disciple shall become a beast (*paśu*) for the *yoginīs*;
being deluded in soul, he desires liberation while not knowing the Left-hand Path (*vāmamārga*).
He wishes to cross over both this shore and the further shore with his two arms alone.
Those who are free from all ritual actions and devoid of the system of castes and stages of life,
whether they follow the Kaula path or the Vāma path, are the vessels for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Let all kinsmen revile me; let wives, sons, and others abandon me;
let people insult me upon seeing me, or let kings punish me.
Even though I am constantly oppressed by disease, poverty, suffering, and the like,
whether Fortune remains or departs, do not abandon these feet of yours.
Thus, one who possesses firm devotion shall attain all success,
and not [from] the gain of wealth, nor from new anger, nor from hatred, nor from envy.
One should not abandon one who has attained the path, whether out of desire or even out of fear;
otherwise, O Goddess, one will encounter obstacles on that very path.
One who is purified by the duties toward the guru, whose body is cleansed of the impurities of the kalpas,
who is devoted to the worship of the Kula, and who does not deviate from the Kaula path— he is a true Kaula.
Who knows what will happen to whom in their absence?
"That which indeed yields immediate fruit is the supreme vision;
some say that the great ones are those in whom the teacher's instruction has been firmly established."
Some, deluded by their own past karma, chant [mantras] while causing delusion;
they consider liquor to be drinkable, meat to be edible, and the face of a beloved woman to be worthy of gazing upon.
Thus, the supreme ones declare this conduct to be the best;
for if a person should attain perfection through intoxication, [then this would be the way].
If the mere eating of meat were to result in the attainment of beauty, then all those who delight in drinking liquor would have attained perfection.

Liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—

He should be worshipped with great effort by those who know the scriptures of that lineage;

"O Lord, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is better than untruth;
by the mere sight of you, I speak the truth—truly, I speak the truth."
O Lord of Gods, O Radiant One, although my very self is all-pervading,
nevertheless, I feel powerless at every step in that regard.
It is better to abandon one's lineage; it is better to bring harm to one's own family;

One should not, through body, mind, or speech, exert one's strength to cause the downfall of one's own family,
nor engage in the company of a beast for the sake of a momentary pleasure on the path to liberation.

These two family scriptures are sinful and most excellent, yet they bring about the destruction of the lineage; O Lord of the Family, through their practice by another, great infamy falls upon one's own family.
Therefore, even greater sin arises from association with animals; for that reason, O Lord of the Kula, one who is pure in disposition should never manifest [such behavior] there.

A beautiful woman, however, should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) four times a day:
in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight.

"Vāgbhava, O Goddess Tripurā, we know;

Having uttered the word "Mahālakṣmī," one should then say "vidmahe"; having spoken the word "mahāśriyai," one should utter the word "dhīmahī."
From that, one should give the word *śabda* to us; from that, one should give the word *śrī*; and from that, by means of the thirteenth [syllable].

Thus ends the duties for the Brahma-muhūrta.
Thereafter, the wise one should perform the ritual bath for the sake of attaining supreme consciousness and bliss;
he should bathe in the pure sacred ford (tīrtha) situated within the heart.
A person should bathe at Bindu Tīrtha; for such a one, rebirth does not exist.
Thus concludes the ritual of bathing.
O Śivā, when the unborn [Śiva] raises the Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra and attains victory,
at that time the union with Śakti occurs.
For those devoted to the Kula, that twilight is proclaimed as their meditative absorption (samādhi).
Thus ends the section on twilight (saṃdhyā).
With that divine nectar which has flowed forth from the union of the moon, the sun, and fire,
one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
49b) Having filled the lunar vessel situated below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) with the essence of the digits (kalāsāra), one should satisfy the Khecarī with it.
Thus ends the libation.

The placement of the *mātṛkā* letters begins with "on the navel, the embrace" (*ādhāliṅganābhau*) and "the moon-disc in the heart" (*hṛdaya śaśakalā*), and so on, up to that point. Now follows the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement.
In the thousand-spoked [wheel], resembling a jewel and adorned with all colors,
there is then the primordial [syllable] enriched with three lines and adorned with three plow-marks (halas).

In the center of that, one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the supreme bindu, which consists of the nature of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal; this is the internal ritual placement (nyāsa).

One should visualize the Bindu, whose nature is consciousness, extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra); one should satisfy it with the streams of nectar flowing from that Bindu and then perform the placement of the Mātṛkās.
Having uttered each group [of syllables] one by one from the *mūlādhāra* to the end of the eyebrows,
ending with "namas," this is proclaimed as the internal placement (*vinyāsa*).
The heart-essence (hṛdya), which is captivating to the mind, is the illusory power (māyā) residing within the heart; it is from that [power] that my light is given.
That [light] is not made for another, nor is there anything beyond that mantra of the heart.
50a) In the Supreme Self, whose form is pure consciousness and whose lofty peak is twice that of omniscience,
the teachers effect the removal of objects through ritual action by means of the mantra placed upon the head.
The teachers perform a firm visualization of the heart, head, face, and abode as being dissolved,
upon their own bodies, using the Śikhā-mantra.
By means of the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*),
the body of one who possesses the mantra is protected on all sides from the external brilliance of others, so that it remains unassailable day and night.
That which bestows supreme knowledge within the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, is the light consisting of the heart and so forth; it is designated as "Da" therein.
It destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner;
that mantra, impelled by the smoke of its own fruit, is a net of ignorance.
Now, meditation.

Having caused that which resides in the *kīla*, that which resides in the fire of *ṇa*, and that which is situated between the moon and the sun to dissolve into the great void, the yogi should remain in the state of fullness.
The knowledge that "I am He," which is the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—
that, O God, is the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), the knower of the Divine, the Bindu.
Thus concludes meditation. Now, the worship.
One should worship with various flowers; at that very moment, one becomes identical with That.
Nyāsa is the realization of identity with That; one should worship with the feeling of "I am He."
By means of Amāyā, one should [subdue] Haṃkāra; likewise, by means of Manāga, Mada;
by means of Amohaka, Mada; and by means of Hastama, Kṣobhaka.
Non-avarice and non-greed are the flowers of the new moon; the wise know the drops to be the flowers.
Non-violence is the supreme flower, and likewise, the restraint of the senses is a flower.
Compassion is a flower, forgiveness is a flower, and wisdom is the fifth flower;
with these supreme flowers thus described, worship the Supreme Goddess.
Thus ends the worship.
The garland is said to be the *pāṃśikā*; the thread consists of Śakti and Śiva. The knot is the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti, and at the end of the Kalās stands Meru.
Thus ends the recitation. Now, the fire offering (homa).
In the pit situated at the *mūlādhāra*, blazing with the fire of the deity,
accompanied by merit and demerit, preceded by the root mantra of the Ṛṣi; 51a)
The wise person should offer each oblation individually with the mantra "I offer, Svāhā!"—
offering as the sacrificial oblation (havis) such things as falsehood, backbiting, lust, anger, and the like.
The mind alone is declared to be the *sruva* ladle, while the state beyond the mind (*unmanī*) is said to be the *sruc* ladle.
Here, at the end of the root [verse].
In the fire of the nature of consciousness at the navel, eternally kindled by knowledge, I offer the activity of the senses as an oblation with the mind as the ladle.
Svāhā! This is the first oblation. At the end of the root mantra.
With the mind as the ladle, the self as the horse, and dharma and adharma as the clarified butter, I perpetually offer the activity of the senses into the blazing fire by means of the *suṣumṇā* path.
With "Svāhā," [he offers] the second oblation at the end of the root mantra.
Holding the ladle (sruva) in the hands of light and space,
I offer into the fire that which is filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit.
"svāhā"—this is the third oblation. At the end of the root mantra:
When consciousness has been perfected by that which increases through the uninterrupted and continuous application of fuel, it stands as the adversary to the darkness of illusion.
"In some ground that is the expansion of the illusory manifestation of the elements, I offer the universe, from the earth up to the ether"—
this is the fourth oblation.
Having performed the sacrifice up to this point, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person, there are neither sins nor merits, and he certainly becomes liberated while living.
Thus concludes the internal sacrifice.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Śrī Kaularahasya.
I shall now describe the auspicious and inauspicious results of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings:
gold yields the fruit of all desires; silver bestows long life and sons.

Good fortune is attained through a copper vessel, while the increase of dharma occurs through one made of clay; satisfaction is gained through a coconut shell, and that which is produced from glass bestows nourishment.

The attainment of fortune comes from an offering in a bilva vessel; devotion to Brahman from one made from the brahmavṛkṣa tree; the power of killing from one made of iron; and the immobilization of enemies from one made of stone.
In the practice of mantra, the left-hand path (*vāmamārga*) is the ultimate resort;
this is declared to be the *arghya* vessel, which is pleasing to all the gods.
The measurement of the supporting vessel is sixteen or twelve finger-breadths.
The Vasu-ṛtu-tauvika [sāman].
One should prepare vessels for the jewels and other offerings, marked with auspicious lines, using clay today for the purpose of worship and for the offering of bali.
One should show respect toward worthy recipients, for they are indeed most excellent;
for without a worthy recipient, the performance of offerings, oblations, and other rites does not succeed.
A bowl measuring thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed as the best;
the middling is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths.
One should never have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths [in height].
The measure for the *arghya* vessel is one *pāda* (four finger-breadths) in height, while the disc is four finger-breadths; this is according to the distinctions of the superior and other grades.
One should prepare a vessel for flowers and a vessel for perfumes according to what is available;
white and other colors are recommended for the Brahmins and the other castes in their respective order.
One should recite the root mantra and the Astra mantra over the vessel for the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī),
as well as over oneself, the sacrificial ground, the articles of worship, and the mandala.
One should display the bow mudrā; this is considered the purification of the substance.
Then, one should worship the deity with the six types of offerings, having offered the śakti.
A seat, a welcome, water for honoring the guest (argha), water for washing the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Likewise, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the bath, clothing,
ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood paste.
One should employ the sixteen-fold services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) in formal worship;
the ten-fold service (daśopacāra) is considered intermediate and is prescribed for householders.
The arghya, the pādya, as well as the ācamanīya, the madhuparka,
and those beginning with perfumes (gandha) to be offered— these are remembered as the ten services (upacāras).
Now, the secret flower.
O Maheśānī, the menstrual flow is called the "vajra-flower";
for a woman who has reached her first menses in the month of Āṣāḍha, it is the most excellent of all.
For a woman married by force or in due order, the middle [period] increases enjoyment; through the power of the union with *rajas*, another [period] bestows both merit and happiness.
O Goddess, the *svayambhū* flower is born on earth in three varieties;
she is always to be worshipped with all flowers, whether they are prescribed or not.
Devotion to all the gods must be practiced; in this matter, yoga is the cause.
He states the means for grasping this error:
With a thread of fine cloth, O Pārvatī, with a thread of *vīra* cloth,
O Pārvatī, or with a Kashmiri cloth thread or a silk thread, O Pārvatī.
Having offered kastūrī, kuṅkuma, mantra, sandalwood, aguru, and so forth—
various fragrant substances— the practitioner should then combine them together.
One should bring flowers together with the eight fragrances;
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with this combination of unbroken rice grains.
For the purpose of the seat and for the purpose of the fire-oblation, the drop (bindu) is worshipped in the sequence of the wheel;
the wise know that when it is joined with the self-born, it is the perfected flower (siddhapuṣpa).
O Goddess of the gods, garlands of flowers should not be worn;
rather, fresh flowers that are always pure should be offered day after day.
Having taken all of this together, one should worship Tārā and Kālī;
by the merit of offering flowers, one shall obtain fruit multiplied ten millionfold.
Now follows the procedure for the incense of the ten Vidyās.
Now listen, O brahmin sage, to my description of incense:
guggulu, sarjarasa, devadāru, and sandalwood produced from Mount Malaya.
Hrīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, refined sugar,
haritakī, nakhī, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja;
In rites for the gods and the ancestors, the wise one should offer incense consisting of sixteen ingredients:
honey, *muṣṭa*, ghee, fragrance, *guggulu*, and *gurulajana*.
Śaraṇa, śāla, siddhi, and daśāṅga are said to be made of wheat;
mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and honey, along with guggulu and heavy sandalwood.
This six-ingredient incense is always dear to all the gods:
guggulu, agallochum, pine resin, sugar, honey, and sandalwood.
The preceptor should fumigate the deity with substances mixed with clarified butter;
for the threefold knowledge (trividyā), iron and lead are proclaimed as the sixteen-fold [ingredients].
O Goddess, in the ritual of the Kālī-vidyā, agallochum (aguru) is prescribed as the tenth part;
in the ritual of the Śrīkhaṇḍa-Tārā-vidyā, it is remembered that [the offering] consists of eighteen parts.
O Goddess, for the rite of severing ignorance, the five-fold ingredients are guggulu, black agallochum, and yellow sandalwood; this is the range of the Brahmā-astra mantra.
Having stirred together camphor, sandalwood, and musk— this is proclaimed as the "Mātaṅgī" [incense]— as well as musk and camphor, which likewise constitute the "eight-fragrance" (aṣṭagandha).
O Goddess, [the mantra] is carved upon Bhairavī; indeed, it is on Śilānasī;
it is declared to be of iron for Bhuvaneśī, and of sandalwood for Kamalāmatī.
Indeed, the *lakṣāguḍā* is a perfected lore (*siddhavidyā*) in the rite of *dhūmrā*, O Śivā.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the lamps.
Because it abandons the great darkness of long-standing ignorance and because it illuminates the supreme reality,
it is called a lamp.
First, there is the ghee lamp; then those produced from sesame oil,
mustard oil, resinous extracts of fruits, or those originating from *ucūrīja*.
Dadhijagdha and Unnaja are indeed proclaimed as the seven lamps.
It may be made from lotus fiber, or from *darbha* grass,
or from *jālājāvāda* fibers, or else from the fibers of the earth-cocoanut (*bhūlakoṣa*).
The wick is always prescribed as the fifth among the functions of the lamp. Now, he describes the mudrās for the sixteen services (upacāras) in their proper order.
I shall now describe the place for the gift of material substances; listen further to me.
One should offer scents, flowers, and ornaments into the mouth [of the deity].
O twice-born one, a lamp should be offered on the right and incense likewise on the left;
one should carefully present the cooked food offering (naivedya) in the southern region.
Now listen further regarding a lamp that is unrefined and placed on the left side:
it is a lamp provided with ghee and also equipped with a white wick.
One should place that [object] in the right region, and the other in the left region;
on the seat there should be the lotus mudrā, with both hands facing downwards.
55a) This is the *mudrā* for inquiring about one's welfare; at that time, it is again with the face turned upward. The noble *mudrā* for welcoming consists of the form of the *añjali*.
By joining the ring finger and the thumb, that same [mudrā] is called the *padya* (lotus) mudrā;
the wise one, having turned the right hand upward with its palm facing down...

With the little finger lowered and not joined [to the ring finger], and the other four fingers raised, this mudrā is declared for the act of rinsing (acamana); it should be turned downward and free from disease.
O fair-faced one, the *madhuparka* mudrā is formed by touching the thumbs;
it consists of making a fist with the right hand, with the little fingers [extended] and the palm facing downward.
O Supreme Goddess, this is declared to be the Svāna-mudrā (Dog-mudrā).
Having placed the right hand face upwards, one should then join its middle finger...
One should touch [the heart] with the thumb; this is the mudrā known as *vastra*.
Or, touching with the ring finger is the mudrā known as *bhūṣaṇa*.
The mudrā of one's own wife is formed by touching the tips of the little fingers together;
the mudrā of perfume is formed by touching the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb.
Having turned the hand downward, one should join it with the tip of the index finger.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā called Puṣpā is formed with the tip of the thumb;
O Maheśvarī, one should touch the tip [of the other fingers] with the tip of the thumb and the forefinger.
This is declared to be the incense mudrā, which brings pleasure to all the gods. O you who are worshipped by the gods, one should touch the tip of the middle finger with the tip of the thumb.
This auspicious Lamp Mudrā is the support of all the gods;
O Goddess, the preceptor should touch the tip of the ring finger with the tip of the middle finger.
The *naivadya* (food offering) mudrā is called the *tattva-mudrā*.
Now, the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
For those who possess [the consort], however, one should not perform the libation (tarpaṇa) today at the conclusion of the ritual service;
for them, there is the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), as well as the constant practice of libation and service.
Having performed [these], having praised, and having paid homage, [one should place] the drop in the mandala.
Circumambulation.
A triangular form is everywhere declared to be the power of Inclination (nati);
and that of Maheśvara is declared to be the half-moon behind it.
Whether out of delusion or through desire, a Śūdra who recites the Purāṇas along with the Smṛtis becomes a doer of evil and attains hell together with his ancestors.
One may worship or bow to a Liṅga installed by a Śūdra;
by accepting all that comes from it, such as its grace and so forth, one incurs no transgression.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Śrī Kaularahasya. || 12 ||
Now, he describes the daily worship of the Kaulācārin (or Kauravāmin).
O Goddess, when Dakṣa’s sacrifice was abandoned by you,
I took that sacrificial vessel upon my shoulder and prepared to enter the funeral pyre.
Wherever that submarine fire might be sought,
there Śakra extinguished it with waters as its ornament.
As I wandered in this manner for a year, my perspiration became great;
by the falling of those drops, the earth will be scorched.
Then Viṣṇu was entreated by the Earth for her protection; at that time,
your limbs were pierced all over by arrows swift as the wind.
Having divided [the earth] into eighty-four sections, he cast them down upon the ground;
fanned by his departure, I was then entirely delighted.
And Viṣṇu, having manifested himself, fell at my feet;
having raised me up, he embraced me, and my grief was forgotten.
At that time, O Pārvatī, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as Nārada and the great sages, praised me;
then Viṣṇu spoke these words.
O servant of knowledge, how have you, who possess the nature of Maheśvara, fallen into delusion?
You desire to enter the fire suddenly with the body of Satī.
"A woman may follow her husband, but a man does not go to her"—
disregarding this scriptural injunction, O Lord, how have you been so deluded?
Thus he spoke to the Lord of Gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva, with words full of double meanings and ornaments, devoid of intellect yet accompanied by it.
"O twice-born one, we then urged you to ask for a boon;
it was because of that which those brahmins did that this violation of dharma has arisen."
The Śaivas, who were the destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, struck down the Brahmins;
and all seven classes of twice-born who had come to the sacrifice were likewise struck by the Śaivas.
If this surface of the earth were truly composed of portions cut away by Viṣṇu,
then at every step there would be contact with corpses, and all ritual action pertaining to Brahman would be abandoned.
Therefore, act in such a way that the purification of the earth, the purification of the Brahmins,
and the truthfulness of Brahmā’s word are all realized.
Then, having reflected and having reached an agreement with Viṣṇu, I declared:
"Where the Vedic rites have been destroyed, there let the Tantra be practiced."
For those Brahmins who have been consumed by curses and deprived of the performance of Vedic rites,
this Kaula dharma is the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
57b) Those brahmins who were born at the sacred seats (pīṭha) and whose curses have been consumed by the fire of [the Guru’s] curse—
for them, the right to this path arises within their lineage.
Because it is honored within that very family, this path is called Kaula;
the Vāmamārga is inferior to that, as are the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas among them.
The entitlement of the sacrificer and his wife to those two [rites] has been declared therein;
however, in that which is inferior to that Siddhānta, there is the entitlement of Śūdras.
Those who enter the Kaula dharma without knowing its lineage will undoubtedly become breathless, destitute, and afflicted by disease.
O Goddess, he who desires to consume the substance belonging to one who has attained perfection through the knowledge of the Kaula is a great sinner, excluded from all ritual acts.
For one who is deficient in the conduct of the samaya, who is self-willed and evil-minded, there is no accomplishment; his lineage perishes, therefore one should not associate with such a person.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains no perfection in this world, nor the supreme goal in the hereafter.
Those who, having taken refuge in my teaching, enjoy the wealth of their families,
shall be honored among the sources of beings for as many eons as there are hairs on Daṅga’s body.
58a) And if one whose self is stumbling with pride does not abide in anything at all—
neither in meditation, nor in the practice of austerity, nor in dharma, nor in sacred rites;
If there is no consideration for destiny, nor for the guru or the mantra, in the Kaulika path,
one who is merely attached to sense objects falls to the earth without a doubt.
Having correctly understood the latent impressions from the Kula scriptures of the venerable Guru, one should be consecrated in the five mudrās; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
If one does not worship the lineage of gurus, the circle of teachers,
Vaṭuka, and the others— even a Vīra— by drinking liquor in vain, the deity will incur sin.
Now, the taking up of the shaven head.

At the time of the ritual striking with the *muṇḍa*, however, an offering (*bali*) should by all means be made to Śivā; and having worshipped Śiva and Śakti, one should offer the *bali* together with the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*).
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship [the deities] along with their weapons and other attributes in due order;
thus, O Lord of Heroes, one should offer the bali-oblation for all of them in this sequence.
Having uttered "Vaṃ Māyā Kamalā," the Yajus mantra of the Goddess's mouth proceeds;
[recite] "Pravartate imaṃ bhāva, valiṃ gṛhṇa" as a pair.
Now, the procedure for the seat.
O Goddess, for three days during the menstrual period, the practice on the seat has a threefold form;
O Goddess, the practice on a cloth seat for three months yields fruit.
O Goddess, the fruit of the *muṇḍāsana* occurs within six months, that of the *śavāsana* at the end of a day, and that of the *naracarmāsana* at the end of a fortnight.
O Goddess of gods, by using a soft seat for one month, the result is the removal of jaundice;
and for ten years, the result is that which is called "the woolly" (*ūrṇā*).
O Goddess, on the seat of the womb (yonisthāna), the fruit [of practice] occurs within seven days;
on the seat of the vulva (yonyāsana), it occurs at the end of a fortnight, specifically during the eight days known as Surātā.
In the reverse order, it takes six days; the touch of the tongue occurs after twelve days.
O Goddess, in the case of seven kisses, the fruit arises after seven causes [days].
O Pārvatī, when performed on a seat with the six limbs of the month, the fruit is attained.
Now he states the method for preparing the seat.
O Goddess, if a man should practice the worship of Kālikā without the corpse-seat (mṛtāsana),
he is to be known as a denizen of hell for as long as the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
Now, he states the alternative procedure in the absence of a soft seat and other such items.
In the absence of a corpse, one should imagine a seat (viṣṭara) in the form of kusha grass;
having worshipped that seat known as the viṣṭara, one should worship the supreme goddess Tārāvikā.
O Goddess, the expansion of the Śrī-devī is her stream, which has become manifest;
now listen as the *viṣṭaka* for the sake of the practitioner is being told. 59a)
Upon which the leaves of living beings rest and are supported according to their destiny.
Ten fingers and so forth are prescribed for the hands and feet; twenty are declared for the heart, the king of the mantras, and thirty for the head, the bestower of all boons.
In the secret place, the tongue, the mouth, the teeth, the nose, the letters, the breasts, and the penis, the *candrā* and *kuśa* blades, measured by pairs, should be joined together.
Thus, this seat (viṣṭara) bestows all perfections;
O Supreme Goddess, the binding should be performed with kuśa grass or with a cord.
Furthermore, having fashioned a seat with a thread mixed with blood or with silk thread,
one should perform the recitation upon it.
I have explained to you the detailed ritual for the lotus;
by performing it according to the rules, a man shall become a poet and an eloquent speaker.
The composition of the sūtra should be performed by oneself for the sake of all accomplishments;
its detailed nature is proclaimed in the form of Śava.
59b) Indeed, the sacrificial seat (viṣṭara) is proclaimed to be the very form of Śiva;
the seat is the form of Śiva, for it is the conceptualization of one's own power (śakti).
What cannot be accomplished on this earth through the union of Śiva and Śakti?
The finest garment of a Śavarī woman is considered the second seat.
Listen, O Goddess of gods, to the third [mantra], which bestows all accomplishments:
Viṣṭara is the form of Śambhu; he is the seat (viṣṭara) of both Śivā and Śiva.
Having performed the purification of the *samaya*, one should perform the purification of the *śakti*;
having performed the purification of the *śakti*, [one should perform] the purification of the wine (*surā*).
Vijayā: Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī, svāhā! Aiṃ, obeisance to Kṣatriyā, svāhā! Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiśyā, svāhā! Klīṃ, obeisance to Śūdrā, svāhā! Now, the meditation (dhyāna).
I bow to Bhairavī, who awakens one to Śiva, whose hands shine with the noose and goad,
who is skilled in granting the strength of desired boons to her devotees, and who bestows stability against the bonds of saṃsāra.

O Enchantress of the World, meditate upon the victorious Suvi-jayā, whose sandals are worshipped by the heroes, who severs the bonds of saṃsāra, and whose essence is the nectar produced from the churning of the intellect.
Now, the purification of the *śakti*.
One who practices with the three liquors is a rare and wondrous achiever;
however, if practiced at dawn, there will be a loss of accomplishment, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.
O Maheśānī, during initiation, the power of the mantra arises from the consecration when its recitation is heard;
and at the time of initiation, it resides in the maiden who brings about delight.
One should perform the specific rite for the sake of satisfaction with greater effort;
even for the drinking of liquor or [the emission of] semen, one should do so with water while reciting the ancient mantra.
First, having uttered the vowel *ā*, one should utter *tripurāyai*;
then, having uttered the word *namaḥ*, one should thereafter speak this mantra: *śaktim*.
60b) "Pavitrī kuru śabdānte mama śaktiṃ kuru priye," having uttered [the word] vahnijāyā (svāhā), this is proclaimed as the purification mantra.
O Goddess, women who are constantly consecrated by this rite shall always enjoy themselves here and attain all perfections.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one shall attain liberation in the next;
into her ear, with the intent to create a sense of duality, one should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā.
By this, a woman shall indeed always be pure and worthy of worship.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Śrī Kaularahasya. 13.
Now, regarding the acceptance of substances, he states the purgative for those who are qualified.
A Brahmin should never worship Śivā with material substances belonging to a Sāttvika Brāhmaṇa; O Lord, by giving liquor to a Brāhmaṇa, one is fallen from the state of being a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin, however, by performing even a secondary rite (anukalpa), would fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla;
likewise, a Kṣatriya should never offer an image made of flour (paiṣṭikī).
61a) Thus, by merely giving [this], one becomes a Brāhmaṇa of long life. In rites for the gods and ancestors, cow's milk mixed with honey does not cause any fault.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, the copper used for the *homa* is taken up;
likewise, it must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa, so that his Brāhmaṇahood does not perish.
Furthermore, distinctions among substances arise according to the sequence of the castes:
Brahmins should be gratified with milk, and those born of the royal lineage with clarified butter.

therefore, at the conclusion of my worship, people shall address you with words of high praise.
O fortunate one, he who sports while abiding in a tranquil mind,
even though reciting the word "bhaga" repeatedly, speaks of it as "bhaga" [in its true sense] because of his gentleness.
By repeatedly saying "liṅga, liṅga," one causes [the seed] to be emitted;
from that emission, whatever is seen there is born.
"His fortune is such that he deserves to be censured even by the poet of the three worlds"—
by such words as these, people may sport at will with the Goddess.
Now, the meditation on the ten Vidyā-Bhairava mantras is as follows. Among them, first is Akṣobhya.
Having extracted the unsurpassed [seed-syllable] which is unadorned by conceptual proliferation (*papañca*),
the Great Mantra ends with *akṣobhya* and *svāhā*, bringing delight to *Ramā*.
Now I shall explain meditation, which bestows all prosperity.
Resplendent like a thousand suns, bearing the auspicious form of a serpent,
his face was equal to ten million flashes of lightning, and his eyes blazed with the brilliance of fire.
Endowed with three folds and a half, situated at the tip of the *japā* flower,
possessed of great loveliness, and saluted by gods and demons.
Upon his head is a great, radiant jewel equal to the sun and lightning;
this form of great body is well-worshipped even by the gods.
Now he states the mantra of Krodhabhairava.
Now I shall declare the mantra of Krodha, by which even the unattainable is accomplished:
first take the seed-syllable Hālāhala, and after that, the seed-syllable of Krodha.
Having addressed the one who stands with limbs smeared in blood as if causing fear,
and having addressed the one with great flames like the fire of universal dissolution, one should extract the mantra from the head.
When the wrathful deity is thus invoked, he becomes manifest by himself.
Now, he speaks of meditation (dhyāna).
There, in the midst, was a terrifying [being] filled with blazing flames,
laughing with loud boisterous laughter, most fierce, and resembling crushed collyrium.
He stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, possesses four arms, holds a wheel in his right hand, and makes the threatening gesture with his left;
he is terrifying with his sharp fangs.
He who has a crown-jewel of a skull, the leader of the three worlds,
resembling ten million suns, and adorned by eight nāgas.
One possessing the mudrā of the trampled Aparājita should encircle [the hands] with the palms;
having joined the two ring fingers, one should bend the two index fingers.
By joining the little finger and the middle finger with the thumb and ring finger in the manner of a wheel,
one who holds this mudrā becomes a subduer of the three worlds, capable of both achieving and being achieved.
Now, he states the mantra of Tripurabhairava.
Māyā, Lakṣmī, likewise Haṃsa, and the seed-syllable Prāsāda;
with Vahni, Jāyā, and Antaka, this is the mantra of Tripurabhairava.
92a) The six-limbed [rite], as well as the offering of bali, worship, and so forth, should be performed with the root mantra.
Now, the meditation:
He has one face, three eyes, and is endowed with four arms;
in his right hands he holds a goad and a sword, and in his left hands a shield and a noose.
They meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, red in color, seated upon a bull,
with hair standing erect, wearing a necklace of skulls, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
O Goddess, one should always meditate upon Tripurabhairava in this manner.
Now, as for the group of four.

Māyā (māyāyai) and vaṭukaṃ (vaṭukāya), with the suffix ṅe; for the purpose of the recitation of the Māyā-buddhi, there are two *kuru*s, followed by *vahukāya* and *hrīṃ*; this is the color of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The sage is Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Bhairava; Hrīṃ is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), Āḥ is the power (śakti), and [Hrīṃ] is the proclaimed pin (kīlaka).
Thus, one should meditate on the body placed [in its proper positions], pure and resembling crystal,
wearing radiant white garments, and adorned with anklets and a network of tinkling bells.
Endowed with a supreme, jewel-encrusted vessel of fearlessness,
his lotus-like face is most serene, and he is seated upon a cushion of *kuśa* grass.
I bow to Bhava, who is praised with devotion by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as by gods and demons;
he is the primordial source of the universe, whose body is the universe itself, and who removes the fear of worldly existence.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantra known as Aghorāstra:
one should utter Māyā (Hrīṃ), then "Sphura" twice, and "Prasphura" twice.
Afterwards, say *turuturu* at the end of the form (*rūpa*), and then that pair (*tadvaya*).
After that, two *pracaṭas*, then two *kahas*, and two *vamas*.
The mantra "vandha dvayaṃ ghātayadvi hūṃ phaṭ," consisting of fifty syllables,
is for meditation.
Then one should meditate upon the three-eyed Bhīma, who is like a dark cloud,
adorned with serpents, and beautified by red garments and unguents.
Holding an axe, a sword, an arrow, and a trident respectively in her right hands, starting from the uppermost and proceeding in order with the others.
The hand-drum, the shield, the bow, the human skull, and the [gesture of] playful movement.
Now, for Tryambaka.
Mounted upon the serpent, O Pūtanā and Earth,
we worship Vaka, who is fragrant and increases nourishment.

One should say "ruvārukam iva" for the word "randhanāt"; one should say "mṛtyoḥ" for the word "mṛtyu"; one should say "abhyukṣīya" for the word "abhi"; and one should utter "amṛtāt" for the word "amṛta".
The three-eyed Lord has been proclaimed by Manu as the destroyer of death for those who worship Him.
[Meditation:]

I meditate upon the supreme Lord Śiva, who is as beautiful as Mount Kailāsa; he bathes two jars with the nectar of immortality held in his two hands, while holding those two [jars] at his two ears; he wears a garland of deer-skins on his waist, has his two hands placed upon the lap of the Goddess, carries a jar of nectar, is seated upon a pure lotus, wears a crown of the new moon, and possesses three eyes.
One should worship.
Now, [the ritual] of Mahākāla.
HŪṂ KṢĀṂ YĀṂ LĀṂ ĀṂ KROṂ Mahākāla Bhairava, destroy all obstacles! HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
Meditative absorption.
Oṃ! To the Lord of the Topknot, the Great God, seated upon the pericarp of the lotus,
the deity who has entered the liquor of the hungry ghosts (preta), resplendent with a white complexion.
The southern face is red in color, the northern is adorned with yellow, and the northern [face] is like a dark blue cloud; thus is Maheśvara with four faces.
Endowed with twelve eyes, her face slightly visible, auspicious, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair, she is great, fierce, and possesses a terrifying radiance.
And likewise Raktākalatalā, Śarvā, Lambodarāṅgikā,
Vajrajvālā, Gatā, Jvālā, Mahājvālā, and Sajājvalā.
All the weapons were blazing, resplendent with flaming tongues of fire;
the great god had ten arms and was holding a sword and a shield.
Holding an arrow and a bow, as well as an ankusha and a noose; likewise, bestowing the boons of protection and fearlessness, and holding a vessel and a khatvanga staff.
Thus, the hand-drum (ḍamaru) extends ten yojanas;
pervading the body, its forms are entirely peaceful and black in color.
Thus, the ten vidyās constitute Bhairava.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Śrī Kaulārha-rahasya. || 18 ||
Now, the worship of the Kaulika.
Having beheld Maheśvara, one should worship him according to the prescribed rites,
and having offered the five elements (pañcatattva) in accordance with one's means.
The goddess shall always be pleased and she shall even grant all desires;
otherwise, there will be no accomplishment at all, for the Yoginī becomes enraged.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving the entire earth to a Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas,
that same fruit is obtained in the worship of the Kaulika.
The fruit that one obtains by witnessing thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, that same fruit is obtained from the worship of Kaulīśa.
Whatever fruit one may obtain by constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like,
that fruit is multiplied a hundred thousandfold by the worship of the Kaulikas.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving a tawny cow,
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by worshipping the Kaulikas.
Now follows the sacrifice of the messenger (dūtī).
Indeed, nothing whatsoever is produced by primordial nature (prakṛti) without a person (puruṣa);
likewise, the Lord cannot bestow fruit through his sequence [of grace] without power (śakti).
Therefore, having established union with the power of the male (*puṃśakti*), one should accomplish the mantra;
for on the Kaulika Vāmamārga, the male deity does not attain success.
Meditating upon the Self as Śiva and the deity in the form of Śakti, one should sport with the five makāras; thus the deity becomes well-pleased with him.
The deity is pleased with him in whom the perception of [the guru as] a mother and the perception of [his consort as] a woman have become most firm on the path of Dakṣa and on the Kaulika path.
This secret has been declared; it must be kept hidden like a lover's affair with one's mother.
O Pārvatī, neither the Śaivas, nor the Smārtas, nor the ritualists perform that [rite].
To those who know the Kaula scriptures, who abide by the Tantric conduct,
who provide alternative ritual procedures (*anukalpa*), and likewise to those who remain impartial;
The goddess is the intellect of women, while Suyāmā is the fickle-minded one.
O Goddess, for those who are devoted to Kālī and whose minds are always resolved [upon her],
the worship of Śakti and the worship of the Pīṭha are mandatory.
Kālī is to be worshipped with the intellect alone, not with a mind agitated by desire;
except for one in the fourth stage of life, those who are devoted to the worship of Kālī [should do so with pure intent].
O enemy of the city, those who follow this doctrine— whether they be Kaulas or Akaulas— for them, the worship of Nityāśakti is as I have described.
That power (śakti) should be known to be of two kinds: one's own and the wife of another.
She who belongs to one's own caste and has been married should be cherished as dear.
She who is designated as one's own is not praised in that way;
I shall now describe in order the five kinds of women belonging to others.

Another [type] is one who has brothers-in-law; likewise, a beloved wife who is similar [to the former] is also [a type]. A female servant, a courtesan, and one who is not well-bred are each more praiseworthy than the one preceding it.
Among them, a young woman who has not yet given birth is praised as the first to be eaten.
Sometimes, even one who has recently given birth is considered equal to all [others];
indeed, in the absence of each preceding one, the succeeding one is to be accepted by practitioners.
In this very same way, even a man [may be] a *sādhika* of the *kaula*;
however, there is no noble woman (*anārya*) without a male practitioner (*sādhaka*), nor is there a female practitioner (*sādhikā*) who is a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*).

O Goddess of the gods, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas, mantras do not attain success through such acts as sexual union with another’s wife, causing miscarriage, or the killing of living beings.
If for one's own sake it leads to hell, and if for another's sake it leads indeed to merit—what is the reason? I do not understand, O Goddess; these [actions] are pleasing.
Just as the slaughter of animals for that purpose does not produce sin,
so too there is no remorse regarding such things as union with another's wife.
The specific genus of the *arśas* powers.
An actress, a courtesan, a washerwoman, the mother of a father,
a Brāhmaṇī woman who is the daughter of a Śūdra, and likewise the daughter of a cowherd.
The daughter of a garland-maker is proclaimed as a "new bride" (navakanyā);
she should have neither too few nor too many limbs, and she should be neither too stout nor too emaciated.
Nor one whose nose or fingers have been cut off; nor one who is tall, nor one who is short;
nor one who is shaven-headed, nor one who is hunchbacked; nor one who is foolish, blind, or deaf.
Those who are squint-eyed, lame, born of a mixed womb, or have sagging breasts;
those with young children, or who are excessively talkative—these should not be appointed as Śaktis.
I speak of those who are worthy and superior, by whom the Lord is pleased:
fair-limbed, youthful, beautiful, smiling, and of lovely form.
She has large, rolling eyes and full, elevated breasts;
she has broad hips and is adorned with three folds of skin over her belly.
She has a beautiful, very white complexion and is slender; she possesses a melodious voice and curved, vine-like limbs.
She wears various garments and diverse ornaments, and is clad in variegated attire.
It is strewn with various garlands and bestows manifold delights.
Always possessing a serene countenance, she was devoted to the Goddess,
knowledgeable in the Kaulika practices, and intent on devotion toward the practitioner (sādhaka).
Free from fear, with a smiling face, always speaking kindly,
perfected in the conduct of the observance (samaya), knowing the mantra, and devoid of all dread.
One should worship all women who are wise, eloquent, endowed with fortitude and independence, and possessed of such qualities.
Now, he states the specific power resulting from the specific nature of the knowledge.
The Great Vidyās are proclaimed to consist of the classes of *gandha* (fragrance) and *rūpa* (form).
O Goddess of the gods, listen now with diligence to their sequence.
O Maheśvarī, one should give a name according to the sequence of form and scent;
O Pārvatī, having abandoned the name given by the mother and father, which is born of ignorance.
98a) One should indeed personally bestow a name according to the appropriate method as before:
she who is black, or dark-blue, with eyes that are tawny like honey.
The practitioner, with a longing heart, [should apply] the scent of a man and a censurable odor;
Kālī is to be joined within that, and she is proclaimed as Kālī. (1)
That woman who has the scent of liquor, whose eyes are red, and who is extremely fierce, is called Mahogratārā; she is the destroyer of great sins. || 2 ||
Always capable of eating, yet fickle despite consuming much food;
possessing a form that deludes the three worlds—this is proclaimed as the severed Vidyā.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, filled with various fragrances,
beautiful, with lovely hair, long-eyed, and captivating.
Skilled in various arts of pleasure, discerning in the treatises of the Kula,
she has traversed the ground of the Guru’s mouth and perceives the stainless center.
That beautiful woman shall be Gaurī, the promoter of all undertakings.
She who is the third, fair-limbed and anointed with fragrant honey-scented unguents,
is the goddess named Tripurā, the accomplisher of the sequence of her own flower.
With beautiful limbs and lovely eyes, seated upon a lotus throne,
her body adorned with golden ornaments— she is celebrated as Kamalā.
O Maheśvarī, Mātaṅgī is renowned as a Vidyā who is adorned with necklaces of guñjā seeds, is dark-complexioned, has tremulous eyes, and possesses a beautiful smile. 7.
Divine in complexion, slender-limbed, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
and adorned with various ornaments— she was described by me as Bhuvaneśī.
With tawny eyes and tawny hair, laughing slightly and very tall, she is called Dhūmāvatī; O beloved, listen now to the vidyā of accomplishment.
O Great Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, she who is celebrated as Vagalā is long-faced, long-lipped, yellow-hued, and motionless.
O Pārvatī, the ten Vidyās are declared to be the tree known as Umā in the form of Śakti;
O Maheśānī, they are, in sequence, the mother, the wife, and the sister.
O Goddess, they play constantly with the Vidyās alone; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, the sequence of ten consists of the ten Vidyās through diligent effort.
O Goddess, one should perform it in every way; otherwise, not even in ten million aeons will they be accomplished, O Mistress of the Gods, by merely reciting the ten padmas.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the sequence of one's own respective knowledge;
for both one's own and the supreme [knowledge], O Maheśvarī, are merely Śakti.
One should worship the presiding deity of the mantra with all ritual offerings,
including various fruits, betel leaves, garments, ornaments, and gold.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, one should cause many offerings to be presented;
he who performs the worship of Śakti while maintaining the latent desire for enjoyment [shall attain his goal].
One will incur perpetual poverty and will certainly become a denizen of hell.
What is the use of many nets of excellent verses? Listen to the summary.
The worship of Śakti is prescribed for the Kaulikas to be performed day after day.
O Goddess, the daily extraction of the *sūradāna* and its acceptance by me are likewise declared to be eternal for those devoted to the Kula path.
O Dear One, the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is not to be abandoned is likewise rare among those who possess power;
for even among those who provide alternative means, it is indeed constant.

Having abandoned those things that are censured, one should indeed accept only what is appropriate to one's capacity; for others, the worship of Śakti may be performed either as a matter of desire or as an occasional rite.
For those whose minds are established in samādhi, there is the rejection of all else;
O Pārvatī, one should now dissolve even the mantras into the single method.
She was bathed, wearing divine garments, adorned with various ornaments,
youthful, with full breasts, and likewise possessing a beautiful form and a pleasant countenance.
Taking hold of the hand, one should place the supreme Śakti upon one's left thigh; if unable, one should carry her on the left hip, or otherwise, onto the seat of the Goddess.
Having drawn a triangle, a lotus, and a circle on the left side.
The stalk, joined with white and red [threads] and smeared with vermilion,
the practitioner, facing east, should worship the Goddess facing west.
One should worship Uḍḍiyāna in the Tretā age, Pūrṇagiri in the Kṛta age,
Jālandhara in the Dvāpara ages, and the seat of Kāma in the Kali age.
I shall describe those four, which are more secret than the most secret:
the entire body of Śakti is considered to be the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇagiri.
On the portion of her head, the moon, the garden has been described by me;
her two breasts are called Jālandhara, and her vulva is remembered as Kāmapīṭha.
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements;
one should first perform the assignment of the seers and so forth, and thereafter perform the purification.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this worship of the venerable Śakti, which begins with "Ṛṣyādi kaṇṭhaścit" and is praised by the gods, is declared to be Gonarda. 100b)
The modification is called *chandas*, following the words that constitute the form of the power.
The deity is Mahākālī, Kāma is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja),
Vadhū Bhuvaneśī is the power (śakti), and it is declared that [the same] is the pin (kīlaka).
The application is in the light of the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti;
the six limbs [of the ritual] are formed with the seed-syllables of the Vadhūs enriched by the five long vowels through their conjunction.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon oneself by means of the limbs of the Power (*śakti*), one should then perform the recitation (*vācya*). In place of the word "Power" (*śakti*), one should utter the word "Bhairava" as if it were feminine.
O Goddess of the Asuras, the conceptualization of the *liṅga* in the place of the woman's womb may occur either through the instruction of a guru or by means of one's own intellect.
Modification (ūha) must be performed everywhere—in the gender and in each respective word—but it is the same for the Gāyatrī; indeed, it is the same in both cases.
101a) Now,
listen attentively to this extraction of the nyāsa-mantras:
Trayā, Kāmo, Ramā, Rāvaḥ, Yoginī, and Roṣayoṣitau.
The Ḍākinī is Pralayohāra, Phetkārī, and Karṇikā;
the Preta is Nṛsiṃha and Kulika; and Cicchukti resides at the end of all.
One should offer each seed-syllable of the names individually to the deity worshipped by the gods; following those, one should offer *aulikī* and immediately thereafter *bhagamālinī*.
Ratipriyā, Tathānaṅgā, Akulā, Samayapālinī,
