Madanotsādinī, and Kāmāveśinī follow immediately after that.
Then [there are] Cintonmathinī, Mohanī, Karṣaṇī,
Smarā, Tarā, Anaṅgabhūpā, Hṛtpramodinī, and immediately after that, Divyā.
Then there is Santāpinī and Saṃkṣobhinī, worshipped by the thirty gods;
at the very end of all, she who is the embodiment of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) is to be fully known.
These sixteen should indeed be formed with feminine endings and joined with the word *pūrvāṇa*;
however, in the rite of worshiping Bhairava, they take masculine forms when referring to the state of being female.
Salutations to all the remaining [deities]; now, assign their respective positions by means of a portion.
The head, the cheeks, the throat, the shoulders, the chest, the breasts,
as well as the sides, the belly, the navel, the bladder, and the penis.
The thighs, knees, shanks, feet, and the remaining parts [of the body] including the generative organ—
over these one should perform the placement (nyāsa) as described for the living soul (jīva), and likewise practice the state of aesthetic flavor (sāmarasya).
"O Goddess, having uttered 'These are the deities,' one should perform the purification of the Śakti;
then, making a respectful salutation with folded hands, one should place them upon the heart and the lotus of the navel."
Or else, O Goddess, [one may worship] Kāmapīṭha at the navel, according to the Māulīyaka tradition;
reciting the mantra to be described hereafter either once or three times.
One should perform this purification of Śakti consisting of the *jīvan nyāsa*;
by this alone is Śakti purified, and not otherwise, even by ten million mantras.
One should visualize in front the eight seed-syllables: Māyā, Kāma, Avadhūtī, Lakṣmī, Kūrca, Prāsāda, Śākinī, and also Ḍākinī. 102a)
The bliss of enjoyment, the expression of the kalās, the individual self, and the supreme self.
Having declared that the ten peaks (of the mantra) consist of the non-dual designation of reflections, the totality, and the abode-less, one should then state Brahman as being the opposite of that.
One should utter the pair at the end of the ten; thus it is measured by half of half.
Then one should say "mamānu hṛdaya" and then "tavānu hṛdayam."
Having first uttered the words "Dadhātu mama," one should then address these words to me;
thereafter, O lady of stainless face, one should speak [the mantra] while the senses are focused on me.
And having consoled my senses, offer my words as an oblation;
then, O lady of shapely breasts, you shall be known to me as Siddhikarālī.
One should say, "Whoever you are, that indeed am I; whoever I am, that indeed are you. Then, joined by the *sandhi*, one should recite both [names] accordingly.
Having begun with Śiva and Śakti, immediately thereafter,
having proclaimed their unity (*tadaikya*), one should utter: "and may [I] accomplish [it]."
O beautiful one, that is the junction, the heart, the head, and the mantra which follows.
This mantra has been prescribed for the rite of purifying the power (śakti);
it consists of one hundred and eight syllables, neither fewer nor more.
One should meditate upon that meditation previously described by me to you, O Blessed One,
visualizing your power in such a form and observing the collection of its limbs.
One should visualize oneself as being identical to Bhairava in meditation;
then, one should invoke the Goddess into that which resembles the seat of the limbs of Śakti.
With the mantra to be recited hereafter and the añjali mudrā,
[the practitioner should invoke] Māyā, Kāmavadhū, Rāvā, Kamalā, Yoginī, and Ruṣā.
The Ḍākinī and Phetkārī—these nine are indeed the primary songs. Having uttered "Come, come, O Bhagavatī," one should then invoke Mahākālī.
One should cause [the deity] to enter by means of the proximity of the Śaktipīṭha and then extract [it];
thereafter, having written "thou" and "I," one should invoke and proclaim [the mantra].
Having addressed Sarvaśakti, one should then speak to her in her essential form (svarūpiṇī).

Listen to the mantra: *tāra* (oṃ), *pratiṣṭhā*, the head (*śīrṣa*), the root of power (*śaktimūla*), *manu* (namaḥ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *rāvaḥ* (kroṃ), *smaraḥ* (klīṃ), *nārī* (strīṃ), and then *śaktaye* (śaktaye) for the heart (*hṛdaya*).
The mantra for the rite of worshiping Śakti is declared to consist of nine syllables; it has no seer (ṛṣi) and so forth, nor does it have a meter, seed-syllable, or power.
This mantra, which is the cause for the offering of water for the feet, the oblation, and all other services,
as well as for the removal of sins, must certainly not be recited by one who has not been instructed by Tripuraghna.
He should offer all the ritual services according to his capacity;
indeed, whatever is desired, such as the offering of water for the feet (pādya) and the offering of food (naivedya), should be given.
O Goddess who wields the mace, in my opinion there is no other mantra distinct from this;
that which is called the *kūrca* mantra at the head [of the sequence] should be understood as being without foundation.
Whatever remains from the worship of Śakti— such as flower garlands and unguents—
that which is offered to oneself becomes the worship of me, Sāmarasī.
That mantra-less [rite] should be performed; such is the command of Īśāna. Then, having placed the hand upon the śakti-yoni-pīṭha, one should perform the recitation (japa).
The practitioner should recite the Śakti-gāyatrī one hundred times, or even fifty or twenty-five times;
there is no recitation anywhere that is as renowned as the recitation at the Yoni-pīṭha.
This is the supreme seat (pīṭha) for mantras,
which generates the power of truth for those whose mantras have lost their strength and whose minds are exhausted by ritual application.
The non-extraction of debts from debtors who are deficient or excessive in their obligations,
as well as the granting of desired gifts even to teachers, likewise results in a loss of vigor.
This is the procedure for the worship of those who have received the vessel-offering,
as well as for those who have renounced, those who are filled with wonder, and likewise those who lack spiritual power.
For the purpose of kindling [the fire], both have been taught by the enemy of Tripura:
one is the recitation of that [mantra] encapsulated by the Nirvāṇa mantra.

104a) Furthermore, there is the Kaulāsana; the practice of recitation (*japa*) is performed upon the seat of the womb (*yonipīṭha*). The Kaulāsana is the grace of the mantra [bestowed] by women upon the seat of the womb.
O King, one should recite the mantra of both [the Guru and the Consort] while they are united;
when kindled by other mantras, it produces supreme and extraordinary power.
Now, therefore, O Goddess, hear the Śakti-gāyatrī of great fruit: one should first utter the Bhagavatī born from the seed-syllable of desire (Klīm), ending with the feminine suffix -ī.
"Vidmahe yonimālinyai dhīmahi," and after that,
"tannaḥ śaktiḥ," having uttered this, one should conclude with "pracodayāt" at the very end of all.
For this power is Gāyatrī, well-guarded by all the Āgamas;
without these powers, there can be no recitation (japa) consisting of the three limbs.
Having empowered her according to one's ability and having offered her to Śakti,
one should seat her on the left lap and perform the recitation of the root mantra, O Beloved.
One should worship the temple of Madana, anointed with red sandalwood;
it should be known that there are three channels (nāḍīs) flowing [there] at the time of the half-measure.
The lunar day is indeed one more than the solar;
another is known as the Vāhikā, and yet another is to be known as the Āgneyī; the practitioner should worship that [lunar day].
The lunar [power] flows as a missile, the solar flows as a flower, and the fiery flows as a seed; one should worship them by their respective names.
With a well-pleased mind, one should worship using the syllables beginning with Vāgbhava joined with "namaḥ";
O Maheśānī, one should perform meditation upon Gahvarī, who has one face and four hands.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon that Vidyā who deludes the worlds, situated there, possessing the radiance of an elephant-faced one and the sound of a copper-crested cock.
The mantra of Bhagamālā, however, is as follows:
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word *gaśat*, followed by *bhage* and *bhagini*;
then *bhagodarī*, *bhagāketu*, *bhagamāle*, and *bhagāvahe*.
In the secret part of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, at the edge of the womb, and at the end of the vulva;
in the *niprāti* and at the very end of all— thereafter, [one should worship] the body of Bhagavatī.
Then, O lotus-eyed one with long eyes, one should draw the form of the vulva;
one should paint everything, including the edges of the vulva, which are eternally moist and well-formed.
One should write "Bhagavati me hyā na moṃte varade" at the end;
then "Ratesvarate bhagavat klinne klinne drave."
O Mistress of the Bhaga, draw forth and cause all sentient beings to melt;
O Amoghe Bhagavicce, agitate the eyes and agitate them all!
Bhageśvarī should address sentient beings with the Vāgbhava mantra beginning with *brūja*,
followed by *bhaṃ*, *vlūṃ*, *mauṃ*, *vlūṃ*, *haiṃ*, and then *krinne*.
And at the end of all the *bhagas*, one should recite "meva śaṃcānaya," and at the end of the seed-syllable of the woman (*strībīja*), the syllable consisting of the letter *va*.
Having drawn the *bhuvanaśī* [mandala], one should worship this Vidyā Bhagamālinī at the end of the dative case; O Goddess, one should cast a flower upon the *bhaga*.
Having washed [the image] with family substances (kuladravya), one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the enclosure (āvaraṇa).
O Maheśvarī, here too there is no invocation (āvāhana) nor the placement of the vital breaths (jīva-nyāsa).
Then, according to this procedure, they [should be worshipped] with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Having worshipped one's chosen deity, one shall become a master of all accomplishments;
immediately thereafter, one should worship one's own Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Now I shall proclaim the ritual placement (nyāsa); one should contemplate the Great God as the very self of Śiva. One should perform the placement in sequence upon the five faces, conjoined with the [sixteen] kalās.
Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, is the first digit, Śaśinī;
Īśvara, the Lord of all beings, follows immediately after as Maṅgalā.
At the end of the word *brahmādhipati*, one should again place *brahmaṇodhipatiḥ*;
then, one should install *brahmeṣṭadāśivo'stu* as the enclosure for Marīci.
Having first uttered *Sadāśivom*, then *Muṇḍamālinī* as the supreme [mantra],
and then *Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe*, it is declared as ending with *kalānti*. 106a)
We meditate upon the Great Giver, as well as upon the arts and sciences.
After that, the word *rudraḥ* is the *pada*; then the *kalās* are said to be *pratiṣṭhā*.
Having uttered *pracodayāt*, there shall then follow *nivṛtti*.
O Goddess, one should sequentially place the *aghorebhyaḥ* mantra and the *stamaḥ* digit upon the heart in the east, west, south, and north.
Then, one should dissolve Moha into the neck from the Ghoras;
thereafter, the ritual should take place at the end of the Ghoras, and then one should install [the deity] in the southern part.
At the end of Ghorā, the Kriyā [kalā] should follow; thereafter, one should duly place the southern portion.
After that, one should place Namastestu [kalā], and then Kṣudhā; subsequently, one should place Kalā on the back in due order.
At the end of "to those of beautiful form" (bhadra-rūpebhyaḥ), there should be "to the end of thirst" (tṛṣāntāra) ending with "namas";
for the secret teacher, there should be "to Vāmadeva" (vāmadevāya) ending with "namaḥ".
Having placed [the mantra] on the right side of the face, one should protect it with "Homage to Jyeṣṭhāya";
then, behind it, [one places] "Homage to Rudrāya" and this left-hand mouse-portion (uṣakalā).
At the end of "Salutation to Kāla," Pālinī is on the right thigh;
O Goddess of the gods, Kalakāmā is on the left, and [salutation] to Vikaraṇa.
Having uttered the word "namaḥ" at the knee of the right leg of Saṃyamanī, the movement known as *valakriyā* is prescribed; and on the left, it is for *vikaraṇa*.
Having uttered "namo 'stu vṛddhaye," one should place [the syllable] on the right;
with "balapramathanāya namaḥ," one should place Rātri on the left.
Having assigned the *kalā* "Brahmā" at the end of "namas" for the subduing of all beings (*sarvabhūtadamana*),
one should assign the *kalā* "Mohinī" at the end of the mantra to the region of the hips.
Having placed [the syllable] *jvalā* on the right side with "Salutation to Unmanā," one should place [the remaining syllables] on the two feet, the two breasts,
the nose, the head, and the pair of arms.
107a) The mantra practitioner correctly [attains] the eight kalās arising from Sadyojāta in sequence.
I shall explain Sadyojāta; the first kalā is Siddhi.
To Sadyojāta indeed belongs further glory; prosperity is said to arise from him, and from him comes splendor as the third, immediately thereafter.
The fourth is said to be Lakṣmī; from her comes the state of non-existence (nirvāṇa).
The fifth is called Medhā; she is the Kalā who bestows the abundance of existence.
Impelled by wisdom, the sixth ray shall be the final one of existence;
after "Salutation to Udbhava," the eighth ray shall be Suddha.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) beginning with the syllable Om, ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namaḥ.
Having thus performed the rite of placement, one should contemplate oneself as Śiva.

Placing the five-syllable mantra at the forefront and being devoted to the meditation on Rudra, one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) for the sake of protection, having established a state of aesthetic rapture (sāmarasya).
Having sealed the agitating [power] with the bride (*vadhū*), one should never cause Kālikā to enter within;
for from that very moment, through her presence, [the goal is attained].
One should perform the libation for all the gurus and practitioners;
by that divine nectar, they all become satisfied.
Whatever desire the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) undertakes, that very thing is accomplished in an instant.
Having taken the nectar of the Kula, the wise one should pour it there as an offering (argha).
Thereupon, practitioners of pure disposition should worship the digits of the Moon with thousands of jars of honey and even hundreds of loads of meat.
O Goddess, she shall not be satisfied at all except by the nectar of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*;
O Beloved, having purified the *kula*-substance which consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Having cast the supreme Brahman, which is the nectar of life, into the form of the beautiful woman,
the ever-pure one, free from conceptual construction, becomes heated by the nectar of the *arghapātra*.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the Goddess in the vulva with the substances for the *argha* offering.
Without the worship of the *yoni*, even that which has been performed becomes as if unperformed;
yet when the union with the *dūtī* is accomplished, the practitioner of mantra certainly becomes all-knowing.
There is no returning for him again, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas,
by those who have performed worship through the messenger (dūtī) and completed all the desired sacrifices.
It is said that he embodies all sacred fords and embodies all the gods;
by him, the entire rite of *puraścaryā* and so forth has been performed—of this there is no doubt.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, as well as the entire earth reaching to the oceans— by that he [performed] those sacrificial fees.
O beloved, the merit that arises from the gift of ten million cows is indeed produced by those who have offered gold equal in weight to Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the sacrifice of the messenger (dūtīyāga), O auspicious lady;
it bestows the perfection of worship and reveals all misfortunes.
A worship performed even if it lacks the *yoni-pūjā* shall become inexhaustible;
such a person obtains long life, health, wealth, and honors. (109b)
By this very procedure, one afflicted by poison shall become free from poison.
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth.
One should worship Mātaṅgī and Śaktimatī, and likewise worship us.
The goddess Mātaṅgī, endowed with the god of love, is the deity of the Mātaṅgī mantra; she should always be worshipped together with Śakti for the attainment of all desires and goals.
But that goddess, being devoid of power, does not grant one's heart's desire;
likewise, the man who seeks to accomplish the power while being deprived of the full consecration.
The impure person who has fallen ill will certainly meet his death,
due to the unassailability of the senses and the arising of desire and greed.
Generally, in this Kali age, this Kaulika path leads to hell;
the daily worship is the best, while worship on festival days is mediocre.
Worship performed monthly is declared to be the lowest; after a month, one becomes a sacrificial animal (paśu).
Whether at the end of a month, or three months, or six months, or a year— 110a) [The text continues: ...or even longer.
One should worship the glorious Guru with devotion; thus one obtains wives, sons, and other blessings.
In his absence, one should satisfy a yogin who belongs to that same lineage or is his disciple with the substances of the lineage,
preceded by the worship of the cakra.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the Śrī Kaularahasya, which encompasses all the Āgamas. || 19 ||
Now, he describes the specific ritual procedure for the wheel.

One who is impure from eating remnants should not touch the cakra, the kula, the ritual substances, nor the guru. Having washed one's hands outside, one should cause the kula-substances to be offered.
Having removed the vessel for liquor, one should not fill it with [other] vessels;
one should never cast away the vessel of enjoyment or the jar of wine.
That foolish-minded person who, with impure thoughts, performs the cleansing of the hands, mouth, and other parts within the center of the maṇḍala, shall indeed become a vessel for calamities.
He who discharges spittle, excrement, urine, or downward wind into the center of the Śrīcakra shall become a beast for the Yoginīs.
If the wheel is destroyed in the center, or the vessel is encircled by serpents,
or if there is the extinguishing of the lamp, there will be oppression by the king; for its pacification, one should perform the worship of the wheel.
One should avoid joking, idle chatter, mockery, excessive speech,
indifference, fear, and anger while in the midst of the assembly.
With the bowl in hand, one should not move about in the midst of the circle with a full bowl;
one should not place it on the ground nor let it slip from the hands of the one holding the bowl.
One should never touch the bowl with one's feet, nor should one ever shake it;
it must not be given by hand, nor should a single drop be allowed to fall to the ground.
One should not move the vessel from its place, nor drink while avoiding the mudrā;
one should drink the liquor making a sound, and one must not cause a confusion of vessels.
One should sound the vessel when it is full of wine, whether it be three-quarters or one-quarter full;
one should strike various other vessels, but one should not strike a vessel from below.
That which is common to all does not bestow increase. || 1 ||
Folio 111 not found.
112a) Endowed with the entire collection of the arts of all traditions, revealing wonders, [it is worshipped by] Candra, Upendra, Śambhu, and Varuṇa.
Worshipped by Brahmā and others,
meditated upon always by hosts of gods seeking liberation, increasing the prosperity of the worlds and bestowing happiness—
salutations to this second vessel. || 2 ||
Wine, meat, and fish are filled by Harihara, Brahmā, and the other gods; they provide the bliss of dharma through the mudrā of sexual union, and consist of salty, sour, and bitter flavors.
By means of the purification of the eight Bhairavas through the placement (*nyāsa*) of their digits (*kalā*), they are honored by the Master.
This third vessel, joined with the five *makāras*, is saluted. || 3 ||

Manifested as that which bestows the bliss of the Golakuṇḍa, worshipped by Brahmā and Rudra, worthy of the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the first flower born from the elephant, possessing a divine and supreme peak beyond all others,
my own longing, the most excellent of essences, and once again the celestial nectar of the assembly.
This fifth liberation, which fulfills all desires, is for the joy of the fourth state.
112b) The vessel is the mandala of the earth upon the supporting base of the serpent-king’s coil; the wine is the water of the seven oceans, and the meat is the eight elephants of the directions.
Thus, worshipping Bhairava daily—He who is protected by hosts of stars and by the throngs of gods and asuras led by Āditya, who stand ready to execute His commands—I [attain this]. || 5 ||
O illustrious Sundarī, [this] parasol, chowrie, and auspicious throne bestows supreme bliss; it grants the kingdom of Rāma and the union with the essence of enchanting happiness;
it dispels the darkness of various diseases and destroys future births.
One should worship the sixth vessel as Tarpaṇendra Varada.

The direct bestower of consciousness before the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turya), resembling lightning, the sun, fire, the moon, and a rainbow, described in the sacred narratives;
she who is the triple-folded body situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, the true *Kuṇḍalinī*, with her vessel turned upward by the filling of the seventh [chakra].
May he, whose bliss increases with his body, protect me.

The sword, the sandals, the collyrium, the pill, the eternal eloquence of Sarasvatī, the attainment of the true state, the evasion of death, the accomplishment of formidable tasks, the seizing [of power], and the stabilization of the body— these are the causes.

May [He], who bestows accomplishment, stabilizes the mind, and brings the world under control; who is the vessel proclaimed by the world, the means for attaining the eightfold perfections, and who is ever mature and gracious—protect me. (8)
O Śrī, you are the vessel that always bestows all bliss, grants liberation through the singular union in the state of Śiva, provides sovereign dominion and happiness,
fulfills desires, destroys ignorance,
increases longevity, fame, and glory, and cuts through the delusion of saṃsāra.
The group of nine powers of the nine lords is fully manifested as the counter-position.
One may drink from three vessels, five vessels, or even seven vessels;
one may also drink from nine vessels, but one should certainly not drink from sixteen or half of that.
As long as the sight does not move and as long as the mind does not move, one should perform the drinking; beyond this is the drinking of the *paśu*.
For those who are endowed with the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*, [the state] is declared to be *ānanda*;
having lifted the vessel with both hands while recollecting the *mūlamantra* and the *pādukā*.
One should drink wine until the throat is filled, along with pearls; of this there is no doubt.
Having drunk again and again, one should continue drinking until one falls to the ground.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth is no longer found;
Bhairava himself is intoxicated by the bliss of the Goddess's swoon.
Since all the gods vomit [at such acts], one should therefore perform these three;
the knower of Brahman, following the Kula practice, having drunk wine, stumbles repeatedly.
If dust particles fly from his body as he falls to the ground, for that many thousands of years he rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
Having drunk [the nectar] repeatedly and having recited [the mantra], one is liberated along with ten million kulas;
O Goddess, one shall dwell in the world of Brahmā—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
In that very state one attains pervasion (vyāpti), and shall not fall back into this world again;
having drunk [the nectar] and worshipped the Lord, one certainly attains lordship.
Therein alone one attains dissolution and never returns again;
there, among the intoxicated heroes, there exists neither what should be done nor what should not be done.
In that regard, whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all of it arises for the pleasure of the deity; of this there is no doubt.
Idle chatter is the fruit of recitation; drowsiness is declared to be meditative absorption (samādhi).
Physical agitation is said to be worship, and vomiting is the bali offering to Bhairava.
Liberation is the union with that power; praise is the recitation of its hymns;
ritual placement (nyāsa) is the touching of its limbs; and the act of eating is the performance of the fire-oblation (havana).
Meditation is said to be gazing, while lying down is salutation;
and whatever movement is performed out of joy in that [state] is considered a virtuous action.
He who deliberates upon what should and should not be done is a sinner. Those heroes who have entered this wheel are to be known as supreme yogins.
By means of which human beings directly attain the very form of Bhairava—
[exhibiting] joy and tranquility, falling and rising, and dancing.
The playing of flutes, lutes, and other instruments; the composition of poetry and the like; pushing, speaking, falling down, rising up, and yawning.
O Goddess, movement is called *vikriyā* (modification), and that is designated as *yoga*.
When one abandons the modification of the mind, that which proceeds is *pallāsa*.
At that time, the best of yogis partake in the state of the deity;
however, those of deluded intellect revile the Kaulikas, the Ambhas, the Bhairavas, and the Vaiśyas.
O Yoginīs, there is no doubt regarding that destruction; there is no uncertainty here.
Whatever the Kaulika person speaks out of the possession of divine intoxication is truly marvelous.
For that particular state of existence, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [the mantra is]:
*Tāro namo bhagavati madyamāṃsavihāriṇi*.
"O Cakreśvarī, beloved of Rati, speak, O you who are dear to the Kaulikas! Is the liquor that has been thought of in my mind truly present? Having said this, [he offers] the liquor mixed with meat.
One should bestow [the teaching] upon those belonging to the Kaula lineage; they, being devoted to that doctrine, proclaim it.
Therein, for one who is a true Kaula, the words of wisdom flash forth.
One should rejoice, laugh, and become angry; one should intoxicate oneself with wine, agitated by passion.
One must never reveal to outsiders the conduct of those who have entered this circle.
One should not commit malice toward them, nor should one act for their harm;
rather, with devotion one should indeed serve them and protect them with great effort.
And upon seeing a woman, one should regard her with the thought that she is a deity;
he who rejoices in her and pays homage with devotion shall go to the state of the Yoginī.
When the Bhairavī-cakra has commenced, all castes are distinct from one another:
women, men, eunuchs, outcastes (cāṇḍālas), and even the highest of the twice-born (advijottama).
Within the center of the wheel there is no distinction; all deities are remembered as equal.
(115b) All persons who have entered the center of the wheel possess the form of Śiva.
All women are like Pārvatī; therefore, one should not cause division among them.
A lustful man shall not approach a woman who is unwilling or one who has not been initiated;
however, he may approach a woman who has been purified by the immediate purificatory rite, for such an act is prescribed.
By performing the worship of a thousand wheels, a king who has fallen from his kingdom shall regain it;
by fifty, one obtains a son; and by ten, one becomes free from disease.
If a woman falters while engaged in the worship of this wheel,
she will certainly become a sovereign ruler within the course of a year.
One should perform fivefold worship for the attainment of desired beloveds;
through sevenfold worship, there is the acquisition of wealth—this is the procedure for the Cakra-pūjā.
The merit of one who gives his sister, daughter, or wife to a practitioner of the lineage (kulayogin) at the end of the Cakra while he is intoxicated with honey cannot be calculated.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the venerable *Kaularahasya*, the scripture of all traditions. || 20 ||
116a) Now, he explains the indicative sign (naimittika).
Śrī Mahākāla said:
This much of the procedure for daily worship has been declared by me to you;
now listen to the rules for occasional and optional rites.
O Goddess of the gods, when one proceeds with reference to some specific occasion, that is designated as occasional (naimittika); yet even that is as dear as the daily (nitya) rite.
Having formed some desire within one's own mind, one engages in action;
that which accomplishes the fruit of such desire is designated as "kāmya" (action performed for a specific reward).

Therein, O Śivā, I shall first explain the occasional rites (naimittika). These occasional rites, moreover, should generally be understood by the wise as being like the daily obligatory rites (nitya).
But he who performs the occasional worship established by specific occasions,
as well as the daily worship, augmented by the power of his knowledge;
Therefore, who among the most wicked would be a vessel for hatred toward Kālikā?
Even through the loss of a limb, no loss of form is conceived for that which is eternal.
For one who relies on omens, fruitlessness and loss arise.
Therefore, having examined the scripture according to the lineage of gurus, one should perform the rite with all its constituent parts;
for this [rite], the limbs are these, while the excellence of the recipient is the lineage of Śiva.
The five-fold assembly, the traditional law, the distinctness of the mantra,
the worship, the offering (bali), the animal sacrifice (paśubali), and the sequence of the worship.
The requisites such as incense and lamps, the worship of Śakti, and the recitation of mantras—
these ten are indeed fully present in the daily worship, even if some among them [are lacking].
Indeed, even though there may be regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) offerings by women,
there are likewise the autumnal (śārada), the winter (vāsantika), and the eclipse-related (auparāgika) worship.
Because it is accepted as having a cause, it is considered to be caused;
since these two are not performed, there is no permanence.
Various [systems] are proclaimed in the various Tantras; among them, that [system] is considered the principal.
Thus it should be understood in all cases regarding all these established conclusions.
The pure occasional worship is said to be of twenty varieties.
The lunar nodes (parvan), the great pretas, Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛta, the beginnings of the Manvantaras and Yugas, the Vedāṅgas, the deities, and Bhava;
One should avoid flowers, meat, and the three heavy foods (triguru) on one's own birth day,
as well as the day of initiation during the Navarātra festival.
The conjunctions of the moon and sun (eclipses), the purification of the metals,
the undertaking of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, and likewise the arrival immediately thereafter;
In matters concerning sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and those residing in them, the acquisition of merit, burnt offerings (*homa*), vows, and festivals;
as well as the appearance of portents, the release from bondage, and the rise of enemies.
In times of disease, calamity, fault, ill association, or evil omens,
as well as during planetary afflictions and fear of the king, there shall be peace and great prosperity.
Thus have these various kinds of signs been described by you:
that which is called the binding of the *damanaka* flower, as well as the mounting of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*).
O Pārvatī, the lunar days (tithis) and the names [of the deities] are included within their respective functions.

The lunar days (tithis) and festival days (parvans) upon which occasional worship (naimittikārcana) is performed are now described; next follows the determination of the Kula-days (kulavāra) and so forth.
For those of noble lineage, on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight— and especially on the fourteenth—
the worship of the Yoginīs and the worship of the Kula are paramount there.
The Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are considered non-kula (akula);
Mars and Venus are known as kula, while Wednesday is both kula and akula.
The second, tenth, and sixth [tithis] are declared to be *kulākula*;
those that are favorable to the *kulas* are *kulās*, while the remainder are *akulas*.
The eighth and the ninth, as well as the fourteenth day of both fortnights,
and likewise the full moon and the new moon.
Likewise, twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) are taught, as well as four among them:
two solstices (ayanas), two equinoxes (viṣuvats), and the four [periods] of eighty-four [yogas].
O Dear One, these four [groups] of the Viṣuvat do not precede the first;
thereafter, there are four [groups] of the moving [planets], each consisting of two kings.
Then, for those stable [planets] whose auspicious rise of merit occurs, there are as many [periods] as there are,
including Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, and the very waning of the lunar days (tithis).
All four of these Yugādis grant the fruit of great merit;
likewise, the third day of the bright fortnight, Rādhīpātā, and the ninth day of the month of Kārttika.
The thirteenth day of the dark fortnight is [the day of] Bhrātṛ; the new moon day is for ascetics;
and the seventh day of the bright fortnight, when joined with Sunday, is [the day of] Kṛṣṇā.
The eighth lunar day conjoined with Mercury, the tenth with Jupiter,
the sixth with Venus, and the thirteenth with Saturn.
The Vaiśākha full moon, the seventh day of the bright fortnight, the Jyeṣṭha fourth,
the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, and also the tenth day of Jupiter.
O beloved, the fifth day of the dark fortnight and also the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa—
starting from the second lunar day, it shall continue until the eighth day.
In the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, however, these lunar days (tithis) bestow sevenfold merit; they are generally regarded as the eighth day (aṣṭamī), established as a sacred festival (parvan).
The Durgāṣṭamī is specifically a lunar day that bestows pleasure upon Durgā; on this day, the Mauleyas perform the rite known as the planting of Durvā grass sprouts.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the tenth day of the bright fortnight—
these eighteen lunar days are remembered as being pleasing to the Goddess.
O lady with the downward face, three nights—beginning from the seventh—are especially meritorious;
on these, the great autumnal festival is celebrated by all.
O lady of excellent hips, the three lunar days beginning with the thirteenth of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika bestow infinite fruit.

On the thirteenth day of the month of Phālguna, she is known by the name Aghorā; on the fourteenth, she is called Sukharātrī, or alternatively Dīpamālikā. On the new moon day (darśa), she is likewise named Sukharātrī.
On the day when the moon is in conjunction with the constellation Śravaṇā, one should worship Śivā;
the eighth day of the bright fortnight is called Goṣṭhā, and it bestows abundant merit.
The ninth lunar day is declared to be the beginning of the Yuga; on that day, Kālikā remains awake.
Therefore, an elaborate worship should be performed on that occasion with special care.
Now follows the determination of the lunar days (tithis).
I shall state the determination of the lunar days (tithis) in their subtle essence, and not in detail—
those lunar days which have been prescribed for occasional rites of worship.
Pervading both fortnights until the end of the night,
midnight is indeed highly praised for the joyful worship of the Bhagavatī.
When, due to the midnight conjunction (yogonīśītha), the lunar days (tithis) cannot be determined at all,
then a distinction must be made between both fortnights.
119b) When the sun has risen during the bright fortnight, the lunar days are established;
when it goes to its setting during the dark fortnight, this is considered the general rule.

A lunar day (tithi) of the bright fortnight that exceeds even a single muhūrta by being joined with an even [number of muhūrtas] is accepted for rites such as bathing, giving, and worship because it is prescribed for those purposes.
A lunar day (tithi) that lasts for only a few moments, or even one measured by a single muhūrta, should never be accepted due to its brevity of time.
For as long as a lunar day remains, for that duration the ritual activity prescribed for it—
conducive to the respective rite— should be completed with devotion.
O Kṛṣṇa, when that lunar day (tithi) occurs at such a time,
then the prescribed rite should be performed, whether by night or by day.
If the Niśītha-yoga does not occur during either of the two fortnights,
then the worship and other rites should be performed in the forenoon or the afternoon.
In this world, the forenoon belongs to the gods, the midday belongs to the *ṛṣis*,
and the afternoon belongs to the ancestors; such is the divine determination of the law.
The lunar day (tithi) is indeed analyzed in two ways by means of Madhu.
If both of these [tithis] are pierced by another tithi that pervades the forenoon, then the one pierced by the subsequent tithi is the one to be taken;
there is never any precedence for the one pierced by the preceding tithi.
The fourth lunar day should be observed in conjunction with the third, rather than with the second;
on the day of worship, the fourth day must be performed when it is joined with the preceding [third] day.
One who performs [the rite] on the fifth day together with [the fourth] will immediately cause his lineage to perish;
therefore, Kālikā’s worship should always be performed together with the fourth day.
The sixth lunar day conjoined with the seventh is praised for all ritual acts;
the sixth should be observed when pierced by the seventh, according to my teaching.
O Goddess of the Universe, during the worship of the two Aśvinīs in the month of Śarada,
the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of both fortnights should be observed as joined with the following day.
The ninth lunar day (navamī) conjoined with the eighth is a merit-bestowing date;
the ninth pierced by the tenth is considered to bring all happiness.
One who desires prosperity should not observe an Ekādaśī that is pierced by Daśamī;
nor should one observe an Ekādaśī that is joined with Dvādaśī, nor a Dvādaśī that is joined with Trayodaśī.
The fourteenth day should be observed when joined with the thirteenth;
it should not be joined with the fourteenth, but rather performed when conjoined with the new moon.
Thus, in the ritual procedure for the worship of the Goddess, the lunar day and its required duties have been declared.
Now follows the determination of Vīrarātri and other such observances.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the determination regarding Vīrarātri and the others:
Vīrarātri, Mahārātri, and likewise Kālarātri.
The night of delusion, the terrible night, the night of anger,
as well as the auspicious night, the divine night, and the dreadful night, respectively.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
It is told, O Supreme Goddess, listen, O you who have arisen from the fire:
the fourteenth lunar day, the transit [of the sun], and the day of Kula and Kulakula.
At midnight, according to the appropriate yoga, it is proclaimed as the Hero’s Night (vīrarātri).
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is indeed the Navarātra;
it is the Mahārātri, O Maheśānī. Listen, O beloved, to [the account of] Kālarātri.
On the fourteenth day of the festival of lamps, when it coincides with the conjunction of Amāvāsyā,
O Maheśānī, you are Kālarātri, Tārākālī, and Priyaṅkarī.
O Great Goddess, Janmāṣṭamī is proclaimed as the Night of Delusion;
O Maheśvarī, it occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived.
Mahākāla is proclaimed as his own form, and Ghorarātri is celebrated;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, when Mars is in the ascendant.
O Great Goddess, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight when the month of Phālguna arrives, Krodharātri will take the form of Tārā.
If it is joined by Venus and Mars, it is declared to be an "Avalā" night;
likewise, the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when endowed with the ten yogas.
If there should be an eclipse on the new moon day conjoined with Mars, occurring at a solar transit (saṃkrānti),
and associated with the Kula constellation;
The Tārā [mantra] is said to be obtained through good fortune alone when it is recited three times at midnight on a Friday during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, O Śiva.
Śivarātri has indeed arrived, bestowing all perfections;
it is the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the day of Śukra and the hour of Vāsava.
O Supreme Goddess, if the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is joined with the ten yogas during the night, that lunar day is proclaimed as a divine night.
O Goddess, the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava, conjoined with the lunar mansion Kṛttikā,
is proclaimed as Dāruṇā, the supreme sovereign of all accomplishments.
Furthermore, O Goddess of the gods, the lunar month and others are to be adopted for matters such as ritual impurity;
however, that month which follows the sequence of the zodiac signs is prescribed for matters such as marriage.
122a) Regarding the non-payment of debts, the practice of lending, and journeys to Śrāvastī, Ādhavana, and other such places,
as well as for rites of pacification (śāntika) or enrichment (pauṣṭika), no specific lunar mansion or month is required.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, that time when the oblation to Indra and Agni is offered should be known as the beginning of the month for rites such as the commencement of vows.
O beloved, when the month of Bhomāgnīṣoma is said to be in the middle, it is then that the ancestral rites for the Pitṛs are performed.
This ritual should be understood as occurring within each month;
for occasional worship, the prescribed times are morning, midday, and the period of saṅgava.
O Lord of Obstacles, O Lord of the Night at the onset of dusk, O Source of Power!
Whatever action is performed by transgressing the prescribed root-time [of the rite], [is rendered fruitless].
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, some fruit indeed arises from that;
thus the scriptures declare that such a person becomes a treasury of wealth.
Therefore, at that time, those who desire the fruits of their actions and heaven should perform the rites according to the season,
according to their faith, according to their available materials, and as is appropriate.
O Goddess of the Suras, one should perform worship according to one's strength and according to the place; likewise, occasional and great rites must be performed.
Having conquered his senses, he should eat sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) only once a day, while abstaining from perfumes,
flowers, ornaments, collyrium, bathing, shaving, and the wearing of garlands.
The union of the image, the pedestal, and so forth; the anointing of that temple;
and the purification of the vessels for worship by means of specific substances.
Indeed, one should perform these six [acts] during occasional rites:
when there is smoke, when there are embers, when the teeth are stained with blood, during childbirth, and when there is a discharging sore.

One should not perform occasional rites (naimittika) preceded by worship, nor sexual intercourse, nor when reviling women or the twice-born; for by performing them in such a manner, one shall not obtain the fruit.
One who is devoted to the Kaula conduct should diligently invite all women who travel the path of the Kula; among them all, the Guru must be invited first.
O fair-faced one, one should diligently provide an abundance of food offerings, incense, and lamps, and especially of flowers and garlands.
Whether by night or by day, having prepared the materials for worship, having performed the daily rites,
with darbha grass in hand and his mind focused on nothing else than the sacred scripture—
O Goddess of the Gods, having removed the flowers, incense, and other offerings, one should place them back again;
and having washed all the vessels as before.
Seated comfortably on a soft seat prepared according to one's means,
one should ensure an abundance of *vakula* flowers during the month of Vaiśākha.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform [the worship] with Nāgakeśara flowers;
furthermore, in Āśvina, it should be performed abundantly with Bandhūka flowers.
One should perform the abundance of the *agastya* flowers during the month of Ūrja (Kārttika); one should perform the abundance of *viśva* leaves during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Indeed, in the month of Pauṣa, a collection of sprouts of *durvā* grass bestows fruit;
in the month of Māgha, a cluster of *kaunda* flowers grants all auspiciousness.
The Mādhavī flower in the month of Phālguna bestows all perfections.
In the month of Caitra, the buds of the Aśoka tree destroy the effects of the Kali age,
as do Mālatī, Yūthikā, Damana, and Karṇikāraka.
The kuruṇṭhaka, the kuruvaka, the amlāna, and likewise the pāṭala,
as well as the flower of the navamālika, bestow supreme liberation.
O fair-faced one, these eleven flowers should always be offered during the months of Māgha or Pauṣa, provided that the sun is conjoined with Kārttikeya (the constellation Śravaṇā).
If the conjunction of Vyatīpāta occurs on a Sunday during the month of Bhādrapada, it shall be considered half a year;
that great lunar day (tithi) should be known as equal to ten million Yugādis.
Having offered an oblation there according to the prescribed rite with an *antaphala* fruit,
one shall obtain wealth, grain, and sons, and at the end of the body, attain liberation.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is designated by the name Varā;
for Kālikā, when worshipped on this day, bestows excellent husbands upon young maidens.
The daughter of a potter and the daughter of a water-carrier—these are declared to be the eight maidens; now hear of the eight families.
The royal courtesan, the secret courtesan, the divine-like courtesan,
the playful courtesan, the dancing girl, the pilgrimage courtesan, the hunchbacked woman, and the unchaste woman.
Pañcaliṅga is Hatāveśyā, Daśaliṅga is Bhageśvarī,
and Pañcaviṃśatiliṅga is proclaimed as Liṅgatuṣṭā.
Those endowed with fifty liṅgas are proclaimed as the Liṅgasiddhas;
she who possesses a hundred liṅgas is Bhagānandā, and she who possesses a thousand is Bhagasundarī.
Innumerable [deities] are joined with the *liṅga* and are considered supreme as the *bhaga* and *brahman*.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear from me the truth regarding the eight *kulas*.
In the center, O Maheśānī, is the Liṅga; the Bhaga is born from it as the most excellent.
The Viśvaliṅga is the source of all (*sarvayoni*), and it is superior even to everything else.
O Goddess, within the group of eight Kulākulas, two types are proclaimed:
the pair beginning with royal women and courtesans, and those beginning with cowherds and the like.
The mother, the daughter, the granddaughter, the sister, the wife of the brother-in-law,
Kālikā, Keli, Kuñcī, and the sister of the paternal uncle as the eighth.
This group of eight families has been proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments.
[One should worship] a young woman, beautiful, charming, restless, and eager for desire.
Having brought such a woman— one who is devoted to the guru, endowed with the mantra, and possessed of all auspicious marks— upon a bed of flowers;
The two breasts are said to be the two jars, while the navel is the general arghya vessel;
the vulva and the penis are the two [special] arghyas, and the triangular diagram is declared to be the yantra.
The movement of going and coming is said to be the *vṛtti*; the *puṣpaprahasita* is remembered [as such].
*Ālāya* is declared to be *tapaḥ*, while *nrvavaloka* is remembered as the best.
Anger is said to be suppression, while the grasping of the hand brings fear;
the wiping of her feet, however, is equivalent to circumambulating the earth.
Kissing, the recitation of hymns, the supporting of the breasts, the performance of virtuous rites,
and the placing of the feet upon the neck— this is declared to be the "Lion Throne" (siṃhāsana).
O Maheśvarī, the worship called Dolikā is said to be the reverse;
it consists of dismissal (*visarjana*), the falling of the seed-syllable (*bījapāta*), and the embrace (*āliṅgana*) as the mudrā.
O Goddess, the kissing of the lips is declared to be the Khecarī-yoga;
O Goddess, the kissing of the cheeks is proclaimed to be the Guṭikā.
O Goddess, a kiss upon the forehead is proclaimed as the *pādukā*;
O Goddess, a kiss upon the eyes is proclaimed as the *añjana*.
O Goddess, the kissing of the hand is proclaimed as the attainment of the sword-siddhi; O Goddess, the kissing of the vulva is the power consisting of the fulfillment of desires.
O Goddess of gods, the offering of the tongue is said to be the deception of Time;
O Goddess, that which relishes the essence is the form of Brahman— of this there is no doubt.
Upon looking at the earth, the deity Darśana should appear;
one should always maintain a connection with her and constantly recite [the mantra] while gazing upon her.
O Goddess, the gift of ten million universes and so forth is proclaimed as one thing;
however, the mere sight of her, O Goddess, would be far superior to all of that.
There may be millions of ascetic practices at millions of sacred fords, and even millions of yogas,
yet none of these equal the merit of one who has continuously performed service to temples.
Therefore, O Goddess, this vision of Brahman in the form of the Bindu is obtained;
O Goddess, the vision of Brahman is the most exalted Śabdabrahman.
Out of fear of Rāhu, the nectar of the moon, as well as the nectar of heaven, was drunk;
yet, out of great terror of the Rākṣasas, it remained within the radiant vulva of Kṣoṣṭhī.
O beloved Mistress of the Gods, the nectar of the moon resides eternally upon the lower lip, and the nectar of heaven resides in the womb; through knowledge it is attained, and not otherwise.
From ignorance, it takes the form of poison; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
(126a) Hālāhala is in the mouth, the garland in the [right] eye, and the vulva in the [left] eye.
A woman with protruding teeth [is seen] in the heart, and a row of lamps in the courtyard of the house.
O Goddess, how can one who does not perform [this] for another be a worshiper of me? O Goddess, there shall be no union with a home even until the end of the great kalpa.
Just as during a solar eclipse, O Lord, or when the moon is in an unfavorable conjunction,
whatever word is spoken by her, O Beloved, that you should carry out.
When yoga has been fully attained, and whenever that yoga is present, the person is indeed not born again; therefore, he sports repeatedly.
But that which is swallowed at sunset should be known as the most excellent of all;
however, when yoga is attained by oneself, one's own [life] falls away first.
By her, the ritual must be performed; for her, no downfall occurs. That [time] should be known as "eclipsed at rising," which bestows all accomplishments.
This secret which has been proclaimed— listen, O beloved, to the yoga of the day:
according to its own natural sequence, it arises from the splendor of the half-moon of each respective [day].
Mahodaya, when in its own yoga, is remembered as the "remover of the ten-fold news" (vārtādaśahara);
that which is called the subtraction of the form of that news is proclaimed as the third.
Thus it has been briefly declared; hear now the specific details, O Pārvatī.
The twelve months, O Goddess, have been proclaimed in their proper sequence.
O Maheśānī, in the Śatayoga, the Great Empire (Mahāsāmrājya) is proclaimed;
this has been declared regarding the ten [categories] beginning with the Divine (divya). Now hear another [classification].
Listen, O Great Goddess, to the rule of the kingdom: examine the sun and moon in their proper sequence;
whether on the new moon or the full moon, [observe] Rāhu, the sun, and the maker of night (the moon).
O Goddess of gods, by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, the moon never eclipses the sun; rather, it follows the shadow of the earth.
When there is a conjunction of those two having the same taste (*ekarasa*) and the same lord (*ekabhukti*),
occurring on a Sunday from the end of the new moon until the seventh [tithi], [the result is as follows].
Beyond that, one becomes a giver of the fruit of ten million merits.
O Goddess, there are three divisions of the solar eclipse, and likewise three divisions of the lunar eclipse;
these are known as the total eclipse, the partial eclipse, and the eclipse occurring at sunrise.
In the case of the moon as well, there are three types of division; and in the case of Śākta, it is likewise threefold and threefold.
Two and a half [units] are proclaimed as the state of being eclipsed when the Guru is superior.
O Goddess of the Suras, it should be understood that at the time of bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, giving gifts, ancestral rites, and the worship of Umā, it is indeed a period of great merit.
Having first fasted for a day and night during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
and having likewise recited the mantra, worshipped the Goddess, and given gifts;
Having performed the *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rite, one is liberated from all sins;
whatever one performs at that time, indeed becomes inexhaustible for them.
Even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) rejoices here through merit along with Brahmā when an eclipse of the Sun or the Moon is imminent.
O Goddess of the gods, even water from a well is considered equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
however, pure lake water should be known to be a hundred times more meritorious than that.
Therefore, it is proclaimed that [the merit of] the Ganges water is a thousand times greater than that;
therefore, the purifying water of the Ganges should be known as possessing ten million times the merit.
The wise should know that a fire offering (homa) is a thousand times more meritorious than bathing;
a funeral rite (śrāddha) is a hundred times more meritorious than a fire offering; and recitation (japa) is a hundred times more meritorious than a funeral rite.
The wise say that giving is a thousand times more meritorious than recitation;
worship of the Blessed Lady is distinguished as being ten million times more meritorious than giving.
In that regard, one should never perform worship as a matter of routine;
however, if one observes a fast on the preceding day, the worship becomes ten million times more meritorious.
If one is incapable of observing the fast, worship is considered to yield a hundred-thousandfold merit;
even when the moon or the sun is eclipsed by darkness, one should begin the worship as soon as it is seen.
O Goddess, when the planet is not seen, everything is said to be fruitless; in that case,
there is no conviction regarding one's own conviction in the rite for the deity.
In bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, ancestral rites, and receiving instruction, one should avoid accepting gifts.

O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, there is no entitlement for those who see [the eclipse] after it has begun, nor otherwise; however, O Goddess, when the planet is seen to have entered [the sun], that is a central eclipse.
When the sun is obscured by clouds and devoid of its rays, one should perform ritual bathing, giving, and other such acts;
however, during a partial eclipse of the sun, only the recitation of mantras (japa) should be performed.
O Supreme Goddess, beginning from the time of an eclipsed sunrise until the end of an eclipsed sunset,
one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites after consulting and examining the scriptures.

Having ascertained with effort through omniscience when the conjunction occurs and when the liberation occurs, one should perform bathing, giving, and other rites; such is the word of Śaṅkara, and not otherwise.
O fair-limbed lady, when a planet is in its own sign, or in the thirteenth, sixth, or eleventh house from that sign,
even if it is afflicted, there is no fault if Rāhu is also aspecting it.
Since an abundance of benefits and a reduction of defects arise from it,
one must certainly observe the appearance of Rāhu.
For the removal of defects such as the *nāḍī*, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), the moon, and so forth.
Some gift should be offered for the pacification of those respective obstacles;
O pure one, these Kālī mantras have been proclaimed by me for your sake.
If one recites this even once for them at the sight of Rāhu,
it destroys their sins— even those committed over ten million lifetimes.
Whoever recites the seventeenth [verse] consisting of sixteen syllables even once,
attains the fruit of giving away the entire earth with its seven continents.
Therefore, one should specifically perform the recitation (japa) accompanied by worship;
some, however, consider the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) to be merely secondary to the mantra.
This alone is the duty to be performed;
therefore, those entitled to the worship must observe the fast as a matter of necessity.
The performance of worship is the primary requirement; for its sake, there is an abundance of fruit. One should not eat for three watches (nine hours) prior to the lunar eclipse.
129a) Four *praharas* prior to a solar eclipse,
as well as [the period] when the moon is released from Rāhu and is reddened, are likewise [inauspicious].
One should eat only after seeing [the food]; otherwise, one becomes a denizen of hell.
Furthermore, those two [hands] should be held open or else with eyes closed.
Having fasted day and night, one should thereafter offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed sequence;
regarding this, some who are deluded by the scriptures of worldly existence also express their own opinions.
O Supreme Goddess, one should observe a fast when [the sun] is swallowed by Rāhu at sunset;
its manifestation is through scripture, its full vision is through direct perception, and its complete form is realized in the presence [of the deity].
O Queen of the Gods, even for divine beings, [the distance] shall be two finger-breadths;
however, a three-night fast is prescribed for those devoted to Śiva.
For the Vaiṣṇavas, Gāṇapatyas, and Sauras, a two-night rite is prescribed;
for the Śāktas, however, it should be performed during the first part of the night, joined with the preliminary service (puraścaryā).
O Goddess, previously, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara of the Moon, this two-night rite was proclaimed by me for those who were destitute. 129b)
One whose son is living should never observe a fast for the sake of his own welfare.
O Īśvarī, that man who performs the bath for liberation without performing even a small portion of the two occasional rites or those expressive of specific desires— [is not truly liberated].
He who eats merely liquor eats only the universe; whether you perform ancestral rites, fire offerings, acts of charity, or recitations of mantras, it is all the same.
One who has turned back from the Prātyāṣika rite and is desirous of performing the Kalā rites should remain standing;
having seen the planet [Jupiter] and quickly bathed, he should perform the rites pertaining to death.
If impurity (āśauca) arising from birth or death occurs, one should not perform optional rites, ancestral offerings, gifts, or worship; one should simply practice ritual bathing.
Even when joined with two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka), if a fool does not bathe during an eclipse, he meets death immediately; however, one who bathes incurs no sin.
O Goddess of the Gods, this fault exists everywhere— in recitation, in fire-offerings, in ancestral rites, and in the worship of the gods— but it does not exist during ritual bathing.
In the two months of Bhādrapada and Nabhasya, the vowels of the rivers should be without the letter 'ja'.
When an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs, no fault from dust exists;
having bathed in sacred waters at a holy site, being pure and having previously fasted.
With undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra from the time of touch until liberation;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the recitation count].
Alternatively, one should perform great worship as well as give gifts;
for the sake of accomplishing the root mantra, one should diligently please the gurus.
In this way, the accomplishment of mantras shall occur and the deity becomes propitious;
there is a distinction in that sacred ford, and likewise in the fruits [attained].
Therefore, O beloved, he should perform bathing and other rites by visiting sacred fords (tīrthas);
for all those on the surface of the earth yield fruits equal to the Gaṅgā.
Nevertheless, some specific distinction regarding those various lunar days is stated:
(130b) the sin committed over ten lifetimes is destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā.
The sin committed over thirty lifetimes is destroyed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
The sin committed during a hundred births [is destroyed] at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
likewise, whatever sin has been accumulated over a thousand births [is likewise destroyed].
Having performed a ritual bath during a solar eclipse, one casts that [sin] into the great ocean;
for whatever has been earned by men throughout their births, at the end of life, it does not follow them at all.
At that time, by reciting the name of Vārāṇasī,
one indeed dispels whatever evil deeds have been committed throughout tens of millions upon tens of millions of births.
O Goddess of the Suras, all that is destroyed by the mere act of bathing when the night-stalker [the moon] is seized by Rāhu at the Sannihatī [conjunction]; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
When there is a solar eclipse on a Sunday and likewise a lunar eclipse on a Monday, that yoga is renowned as Cūḍāmaṇi; it is then of great fruit.
O Goddess, among all gifts, the gift of land and gold yields great fruit;
yet, because of its color, the gift of land is praised above that of gold.
O Goddess of the gods, even in the case of worship, because of the adoration of the retinue of deities,
the Kula-worship is praised when performed at sixteen, twelve, or eight years [of age].
Therefore, the worship of the *bindu* should be known to be certainly ten million times more meritorious;
or else, one should perform the installation of the *yantra* during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
The rite of installing the yantra should be performed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, O Śivā;
for the deity residing within that yantra bestows boons and grants true grace.
O Goddess, whatever action one performs during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
all that becomes inexhaustible through the grace of the Queen of Vidyās.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should perform the practice of Meru;
even a wicked mantra, O Goddess of the Gods, will certainly be perfected through this sequence.
When an eclipse of Tārā (the Moon) occurs, as well as during an eclipse of the Sun,
one should perform recitation and other rites, and thereafter carry out the worship of Śakti.
One shall become the lord of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having recognized a woman who has bathed after her menses during the interval between an eclipse of the sun or moon, [one should proceed].
Having reached the day of the new moon (parvan), one should cause the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered to him;
this conjunction bestows sons upon the barren woman and grants all perfections.
O Goddess of gods, during a solar eclipse, one should bathe and perform worship;
O Maheśvarī, having worshipped [the deity] along with the limbs and the retinue, one should conclude with the bali offering.
Having performed the worship of the maiden, one becomes a master of all accomplishments;
O Goddess, having offered the moon during a planetary affliction, one should [worship] a hundred maidens.
One shall become the worshipful Siddhiśvara; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Maheśānī, Śiva, performing the optional fire-oblation during a solar eclipse, [attains this].
Prosperity faces all directions for one who performs the libation;
however, the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) must be performed for the pacification of all suffering.
When a solar eclipse occurs and there is indeed a *parādhī* [lunar day],
that yoga named *parabhṛt* bestows universal sovereignty.
Having worshipped the Guru and the deity within the pollen-mass of the Tārā-piṇḍa,
and having satisfied them, one should accept the boon; thus one becomes the lord of all siddhis.
When the seizing of the Tārā-piṇḍa has been proclaimed,
O Goddess, the practitioner should bring a corpse and recite the mantra upon the corpse-seat, O Śivā, from the first morsel until the final morsel.
He shall become the lord of all accomplishments and, at the end of that, attain the state of Śiva,
O Goddess, provided his inner organ is pure during a solar eclipse.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite and having worshipped the Mother of the Universe,
one should offer flowers from one's head to the deity.
O Śivā, when a solar eclipse has occurred, one who has bathed according to the prescribed method will certainly behold the deity intent upon granting boons.
Having brought the Śakti, one should perform the extensive ritual placement (nyāsa) upon her limbs,
using liquor, meat, fish, and even the nectars of the bhaga and liṅga.
O Śivā, having worshipped the deity there along with the limbs and the weapons,
and having offered the tongue there, one becomes conscious through recitation at the three periods of the day.
O Maheśānī, by means of knowledge of the past and future, one perceives the present;
during a solar eclipse, having respectfully brought a courtesan [to the site].
O Pārvatī, having placed the Śakti upon the Liṅga, one should recite the mantra with diligence;
having thus become a conqueror of the three worlds, there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Maheśvarī, the Śrāddha rite for all Kaulas who have attained liberation is likewise performed by the twice-born who provide the secondary alternatives.
The eclipse of the moon occurs at some time within its own sign;
thus has the determination of an eclipse been briefly explained.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Śrī Kaularahasya of all the Āgamas. || 21 ||
Now, the classification of yantras.
O beloved, for as long as one lives, [the merit] remains in gold; in silver, twenty-two years;
in copper, twelve years; and half of that in birch bark.
By wearing [an image] made of copper for twelve years and by worshipping it,
as well as by offering libations of water and using a copper yantra, the deity remains present at all times.
O Goddess, one should always worship [the deity] after consecrating it upon crystal or similar materials; however,
it is said that on copper the merit is a hundred-thousandfold, and on silver it becomes ten-millionfold.
If the fruit is infinite when [the gift] is made of gold, what more need I say to you regarding [gifts] of gems and the like?
Now, he describes the meditation on the yantra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, O Master, you have previously indicated the meditation on the yantra;
how is it to be meditated upon, what is its specific nature, and what indeed is the object of this meditation?
Is it a circle, a form, or an essential nature; is it the nature of a girdle, or is it composed of lines, or indeed the very nature of the earth?
"Or one may meditate upon the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa); let all of that also be told.
The Lord said:
O Maheśvarī, meditation is said to be threefold: in the yantra, in the mother [mantra], and in the Great Lord.
First, one should meditate on the Virāj of universal form, whose nature is like that of the moon of the universe.
O Goddess, one should honor the yantra everywhere; this has indeed been taught.
O Great Goddess, in the case of the Śrīcakra and other such forms, there is equality with the formless (viradrūpa).
And how does one meditate on the second? Tell me that, O Maheśvarī!
[It is] a line resembling a mass of dust, yet the embodiment of all consciousness.
It should be contemplated as being like a mirror, having the nature of self-luminosity.
O Dear One, one should meditate upon everything from the Bindu to the Earth-fortress as being sentient, possessing the nature of existence,
and non-different from the light of the root-splendor.
Listen to the third, O Goddess of gods, the eternal form of Meru;
it should be progressively higher, and the wise one should contemplate it thus.
O Goddess Śivā, one should meditate on each [deity] individually in ascending order;
O Maheśvarī, one should not meditate solely according to the sequence of the *uttara-krama*.
O Goddess, in the ritual of the Kālī-vidyā, one should contemplate the line as being of the nature of the nine jewels, or like the Meru-prastāra array, O Goddess.
O Supreme Goddess, the Śrīcakra joined with seed-syllables (bījas) is fruitless;
however, a cakra devoid of seed-syllables is "seedless" and does not bestow accomplishment (siddhi).
The wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭi-cakra) comes first; the wheel of maintenance (sthiti-cakra) is the second;
and the wheel of dissolution (laya-cakra) is the third—the wheel is thus divided into three ways.
134a) O Goddess, the withdrawal of the seed-syllables has been explained by me here in three ways;
for without the seed-syllable, it is proclaimed to be lifeless, like a corpse.
A yantra endowed with seed-syllables (bīja) becomes free from curses and bestows accomplishment;
in the absence of seed-syllables, one should draw the letters of the Mātṛkā adorned with nasal dots (bindu).
O Śivā, having drawn that yantra in the center, one should worship it;
for a yantra that has the form of petals is a bestower of success.
O Śivā, in the Kali age, worship should be performed in the form of a *dalā* [lotus]; otherwise, it does not bestow success.
O Goddess, the consciousness of the mantra and the consciousness of the *yantra*—the contemplation of this triad within oneself [is the true practice].
Therein, there is no form of meditative absorption, nor fire, nor machine, nor mental cultivation; for in this manifold saṃsāra, Śiva remains far away, shrouded [by ignorance].
Meditation is declared to consist of being itself, and is considered the bestower of accomplishment.
Now, O Goddess, the Kaulika speaks of the specific distinction.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the most secret of secrets:
the ritual procedure for the consecration of the yantras belonging to both the Vāmins and the Kauras.
134b) Śiva said:
Now, the consecration of the great yantra, which bestows all accomplishments, is described:
having performed a ritual bath on an auspicious day, at an auspicious lunar mansion, and during an auspicious moment; at an auspicious hour.
Having performed his daily rites, the practitioner, facing either east or north,
[should construct] a beautiful and most enchanting [mandala] with the previously mentioned metallic substances.
Having caused a beautiful and auspicious yantra to be drawn according to the prescribed rules,
one should then perform its consecration in accordance with the authority of the scriptures.
On an auspicious lagna and at a meritorious time, in a place such as a mountain or similar location,
the practitioner should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day, according to the ritual manual.
Having performed the formal ritual resolution (saṃkalpa) in the evening, preceded by the installation of the water jar (ghaṭasthāpana),
one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others, and then fully honor the guardians of the directions (dikpālas).
Liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—
these are the substances prescribed by me for the initial rites of consecration and other rituals involving the yantra.
One should perform the worship of the root deity according to one's capacity,
using offerings such as fragrant oils and perfumes, and thereby consecrate it.
Having performed the consecration with the mantra beginning with "Candra," preceded by the sound of recitation,
one should remain self-restrained, having conquered the senses.
Having first performed his daily morning rites, he should then enter the sacrificial ground,
which is crowded with banners and flags and adorned with a divine mandala.
It was resplendent with canopies, yak-tail whisks, umbrellas, and flower garlands,
and adorned with auspicious sprouts, leaves, and other offerings, as well as ritual jars.
O Goddess, one should draw the mandala, auspicious in every respect and endowed with a thousand lines,
either as a common auspicious design or upon the altar.
Alternatively, I shall describe the Varuṇa-maṇḍala on the right or the left:
it is square, consisting of sixty-four squares, and one should place the vidyā therein.
The last [syllables] go to the great directions; one should then sweep away the compartments.
In the center are four syllables, which are called the gates as before.
One should worship with yellow, dark green, white, and turmeric-colored powders,
excluding the corner squares; this consists of fifty-one units of four-footed sections.
One should worship the pedestal with white, reddish-pink, yellow, and black [colors];
in the southeast it is yellow, and the corner squares with red, green, and black.
One should draw four circles in the center with white pigment;
then one should worship them and likewise hang a canopy over their middle.
The first circle is thirty-six digits wide and yellow;
that yellow portion is shaped like a pericarp and is then encircled by a white line.
The second [lotus] has a base twice the width of the first, provided with filaments;
its filaments at the root, middle, and tip are yellow, red, and white in color respectively.
Mark seventy-two divisions on this [line] and draw a line before it;
then, the third part of the third [division] shall be a circle with an equal diameter.
There, [draw] a white eight-petalled lotus with red tips at the ends of its petals; outside,
it is white, and you should draw a black line as before.
Outside of that, one should arrange sixteen spokes joined to the circumference.
These [colors] are dark blue, yellow, and reddish; within them are two [spots] shaped like barley grains.
The five enclosures are white, yellow, reddish, dark blue, and green.
One should fashion five very beautiful [weapons] and fill the interior in this manner;
one should draw the thunderbolt (vajra), spear (śakti), staff (daṇḍa), sword (khaḍga), noose (pāśa), banner (dhvaja), and mace (gadā).
To the east and likewise to the northeast, there is a trident, a wheel, and a goad;
this mandala consists of two Varuṇa-symbols on the left and right.
Facing east and remaining silent, having made a formal resolve for the attainment of his desired goal,
he should perform the fivefold purification and offer oblations of *havi* mixed with *akṣata*.
Having established the maṇḍala there, the wise practitioner should worship it beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti);
having spread the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), he should place the water-pot (kalaśa).

Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the sequence of initiation, one should likewise prepare the consecration jar and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), empowered by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra.

136b) With that [mixture], the mantra-practitioner, while reciting the *praṇava*, should thoroughly bathe the *yantra* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), sacrificial oblation (*havis*), curd, and milk, in due order.
Then, having raised it up, one should bathe it with water;
having brought the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place the yantra there with a concentrated mind.
The knower of mantras should first cast a Vedic thread into gold or other materials;
then, having extracted that gold and so forth, he should place it in a vessel.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with sacred water (tīrtha), and with cool water,
preceded by the root mantra and the Sahasraśīrṣā mantra.
Having bathed [the image] with purifying water consisting of camphor, agallochum,
and sandalwood paste, one should carefully perform the cleansing with water containing all medicinal herbs and fragrant scents.
Then, having pushed back the water with a pure silk cloth, the practitioner,
wearing his kula-robe, [ascends] upon a swing fashioned of gold.
Having led him into the mandala with dances, songs, and cries of victory,
one should then anoint him with saffron and other substances and worship him with all the ritual offerings.
Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) according to the specific rites prescribed for each respective [tantra].

O Goddess, one should recite the previously mentioned Gāyatrī mantra, which resides within the Yantra, one hundred and eight times using either Kuśa grass or Kula grass; by doing so, one attains divinity.
Then, having meditated upon one's chosen deity, one should invoke it with a mudrā;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīva-nyāsa) and worship the designated deity.
Accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music, preceded by the fivefold sounds,
one should then recite the desired mantra one thousand and eight times.
In a sacrificial pit or on a consecrated mound, the mantra-practitioner, having prepared the oblation,
should perform the fire-oblation with the *śrūc* ladle according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
The knower of mantras should offer a sacrificial oblation (caru) the size of a mouthful at the base of the [linga] with the Nākṛkṣa mantra;
then, having poured a stream of clarified butter, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) facing the fire.
One should perform the satiation with the twenty-five principles and with the ultimate reality;
one should also offer the previously mentioned bali-oblation to Indra and the other guardians of the directions.
Then, having turned back, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter to the gods.
At the conclusion of that, O Goddess, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra;
and while reciting the mantra conjoined with the Mātṛkās, one should perform the japa amidst shouts of victory.
Having gone there, one should enter the fire sacrifice (homa), and then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
and having given the bali offering for the attainment of desired goals, one should prostrate before the supreme maṇḍala.
One should satisfy [the deity] with gold, garments, and other offerings, and also bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Goddess, one should perform the worship of the heroes (vīrapūjā) by means of the five "M" sounds.
One should worship the youthful maiden Śakti as the "five-fifths" (pañcapañcaka),
