or else perform the "ten-eights" (daśāṣṭaka) with all the substances belonging to the Kula.
Through the yoga of mantra-worship, one becomes the Lord of the Three Worlds;
having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed in the Kalpa.
At night, there is the worship of Śakti and the Kaulika sacrifice to the Dūtīs;
the worship of Carvāre-yum is performed with the five Makāras.
Having performed these three prostrations, thereupon follows the daily ritual sequence:
the worship of the Sundarī-yanttra according to the order of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The worship of the Kālikā-yantro is performed by way of emanation and reabsorption;
likewise, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and Pītabhā are worshipped by way of emanation and reabsorption.
Thus, in the installation of the Goddess,
this is the procedure that brings about the presence of the Krama for women, Śūdras, Vāmins, and Kaulikas.

That which is endowed with the prescribed rules should be performed; one should not cause that which is devoid of rules to be done. I shall now describe those obstacles that arise for one who is devoid of the rules.
There will be quarrels, pairs of opposing emotions, as well as disease, piercing pain, and burning sensations;
furthermore, there will be trouble from the king, loss, destruction of wealth, and physical suffering.
Crows with disfigured wings, jackals with terrifying howls,
and pigeons alight upon and enter his house.
Remaining hidden, the yoginīs indeed create obstacles for him; they pierce him and he is afflicted by various impediments.
And serpents, scorpions, lizards, and dreadful insects,
as well as fierce and mighty gadflies, were sent forth by the rays of light.
Bull-demons, horse-demons, lordly elephant-demons, cloud-demons, and likewise those with discuses;
wicked ones, as well as fever-demons, bhūtas, and grahas, all cause disturbances.
Scorpions, snakes, and spirits overcome [the practitioner], and not otherwise.
Now I shall explain the garland; it is of two kinds: stable and mobile.
The practice is stable for those with stable minds, but it wavers for those who are fickle;
thus, its cultivation is said to be threefold, beginning with the first garland of letters.
The second is the rosary of recitation (japamālā), and the third is the finger rosary (aṅgulimālikā).
Now, he states the sequence of letters (varṇamālā).
By means of the letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu.
The garland of letters is fashioned by means of those [letters] situated in direct and reverse order;
having uttered each individual letter, the mantra is interspersed with that letter.
With great steadiness, one should then bring [the sequence] from the end of the *valakāra* to the end;
the form of the letter *a*, which is like Mount Meru, must never be transgressed.
One should utter the mantra only once; one should not utter it again at the end.
A rosary that lacks the *meru* bead, or one that bypasses the *meru*, is deficient.
But in this case, the *sāmālā* would be impure and thus fruitless;
it is that which is variegated, devoid of essence, lusterless, and has reached the state of Brahman and so forth.
Thus, when strung together, it should be meditated upon as the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
when recited one hundred and eight times, one should first utter the word *klīva*.
The four letters ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are declared to be neuter;
or else, there is a set of eight groups [of consonants] according to the sequence of the divisions of desire.
The eight groups [of consonants] are *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *sa*;
what else could they be but born from the immortal?
O Goddess, with coral and pearls, there is the rosary called Mahāśaṅkha for the deities of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) and the deities of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
In the Urdhvāmnāya, she is established as Svayaṃbhū; in Pātāla, she is Ratnasaṃbhavā; with coral and Sūrya-mantras, she is Śaktimātraka, adorned with pearls.
A rosary composed of Śiva and Śakti is one made of Rudrākṣa and crystal;
a rosary joined with Rudrākṣa and gold has the nature of both Brahmā and Śiva.
Rudrākṣas are [recommended] for all mantras; however, they are not [recommended] during the day for a mantra dedicated to Śakti.
And so it is said:
Because it involves the separation of Śiva and Śakti, there should be no recitation of mantras with rudrākṣa beads during the day;
for Kālī, when worshipped in separation, does not become pleased.
O Dear One, he who recites a Śakti mantra during the day using Rudrākṣa beads incurs misfortune; his recitation is rendered fruitless.
Thus was the curse given long ago; hear now that story as it is told.
Once upon a time, O Goddess, he was intent upon Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

And she was invited to the house because of her relationship as a daughter-in-law.
Mahādeva did not cause Satyavatī to be brought to the sacrifice;
and Satī, having been addressed by her husband, departed from there.
Śiva said:
O beloved of my life, it was for my sake that he did not do it;
how is it that you feel no shame, that you go there yourself?
The Lord is dear, life itself is dear, and even this ornament is dear;
O Goddess, how can you go there leaving me behind?
"Where is this devotion to a husband, for you are devoid of a rival?
Nevertheless, if you desire to go quickly, please show me your grace."
Having received his husband's command, she set out for the sacrificial pavilion;
in that very moment, she was led by him to the sacrificial pavilion of Brahmā.
Disregarded by him, Pārvatī remained there with a distressed and dejected mind, bearing her form with her face cast downwards. 141b)
All the gods are here, and my husband is also seen.
"O lady of such a heart, this great sorrow has arisen within me on your account.
In the meantime, O Goddess, Dakṣa Prajāpati himself—
Becoming intent on reviling Śiva and striving again for the purpose of censure,
he became one of improper conduct, even though he had been restrained by Viṣṇu.
Constantly intent on reviling others, he rides upon a bee and a bull;
dwelling in cremation grounds, a flesh-eater, naked, filthy, and utterly destitute.
He carries a skull-bowl and a trident, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
his entire body is smeared with ashes, and he is seated upon a tiger skin.
"Gluttonous and fickle"—thus he became intent on much censure;
but she, distressed by the reproach, came out from the pavilion.
Having gone a short distance from the eyes and prepared a fire-pit,
Satī cast off her body there and attained the state of being the form of fire.
I am Śiva, in the form of Krodha, with a mandala radiant with flames.
O Maheśānī, by my wrath the three worlds were reduced to ashes; from the flame [of that wrath], the all-pervading Vīrabhadra was born.
A fire of unbearable intensity at the end of millions of eons, he was born from all the tufts of hair,
having exerted himself for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice of Dakṣa Prajāpati.
Holding a trident in his hand, cruel and devoted to the destruction of sacrifices,
he took the goddess Śivā, who was in the form of a corpse, and placed her upon his shoulder.
Because they wept, tears fell from them;
from those drops of tears were born the great rudrākṣa trees.
Having brought about stability for the sake of bestowing grace, he causes all desires to bear fruit; he is proclaimed as Moraṅgīya.
Born from the middle eye, he is proclaimed as Mālāntī;
with the syllables *dhunāśrīkoṣṭa* followed by ten, it becomes the mantra of Pārvatī.
Up to twenty-one faces, he is proclaimed as Malākī.
Thus one should know the faces [of the deity], arising from the weeping of Rudra;
in the case of the mountain-born [deity] with a clear face, the installation is indeed manifest.
O Lord, one who possesses the signs of wealth, long hair, and beauty will,
at that very moment, meet with the destruction of his impurities through fire while in the midst of water.
He who comes upon the water is proclaimed as Samalākī;
whatever action is performed by him shall have infinite weight.
"In other mantras, success occurs by day; however, in the case of a *śakti* mantra, it is not so. For this reason, O Goddess, recitation (*japa*) is prescribed only at night."
O Maheśvarī, night is of the nature of union, while the state of knowledge (vidyātva) is of the nature of separation;
this is proclaimed in the Mantra-śāstra.
Mahāmālā said:
143a) Hereafter, one should perform the separate consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*).
I shall describe the threefold procedure for the night of the rosary; listen and be attentive.
On an auspicious day, such as one marked by favorable lunar mansions and the like— a pure and propitious day—
one should take up the great garland and bring forth the vessel of the hero.
Having approached the hero’s yantra, one should purify the hero’s garland;
having worshipped the Goddess along with her retinue up to the end of the sacrificial offering, O Maheśvarī.
Having offered lamps numbering ten, twenty, or twenty-five, one should perform the bali offering;
thus, having made the rosary into its constituent parts, one should perform the great consecration (mahāsaṃskāra).
At an auspicious moment and planetary conjunction, one should offer either a garland or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
the five products of the cow consist of cow urine and cow dung.

The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed in the following order: curd, ghee, and so forth. Having offered that, one should wash it with pure water and with mantras dedicated to the Lord.
Having cleansed it with the root mantra, one should place that substance there for a day.
O Goddess, on the third day, one should worship with yakṣakardama pastes.
One should worship with all perfumes, the eight perfumes, and the eight beginning with *ṛddhi*.
O Goddess, on the fourth day, having established the three portions of the eight blue Aśvatārās and the eight Tārās within the fire, one should worship them in sequence.
The Seer (ṛṣi) of this secret garland mantra is the Supreme Lord;
the Goddess Śrī Mahātāriṇī is proclaimed as its Metre (chandas), the Uṣṇih.
*Krīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *strīṃ* is likewise the power (*śakti*), and *hūṃ* is remembered as the *kīlaka*;
this is the application for purification within the garland ending with *Mahāmahālāda*.
O Pārvatī, one should perform meditation and recite the mantra with the three powers;
having meditated, one should apply effort through this mantra with a firm resolve.
One should cast the *kamālikā* with the mantra consisting of the *praṇava*, likewise *lajjā*, *śrīlajjā*, *kāmakurcaka*, *phaṭ*, and *svāhā*.
144a) There, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Kālikālasāradā, along with her retinue and the lords of the attendants, by means of the vehicle-mantras and so forth.
Recalling the third root mantra while forming the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā),
O Maheśvarī, one should transform [the offering] into nectar and veil it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having embraced the goddess Mahāmudrā, one should visualize her as having form;
there one should meditate and cast the drop from the mantra—listen to this, O beloved!
The Praṇava, the pair of Kūrca mantras, and Svāhā; the Praṇava, the Kūrca mantras, Vahnijāyā (Svāhā), Tārā (Oṃ), Astra, Vahnijāyā, and likewise Viṣa.
Then Tārā, followed by Vahnijāyā (Svāhā), then Tāra, Lajjā (Hrīṃ), and Sakuccaka;
then Vahnijāyā, then Tāra, [ending] with Lajjā, Kaṭu, and Vahnijāyā.
Having recited the entire mantra two or three times with the rosary,
one should perform the casting of the drop (bindu) while reciting the mantra one hundred times.
Having offered the filament of the *vahnijāva-stunika* flower along with camphor, agallochum,
and incense, one should remove the flower garland and consecrate it with the vidyā-mantra.
And likewise the Praṇava, Māyā, and the word "Śrīmahāvajriṇi."
Then, one should utter the word "prākarkaṇa" with a most terrible sound;
having spoken [the word] "mahāsthimaṇḍale," one likewise enters the state.
"Grant all accomplishments," followed by the Praṇava, the Kūrca-bīja,
the Māyā-bīja, the Vahni-jāyā, and "Mahākapālinī."
Then, for the purpose of consecration, the Vidyā is declared as: *mahāghorarūpe svāhā* with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīṃ); and *māyā* (hrīṃ), *kūrca* (hūṃ), *strī* (strī), ending with *svāhā*.
Having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should perform the kindling with desire;
having worshipped the Mātṛkā with the root mantra and the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Then, having performed the kindling (uddīpana), one should envelop [the offering] with the syllable *haṃ*;
one should present the oblation (*bali*) with the syllable *ana* alone, and utter the *tāra* (oṃ) followed by two *māyās* (hrīṃ hrīṃ).
One should not pronounce Vāsudeva with the bindu nor the kūrcaka without being encased. 145a) One should not pronounce Vāsudeva with the bindu nor the kūrcaka without being encased.
One should utter "phaṭ" at the end of the *kūrca* mantra, followed by the *carca* and two *praṇavas*.
The *kūrca* seed-syllable, the wife of fire (*svāhā*), the *praṇava*, and the *kūrca* seed-syllables;
then, at the end of the word "mahāyogini," [follows] "tribhuvanamāriṇi."
And the great assembly, established upon the ālā, utters its dwelling in the midst;
it utters the sound "Kuru," grant all accomplishments, O you who are joined with the seat of the *yukūrca* liquor!
O Pārvatī, with this mantra— *māṃso prahāreṇa gṛhṇeti yuku gṛhṇāpaya dvayaṃ kullukā phaṭ tataḥ svāhā*— one seizes [the victim] by striking with meat.
Having offered the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite with appropriate materials,
one should install the rosary for five days using the five substances, reciting "came came" [at each step].
One should perform the ritual of the Garland-Night; by that, the garland is perfected.
One should place the garland in a secluded spot according to the secret ritual of the garland.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Śrī Kaularahasya, the scripture of all [the traditions]. 22.
145b) Now, he explains the consecration of the garland for the sake of women and śūdras.
For the sake of a Śūdra or for a woman, the consecration of a garland is prescribed;
having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā with devotion.

Then, having consecrated that garland with the seed-syllable *hvauṃ* at its center, one should place it in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three days, reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
In the fourth [stage], having extracted it, one should wash it with the Astra mantra;
having tied it with the Hrdaya mantra, one should place it upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
Then, having bathed the garland with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water, one should place it upon the vessel of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇava-pātra).
Then the practitioner should perform the consecration with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and other such substances, using the *hasauṃ* mantra.
Having worshipped the nine planets, one should also worship the guardians of the directions;
thereafter, one should perform oblations according to one's ability with sesame seeds mixed with nectar.
One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor, equal in number to the [total] mantras;
or else, one should feed Brahmins who are reciters of those mantras or those learned in the Vedas.
In the absence of a golden vessel, a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha) should be used;
this is called the consecration of the rosary, and the recitation performed with it shall bestow success.
The mantra for untangling and cleansing.
O Śivā, having bound the Śiva-mantra with the Śakti-mantra, one should recite the Śiva-mantra; O Śivā, having bound the Śakti-mantra with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Śakti-mantra.

O Goddess, the supreme [mantra] which brings about the effect of the garland through the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti— whichever [mantra] one does not bind [with knots], that very mantra one should recite.
"O Lord, have you forgotten what was previously stated by you?
Now it has been declared otherwise; I have a doubt regarding this, O Lord."
Those [mantras] that are distinct from the Mātṛkā-tāra are devoid of Śiva and Śakti;
this is not stated regarding the Mātṛkā, but is considered [to apply] to the procedure for other garlands of mantras.
One should not perform the binding with any other method;
one should recite that very mantra, O Śivā, and thus perform the recitation.
Even in the Mātṛkā and other [scriptures], O Śivā, the goddess Rūpiṇī is woven as a thread upon the *lākrantu*.
A garland for the pleasure of the Goddess should be strung with silk thread;
a Vaiṣṇava garland may likewise be made of cotton or lotus fibers.
Whether made from wool, bark fibers, silk, or cotton thread,
this practice involving cotton and the ritual of the Dharma and so forth is a means that grants all accomplishments.
Listen to the procedure for the production of the thread for almost all the deities: O best of the twice-born, the thread should be spun by a virtuous woman and must be free of knots.
If it is a beautiful woman who loves her husband and has living young ones, or if the thread was spun by a maiden; |||
The twice-born [brāhmaṇas] are white, red, golden-hued, and black in color;
among all these castes, the red [stone] grants all that is desired.
Having tripled the threefold [cord] and washed it thoroughly, it should then be taken up;
it is fashioned from silk thread by means of a *meru*-sūtra.
147a) [A rosary] fashioned from gold and silver, or even from gold alone, is considered auspicious;
however, a thread dyed turmeric or produced from village cotton should be avoided in every respect.
Furthermore, one should avoid using cotton from the Caitra month in the act of stringing [the rosary].
One strung by a preceptor is excellent; that prepared by oneself is inferior even for an ascetic.
O Goddess, it is excellent when strung according to one's capacity, but not by Śūdras and the like;
among these, the Brāhmaṇa is most highly recommended for the purpose of making a rosary for recitation.
In the absence of twice-born men, however, those of one's own caste may be used;
for in the Kali age, Brahmins who follow their own duty are as difficult to find as Brahmins who are not Brahmins.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe her purification in brief,
either according to the path of the Kula or by the procedure prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Having performed the daily obligatory rites, being pure, alert, and with the senses under control,
one should observe a fast, eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), or likewise consume only a single meal.
Having prepared silk and cotton, one should slowly spin the thread;
O Goddess, on the day of fasting, one should worship all of those [materials].
One may perform it twice or thrice, and one should practice that three times over.
The offerings should be made with sandalwood, unbroken rice, incense, and so forth, as well as flowers, oblations, and lamps;
they should be neither too large nor too small.
In the morning, having taken that thread, one should prepare it according to the specific desire and purpose:
white, blue, yellow, and red in color.
Now follows the ritual of ascending the purifiers (pavitrārohaṇa).
The Goddess said:
O Great Goddess, how is the Rohaṇa rite, which purifies those of noble birth, performed?
At what time, in what manner, and for what purpose should it be done? Tell me, O Lord.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Long ago, O Goddess, the Ocean of Milk was churned by the gods and asuras;
there, O illustrious one, was the powerful son of Kaśyapa, Vṛtra, who had eyes like those [of the sun].
O auspicious lady, when the churning rod is applied, [the poison] that causes sleep and fainting is unable to spread even to the edge of the surface during the rainy season.
O you of great mind, I have been propitiated by your pure [devotion];
for a thousand years, O mighty one, I subsisted on air alone.
I am pleased by that, O Queen of the Gods; what was previously mentioned should now be performed.
Then that foremost of speakers fell prostrate upon the ground like a staff and said:
"O Hara, I am able to dwell at the edge of the palm [of your hand] during the rainy season."
Then, O Goddess, he too was taken up from the ground by me with both hands and placed upon my head within my mass of matted hair, O fair-faced Goddess.
Then, O Śivā, having been honored with a bow of the head by all the gods, I, being pure, granted a boon to the serpent: "Your teeth shall be sacred."
If the offering of the *pavitra* is performed by you, there is no fruit for you;
rather, the *pavitraka* belongs to those who have performed ten crores of your worship.

Therefore, the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed for all the deities in due order; on the first lunar day (pratipad) or the full moon (paurṇamāsī), whichever specific lunar date is prescribed for each.

O Śiva, on the twelfth day of the bright or dark fortnight dedicated to Viṣṇu, or during a Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should perform the rites for Hari.
At the equinox, during the time of growth, and likewise upon the arrival of Jupiter.
This is declared to be eternally pure; during the rainy season, one should perform it as a personal obligation from the time of the sun's entry into Gemini until its entry into Libra.
The month of Āṣāḍha is the best; Śrāvaṇa is middling;
the fortnight of Bhādrapada is inferior; and within that, the bright fortnight is excellent while the dark is middling.
On the fifth, the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth lunar days,
as well as on the twelfth, the fourteenth, or even on the full moon day.
"O beloved, the seasons are summer, autumn, and the rainy season—these are considered the most important;
some wise men, however, desire spring to be the intermediate season."
Neither the Hemanta nor the Śiśira seasons are ever praised;
O Goddess of Gods, having understood this one [principle], they are applied in due order throughout the Kṛta and other ages.
In the Kali age, auspicious vessels made of gold, silver, copper, cotton, silk,
or linen are used by kings, while those dwelling in the forest use bark garments.
For the followers of the Sugata, [the staff] is made from the lotus; for the Śūdras, it is ground from flax;
for the students (brahmacārins), it is produced from *adarbha* grass; and for the Vaiśyas, it is born from the *tuśāśa* plant.

O Sovereign Goddess, for those established in vows, [the seat] is made of muñja grass; for those with eyes like a deer, it is made of wool; and for all others, it is made of cotton or lotus fiber—this is prescribed.
O Sovereign of the Gods, the syllables of the Sūtras differ according to the various traditions (amnāya):
the Sūtra is "Smitam" in the first two halves, and likewise "Raktasūtram" in the latter half.
Furthermore, in the six Āmnāyas, the thread is sometimes considered yellow in the west, and likewise in the south; it may also be smeared with blue.
Furthermore, in all traditional scriptures, it is praised that [the thread] should be white;
now follows the ritual of offering the *damanaka* flower.
One is called the "offering of *damanaka* flowers," and the other is the "offering of the single purifier" (*ekāpavitrāropaṇī*);
practitioners should perform these every year.
O future one, the worship performed for him during the year will be fruitless;
even if it is performed, the hosts of spirits, ghosts, and the like will cause it to be destroyed.
Therefore, every year, the practitioner should diligently perform the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower,
as well as the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).
And whoever worships the God with *damanaka* flowers during the middle of the month,
Kāmarāja accepts for him the fruit of a year's worship performed.
Now, he states the counter-argument to this.
Pārvatī said:
O Prāṇanātha Maheśvarī, I desire to know this alone:
having attained the supreme yoga, you shine as the mistress of yoga.
O giver of dharma, we two were desirous of union; why then have you married me after burning away my eyes with the fire of your gaze, and subsequently renouncing all enjoyment?
What happiness would there be for us in that [state] which increases death beyond measure,
if you desire to perform the highest sport with me?
"O Saṃjīva, when my husband takes pleasure as he desires," having heard these words of Girijā, which bring the joy of amorous play—
Having performed this gesture with honor, Bhava spoke to his beloved;
Śrī Mahādeva said:
If such is your faith, O beloved, in this reviver of desire,
then neither Śirīṣa nor Vicakila shall be given to you, O Indrajā.
"I shall restore this man to life; he will be pleased with you, O Pārvatī, and by this deed I shall proclaim your fame."
I shall likewise establish another arrangement for the three worlds:
the constellation Uttaraphalgunī and the lunar day Trayodaśī.
The bright fortnight, the month of Caitra, the conjunction, prosperity, as well as the offering of food consisting of nectar, and even the new moon day— on these occasions one should rejoice.
"His name is Puṣpadhanvan; having conceived him as being present here by means of flowers alone, O Pārvatī, I shall fashion his image while you look on."
Having spoken thus, he commanded his attendants to apply ointments and flowers,
and by fashioning each respective limb, he restored Kāma to life.
Her entire body was adorned with *damana* flowers, her face with lotuses,
her nose with *campaka* blossoms, and her eyes with blue water-lilies.
He adorned both his cheeks with jasmine flowers and likewise his locks of hair with yūthī blossoms.
One should adorn the two ears with *karavīra* flowers, the two nostrils with *pāṭala*,
the collarbones with *mādhavī*, and the pair of shoulders with *śirīṣa*.
Her two nostrils were adorned with *vakula* and *karṇikāra* flowers; her throat with mango sprouts; her pair of arms with *kuruṇṭhaka* blossoms; and her mass of hair with *kuruṇṭhaka* flowers.
The pair of shoulders [was adorned] with *kāñcanāra* flowers, the pair of hips likewise with *kunda* flowers;
the chest with *aśoka* blossoms, and the belly with *ketakī* water-lilies.
Her flanks were like horses, her chest was adorned with jasmine flowers,
her pair of thighs resembled the *tavarga* consonants, and her penis was like a young javā flower.
All the limbs and extremities should be adorned individually with flowers such as the *pārijāta*, *maruvaka*, *kadamba*, and *vandhujīvaka*.
He fashioned the entire body of Kāmadeva from *damanaka* flowers,
and he also prepared arrows and a bow from the same.
One should place the spring season, the female cuckoo, the bumblebee, and the Malaya breeze on the left side, as well as Rati to the left and Prīti to the right.
The Blessed Lord Īśa, the master of the Pramathas, reciting the *mṛtasañjīvanī* mantra,
restored him to life by means of his own power.
Having been restored to life, he rose up and, accompanied by his attendants,
bowed down with devotion before Umā and Maheśvara like a staff.
When that time had arrived, the body addressed Smarohara:
"O Lord, you should grant me permission as to what I must do."
Then Īśāna spoke to him, whose neck was bowed in devotion:
"O Smara, you who eternally delude the three worlds with your flowery bow."
One should wander for the sake of purification, surrounded by those powers and accompanied by friends who have become allies; in this way, you will surely attain it.
Constantly deluding young men with his fivefold arrows, he is ever-intoxicated;
this body has been obtained by you through the grace of the Goddess.
"This lunar day shall be known by your name; those who worship on this day with extensive offerings of perfumes, flowers, and the like, [shall obtain great merit]."

[One should not worship] with offerings of food, incense, lamps, and so forth; nor with singing, instrumental music, dancing, and the like; nor with vulgar speech, verbal insults, singing, instrumental music, joking, intoxicants, or the consumption of [forbidden] substances.
By means of laughter-inducing gestures such as the *yoni* and *liṅga*,
and by words corresponding to various forms, they celebrated the great festival.
O Smara, at my command, grant them their desired boons;
O Dhvaja, on the following day, my worship shall be performed extensively in one place.
Having spoken thus, he approached Hari and,
smiling while honoring her, spoke to Umā who was standing by his side.
By the mere word of your speech, O Goddess, I have restored Smara to life; and I shall also cause your own fame to resound throughout the world, O beautiful one.
Those men who worship you with *damana* plants— known as the body of Kāmadeva— which have been consecrated through ritual perfuming (*adhivāsita*) and whose roots have been planted in the mud;
The annual worship performed for them toward you shall become fruitful.
Those who, out of negligence, have failed to perform the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower,
shall lose their merits and be consigned to the Maṇḍabhā hell.
And all your hosts shall take away the worship offered to the quarters;
just as your autumnal worship is the constant bestower of security.
O beautiful one, from that time forth, the act of planting the *dama* [creeper] shall become like nectar upon the earth.
O beautiful one, from that time forward, the rite of offering the *damanaka* flower has remained as a necessary duty and must be performed, O beloved.
Now, he states the determination of the sixfold tradition (ṣaḍamnāya) of the Ten Great Vidyās.
Bhuvaneśī, Mahālakṣmī, she who is the object of all the Āmnāyas;
Tripurā, Tripuṭā, Bālā, Viśālākṣī, and Pūrṇikā.
O Goddess of the Gods, even today I continue to instill Vagalā,
Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī, and Aruṇatī through my right face.
The tradition known as the Western is recited by means of its mouth;
Tārā, Chinnā, Piśācī, Dhūmrā, and those within the northern sphere [are likewise recited].
The Kālikā division, together with its sub-divisions, belongs to the domain of the Ūrdhvamnāya; the Upavidyās are in Pātāla, and this is proclaimed as the Vidyāmnāya.
Now, the Sūtra on the Ten Knowledges.
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī.
Vagalā, Siddhividya, Mātangī, and Kamalāmbikā—
these ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the Siddhividyas.
Now, he describes the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for the ten vidyās.

If, after receiving initiation, a sinful soul fails to perform the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) within six months, he falls from his status and dwells in the Raurava hell for a hundred thousand years.
If one dies after receiving initiation without having performed the preliminary ritual service (*puraścaryā*),
they shall be cooked in the terrible Raurava hell for as long as the moon, the sun, and the earth endure.
O Goddess, having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in its thirteen forms according to one's own means and endowed with faith;
Having satisfied the guru with effort, the wise one should cause the ritual application to be performed;
having completed the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times each day.
And immediately thereafter, the wicked-natured one is generally made into a nāga;
then the hosts of goddesses, headed by Indrākṣī, devour his flesh.
The great wrathful ḍākinīs and others threaten them again and again;
when they die, they are cooked in the most terrible hell of the boiling cauldron.
O Goddess, in ritual applications, in tasks, and in initiations according to the prescribed rules, one must not allow any interval during the *puraścaraṇa*.
Initiation (dīkṣā), the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), and the ritual application (prayoga) are prescribed according to the rules;
for one who performs them as stated, there is no doubt that the mantra will attain success (siddhi).
153b) Pārvatī said:
Then explain the meaning of the word *puraścaraṇa* and its procedure;
for all mantras, beginning with those of the Vedas, do not attain success without this accumulation of practice.
The illustrious Lord said:
Mantra is said to be the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; that which is practiced beforehand for the sake of its accomplishment is proclaimed as the "puraścaraṇa."

The rite known as *puraścaraṇa*—which pertains to mantras and yantras from the beginning of the Vedas to the end of the Śiva-āgamas—is essential for subjugation; I shall now describe its various methods.
Some, however, say that in this context the five-limbed ritual consists of recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), sprinkling (mārjana), and feeding the Brahmins (viprabhojana).
Mantras consisting of four limbs, three limbs, two limbs, or even those that are solitary,
reside within the Vedas as well as in the Tantras and the practice of the Piśācas.
Some [attain it] through the recitation of the six-limbed mantras whose limbs are not clearly defined,
and by means of the water-offering (argha), the cleansing (marṣaṇa), the offering to the Sun, the drinking of water, and prostrations.
Through the worship of the deities with those same five [offerings], they thus become ten-limbed;
likewise, through the sacrifice of the messenger (dūtī-yāga), the upward-ascending rite, and the worship of the wheel (cakra-pūjana).
Through the union with the *dhvaja-liṅga*, by means of recitation (*japa*), the offering of oblations (*bali*),
and the presentation of the great oblation (*mahābali*), [the results] come to be through these eleven limbs.
The Kaulikas have sixteen limbs, while for the Vāmakas it is said to be twelve;
for the Aghorīs, it is eighteen limbs, including the service to the stone (sevātoṣṭādaśāṅga).
One should effect the destruction of all sins; otherwise, one creates a bond that obstructs accomplishment.
Having brought about the destruction of whatever sin exists, one should perform the preliminary rite.
Through the path as it has been described, his success is said to arise;
by following the Vedic way, there shall be the destruction of all sins therein.
The number prescribed for the *Kṛta* age shall be doubled in the *Tretā*;
it is said to be tripled in the *Dvāpara*, and the number in the *Kali* age is fourfold.
Now, he describes the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for Asitā.
Having become pure by day and having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya), the wise man should recite the mantra;
thereafter, O Dear One, he should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter (ghṛta) ten times that number.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with water from a sacred bathing place, or with milk, or even with ghee, or with honey mixed with water containing sesame seeds.
O Dear One, one should consecrate the Goddess with water from the tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa),
and with the tenth part of that [water], one should devoutly feed her with sacrificial food offerings.
O Dear One, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins who know the Kālī-mantras as one would to a guru;
now hear likewise the ritual procedure (kalpa) concerning the fettered (pāśava), O Beloved.
Having worshipped Māṃsasarvadevī at night according to the prescribed ritual, one should then,
naked and even if covered in sweat, take pleasure with a naked woman.
Then, O Goddess, perform a hundred thousand recitations (japa) and subsequently offer oblations (homa) into the blazing fire;
likewise, place ghee and meat in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a vulva.
The excellent practitioner should satisfy [the deity] with ten parts of liquor mixed with meat;
then, having performed the consecration with a tenth part of that satisfaction, he should [worship] her who consists of the universe.
One should properly feed a tenth part [of the practitioners] who are dear to Kālikā;
one should provide wine, meat, fish, and the ritual libation (tarpaṇa).
Then, O beloved, one should satisfy the guru with devotion by means of gold and other such offerings.
O Goddess, by performing these two acts, the mantra will certainly succeed;
this is declared here as the daytime rite for all twice-born classes.
And for Śūdras, it is likewise declared that the night is highly fruitful when entered.
Now, concerning Tārā:
Eating only at night and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
or, taking up the secret rosary, one may even recite it as many as ten million times.

The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; he should then offer oblations with blue lotuses smeared with the first [substance] for one-tenth of that number, and satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that amount.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with fragrant waters mixed with the liquid extract of aguru-wood; the procedure for that is stated here.
Having offered water for the feet according to the rules with the ritual services, he should satisfy the Goddess and her retinue once, according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped his own self with the *devīvṛddhi* mantra, he should draw down the supreme darkness;
saying, "I shall sprinkle the *tāliṇī*," he should pour water upon his head.
O Goddess, salutation to you, the mudrā named Kumbha; by this, may there be anointment.
Now he states the sequence of the night.
Acting thus, while consuming food that is not forbidden, as well as curd,
honey, meat, and betel-leaf, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.
One should offer ten million oblations with red lotuses soaked in milk and clarified butter;
having filled a human skull, one should perform the recitation at the place of recitation.
Beholding, touching, or walking with a woman during the dead of night, one should offer an oblation;
one must not harbor hatred toward women of beautiful brows, but should worship them with great effort.
There is no restriction of time for recitation; one should recite at all times while remaining in this state.
Now, regarding the case of one who has been cut off.
First, worship should be performed; one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and one should offer oblations in the netherworlds with bilva leaves, flowers, or fruits.
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth; in this way, the mantra becomes perfected.
Now follows the sixteen-syllable Vidyā.
Staying there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while maintaining the form of the Goddess herself;
O Maheśvarī, one should perform an oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers in the tenth part of that number.
Or else, with flowers known as the "three dhurs."
Then, three times for the Bhavyas.
Having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should offer oblations of flowers from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree ten thousand times to the Sun.
Or with those produced from the three central [lotuses], or with those originating from the *karavīra* [flower].
Now, [the mantras] of Mahālakṣmī.
One should recite the mantra of Bhāskara one hundred thousand times, restrained in diet and observing the vow;
then one should offer oblations with ghee mixed with the three sweets in ten parts of that number.
One should offer oblations with ten thousand lotuses and fruits from the *amā* tree;
one should satisfy those two [deities] with well-strained, pure, and warm water.
Now, [the ritual] for Mātaṅgī.
During the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should recite the mantra six thousand times;
one-tenth of that number should be offered as oblations (*homa*) with clarified butter, along with sugar and honey.
With wood produced from the Brahma-tree, together with practitioners and their Śaktis.
Having thus performed the preliminary rites, one should carry out the ritual procedure of application.
Now, [the ritual] of Bhuvaneśvarī.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra while gazing at the sun; he should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with sweets, performing ten oblations for every hundred recitations in due order.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), as well as the feeding of Brahmins.
Now, [the ritual] of Dhūmāvatī.
Performing recitation day and night in an empty house on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
and being intent on fasting, one shall attain success in a single day.
If one mutters a hundred thousand recitations in a cremation ground or a forest, he will become a master of speech; by this, the mantra becomes perfected.
Then one should perform the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites with ghee used in the fire sacrifice;
or else, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times in a cremation ground devoid of clothing.
157a) One who eats at night should perform the fire-oblation with sesame seeds using a tenth part [of the total recitation]. Now, [the mantra] of Vagalāmukhī:
Having put on yellow garments and standing facing the north,
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with a rosary made of turmeric wood.
Constantly devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), having proceeded to the *Prakha* [shrine], and intent upon meditation,
one should worship with *priyaṅgu*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and yellow flowers.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Kaularahasya*, the essence of all the Āgamas. || 23 ||
Now he explains the secret of recitation (japarahasya).
When uttered in their respective sounds, they attain sovereignty;
one should contemplate the protectors of the mantra as strung upon a thread.

One should perform that specific meditation for each respective Ṛṣi;
indeed, that alone is prescribed therein by Manu as the principal deity.
The meditation, the meter, and so forth, as well as the hymn, are all exactly like those of the Goddess.
Ten thousand repetitions of the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) have been completed according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsana*).
Now follows the preliminary practice for the Thousand-Name Hymn (*sahasranāmastava*) and the armor-protective charms (*kavaca*).
The Lord said:
O Pārvatī, among the Thousand-Name Hymns and even within the Kavacas,
that which is proclaimed as the "Kavaca" (Armor) must be performed as the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Where no preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is mentioned, what procedure is prescribed?
For it is proclaimed that ten thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite for a mere hymn.
O Pārvatī, it is declared in the Mahākāla doctrine that if one performs [the rite] while situated there,
everything is accomplished through the mere satisfaction of the Brahmins.
How should the fire-pit be prepared, and what should the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth be like?
O Supreme Goddess, what indeed is the nature of the Thousand Names?
And likewise, O Goddess, what form is proclaimed for the armor? The dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess is celebrated as the "Brahmarandhra."
O Goddess, the other verses are equal to the hair, the seer is said to be the head;
what is the meter, O Goddess, and what would be the deity of the mouth and the heart?
The seed-syllable is declared to be the secret, while Śakti is the supreme protection.
O Goddess, the *kīlaka* (the pin) is proclaimed as the exegesis (*arthavāda*) for the entire body [of the hymn];
whatever is situated within the hymn, all that is of the nature of the hymn itself.
And thus, O Goddess of the gods, it has been proclaimed in the form of a hymn;
likewise, O beloved goddess, having understood the armor (kavaca), one should recite it during the reading.
O Supreme Goddess, if there is a deficiency in any limb, there will be total destruction;
O Goddess, the fruit, the praise, and so forth, are designated as "limbs."
O Goddess, it is proclaimed that without [reciting] from beginning to end, half the fruit is obtained.
In this matter, O Goddess, the proof is as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and others are traditionally remembered.
The offering (havana) of the armor (kavaca) and other [limbs] is prescribed at the end of each verse;
alternatively, it is considered that one should first recite from the beginning to the end, and then perform the offering.
Alternatively, O Goddess, O Queen of Gods, let the name [of the deity] be at the end;
O Beloved, even when the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and others are used, the oblation (*havana*) should be performed at the end of the mantra.
The withdrawal of the ritual procedure is considered to be carried out at the end of the verse;
O Maheśvarī, having first performed the full [rite], one should likewise do so at the end.
The names of the middle [mantras] and those beginning with *pādya* are proclaimed as the *puraścaryā*.
At the end of each verse, one should perform the cleansing and other rites.
Therein, one should perform the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth according to the procedure prescribed for the hymn;
having recited the hymn in its entirety, one should perform the counting at its conclusion.
This complete yoga of the fire-oblation (homa) has been described; one should speak pleasant words, O Maheśvarī, and perform the rites of sprinkling and consecration here.
The Sārūpya, the one called Kavaca, and the Sāyujya hymn have been proclaimed; together with the one named Sānnidhya, these three thousand-verse [hymns] are fully extolled.
The armor (kavaca) is the form of the armor; the hymn (stotra) shall be the companion.
The hymn of names (nāmastotra), however, is proclaimed for the place of worship.
Worship is the true nature of Durgā, while the offering of the *bali* is her slaying;
the king of mantras and the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) are said to be the bestowal of sovereignty.
O Goddess, a king does not shine without a queen;
for it is proclaimed that this [queen] is indeed the very root of all prosperity.
This is declared to be the *homa* mantra, while the *parjanya* weapon is for the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
In the water, the form of Durga herself is indeed proclaimed as the consecration;
the feeding of Brahmins, moreover, is the devouring of the wicked army.
By contemplating the identity of the deity, the guru, and the vidyā, as well as the identity of the self,
one becomes the lord of all siddhis and shall become the sovereign of the three worlds.
And just as fear of an enemy army arises for one who possesses royal power and the like,
O Great Goddess, so too has the attainment of the kingdom of accomplishment been described.
O Goddess, just as there are various opinions regarding difficult places and so forth, as well as countries and kingdoms,
in the same way, there are various opinions regarding the attainment of success in a kingdom and the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth.
The king of mantras is the Guru; the attendants are from Gaṇeśa; the door-keepers are from the Vārapālakas;
the practice is that of the corpse and the skull; this is declared to be the lion-throne.
The practitioner should act in such a way that everything is accomplished;
the horse and the elephant are considered to be for the sake of omens and for desired results.
O Goddess, when there is the smoke of the fire-oblation and a banner, then success shall be the sovereign ruler; why, O Queen of the Earth, would it not be accomplished?
The sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) and so forth is the army that bestows the stars and other [attainments] of the deities.
The *yantra* is indeed the Vajradurga, the piercer of the wheel of life (*jīvacakra*);
the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) beginning with the hair and so forth have been declared; what else do you wish to hear?
Now, he describes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the *aṅka* yantra.
First, for the sake of accomplishing the yantra, one should perform the preliminary consecration (puraskriyā) of its mantra ten thousand times;
thereafter, one should proceed with the yantra.
Just as the vessel, the substance, and the drawing on the yantra have been prepared with care,
so too, O King, having invited the deity there and worshipped according to the prescribed ritual, [one should proceed].
Having meditated, performed the recitation, the offering, and the fire sacrifice.
The wise man, having invoked [the deity] once for each repetition while recollecting the mantra and the yantra, should perform japa and other rites;
when the yantra has thus been perfected, one may then inscribe the name [of the person for whom it is intended].
In a yantra measuring one thousand directions, she should be visualized as being placed in front.
Now, because the mantras have not been mastered through two or three rounds of *puraścaraṇa*, he states the means for that once again:
And likewise, if perfection does not arise through the mantra even when correctly propitiated, it must be performed again by that same [practitioner]; otherwise, perfection will not arise.
One should employ that means which is called "Madhu" by the protectors;

One should recite the mantra encapsulated [by the seed syllables] every day one hundred times;
through a single performance of the fire-oblation and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected.
One should perform the entire daily routine as prescribed for the *puraścaryā*. However, for a mantra dedicated to a cruel deity, one should encase it within the *bhūtalipi* (the alphabet).
One should perform the recitation in sequence, hundred by hundred; success, however, comes within a month.
One should recite the letters of the classes in order—ha, ya, ra, va, and la—as the second, fourth, and third [syllables] starting from the end.
171b) Then,
once these three "heats" (uṣman) have been recognized, [the deity] becomes gracious toward those who have performed worship.
Because of being bound by a curse and pinned down, the eight states of woe (apāya) will exist there.
The falling together, the going forth, the running, the awakening, the subduing, and the making subject.
Pressing, drying, cleansing, and burning—these are said to be the ritual actions therein.
Having procured birch bark, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
With the eight fragrances, or with yellow orpiment and sandalwood paste,
one should inscribe the mantra together with the syllables of the practitioner's name.
One should write the name of the practitioner, beginning with the syllable *tāra*, on the eight petals, starting from the first of those two until their completion.
Two by two, the vowels should be written, and that which consists of nectar (the syllable *saḥ*) should be placed upon them;
then, having properly enveloped it with clay, one should have the Brāhmaṇas and others wrap it around.
Subsequently, one should wrap it with white and other colored cloths and encircle it with a student's garment;
then, quickly place it in a small earthen vessel containing the three sweets (*trimadhu*) during the appropriate season.
One should quickly place it in a fresh vessel filled with milk for a light meal.
Having established the fire and placed that jar near it,
one should establish [the deity] and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the three sweets using the root mantra.
One should pour one thousand and eight oblations into the ritual jar;
then, having completed the fire-offerings, one should cast the jar into a body of water.
One should satisfy one's own guru with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other offerings, ending with the word *brahmaṇāśva*.
Having performed the *saṃpāta* oblation, if success (*siddhi*) does not yet arise, that which has been stated [should be repeated].
One should then perform the rite of driving away; the method for this is stated here: having strung together [the syllables] with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should write the mantra on birch bark.
And with uśīra and rocanā, along with śikhā, karpūra, and kumbha,
one should cast that which has been written into the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
Through worship, adoration, recitation, and burnt offerings, he becomes melted and bestows the fruit [of success].
Even if he is melted, if he is not yet perfected, one should cause him to give half of his wealth.
Having purified it with the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, one should recite that mantra.
In this way, one becomes a perfected Buddha; it need not be said that he brings others under his control.
[The substances are: red sandalwood, great wood, turmeric, madanī, and stone.
This mantra, written by these [scribes] upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf, becomes a means of subjugation when worn around the neck; otherwise, it will cause suffering.
One should recite the second [syllable] with an udātta accent after an anudātta vowel;
the third with an anudātta, and one should recite the *bhūrja* [portion] with an udātta accent.
In this manner, the practitioner should recite all the words of the mantra;
with a voice that is not raised (anudātta), he should meditate on the deity situated below.
Standing up with joy, he should recite the mantra one thousand times beginning with the *uccāra* [of the seed-syllable];
then, he should inscribe it upon birch bark that has been scorched by the sun.
One should step upon that mantra with the left foot and then perform the fire oblation;
when the mantra has been thus afflicted, it becomes propitiated after one hundred and eight recitations.
If it is not yet perfected, that fault must be remedied; now its ritual procedure is proclaimed.
Having written the mantra encircled by the *sauḥ* seed-syllable upon a birch-bark leaf, one should proceed.
One should wear it with *rocanā* and *kuṅkuma*.
This is called the *śokhala*; now the *dahana* is being described.
One should place the individual syllables of one's own mantra, arranged around the four directions,
upon a Palāśa leaf smeared with oil using the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
Then, having fixed it upon a birch leaf, this act of burning is performed by holding it to the neck.
Thus ends the seven purificatory rites (*saptasaṃskāra*). Now begins the section on the meaning of the mantra (*mantrārtha-prakaraṇa*).
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the Yoni-mudrā,
will find no accomplishment even by reciting it a hundred million times.
Therein, first, the meaning of the Guru-mantra, as follows:
Now, therefore, I shall explain the meaning of the mantra according to the names of the gurus:
from the letter *ga* comes the bestowal of knowledge, and from the letter *ra* comes its illumination.
The letter *U* is traditionally taught to bestow identity with Śiva through the Guru;
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the oneness of the Guru and the Deity.
The *iḍā* channel is situated as the moon, while the *piṅgalā* carries the solar heat; the *suṣumnā* consists of various forms of differentiation, and fire is the destroyer of evil.
The supreme reality is attained through the name of the Guru with diligent effort.
Now he states the meaning of the Śiva-mantra.
One should know the syllable *oṃ* as the first, then the syllable *na* after that;
one should know the syllable *ga* after that, and then the syllable *ccha*.
One should know the syllable *va* as the fifth mantra and the syllable *dya* as the sixth;
thus, there shall be the vision of the Immediate (*ruta*) within the five syllables, as well as in Śiva.

One should perceive Brahman in the syllable *praṇava*; "I am indeed Brahman, there is no doubt. The meaning of the mantra is subsequently explained, by which liberation for men is traditionally taught.
The digit of consciousness (citkalā), whose nature is truth, knowledge, and supreme bliss,
is to be known as the most manifest through the word "Śiva," being Śambhu’s consort (Śāmbhavī).
Therefore, this word "vācaka" (designator) is the mind, which is a portion of the consciousness of Brahman;
the word "namaḥ" is proclaimed to be the designator of salutation.
The ancients have declared that the characteristic of prostration (*prahvatva*) is salutation (*namaskāra*),
because the soul of the one who bows becomes humble through Śiva, characterized by [the production of] crops and other benefits.
He says "namas" (salutation) to express the relationship— characterized by identity with Śiva— of that which appears as diverse through Māyā in all its forms.
The Self is eternal, pure, auspicious, and the witness of the true nature of all embodied beings;
therefore, it should never be grasped as an object by the seeker who desires to know the living self (jīva).
Or likewise, even this "sa" is not proclaimed as having reality in fact; thus one should know the meaning of the letter *na*, and now the meaning of the letter *ma* is explained.
The letter *va* is the meaning of my word, while the single letter *ma* has been elided;
having observed this worldly convention, it is proclaimed as "namaskāra" (salutation).
Therefore, the fourth state is called "the corpse" (śava), yet not in a literal sense;
it is proclaimed as the syllable *Oṃ*, the designator of the meaning of all words.
Indeed, O Lord, the application [of the mantra] everywhere is for the sake of all goals, which is Śiva alone;
therefore, the Praṇava is remembered as the designator of the perfection of Śiva.
The relationship between the signifier and the signified, as well as the indicated and the indicator,
does not exist even otherwise when the ultimate reality is investigated.
Alternatively, the claim that "nothing other than Śiva exists at all times" would be subject to falsity; likewise, statements such as "it does not appear" and so forth pertain to the power of Māyā.
The imagined [world], which is the bliss manifested through consciousness, is essentially Śiva in its ultimate reality;
even Māyā and its effects arise from this Śiva, who is characterized by truth and other such qualities.
In the investigation of ultimate reality, there is no establishment of perception at all; now, what is the use of saying more? Nothing exists other than Śiva.
The wise one has told me that this entire universe is of the nature of Śiva;
yet, without knowing the nature of all things, the reality of these two is not perceived.
175a) For this alone is to be cultivated for every purpose, and everything else is not so;
in worldly transaction, it leads to the state of being either the victim or the victimizer. Regarding the moment of another.
"Like waves in the ocean"—this is the summary of the meaning of the mantra.
Now, [the mantra] of Tārā.
He himself, the supreme form of Viṣṇu, shone playfully; and how could he not be thus the moon-crested Lord?
May the three-eyed one, whose feet are like lotuses from which flows a stream of water that is the eternal seed of the universe, protect us.

Since the Creator himself remains as the Self-born (Svayambhū), how could he ever be subject to birth? Thus, the world, beginning with the earth, is produced from the seed of the navel-lotus by him who is swift in action.
He gave to this creator of the world four hands from his own; those which formerly were the Vedas became the worlds.
Therefore, the castes, the ages (yugas), and the Vedas exist, as do the worlds and so forth.
Indeed, they say that the seed-syllable of that [deity] consists of an equal portion [of vowels], while its expansion consists of three-quarters [of consonants].
The single syllable *ci* is the beginning of the Vedas, consisting of the letters and the *jagatī* meter; from that arises the weapon-mantra.
When combined with the half-syllable *sā*, it becomes the five-syllabled mantra known as Tārā, so called because she ferries the world across [the ocean of existence].
"Another [aspect] of his is the eternal Jaṭāsyāja (the one with matted locks), who is the savior of the world," and so forth.
Those people who recite this king of hymns become renowned in both prose and verse praise;
for, being liberated from the form of the world, they quickly go to the state of the Savior within another body.
He who, at the end of the night’s recitation during the change of seasons, should recite with devotion at dawn after reflecting upon its meaning and non-meaning;
The lotus would be blue because of the bees on its feet; the swan would possess life because it is a living thing; and the living thing would be the individual soul.
Thus ends the complete explanation of the meaning of Maktārā, from the *Śrī-Ardhatanirūpaṇa-mantrārthavivaraṇa*.
Now, he explains the meaning of the mantra of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess Earth, you consist of the letters *la*, together with your mountains, forests, and groves;
you are endowed with the fifty sacred seats (*pīṭha*), composed of all holy fords (*tīrtha*), and supreme.
O Śivā, you consist of all the Gaṅgās and all sacred fields and sites;
you are the letter 'Sa', and you embody the moon, the stars, the planets, and the gods.
From the syllable *ha* and through union with Śiva, they are established within the circle of the sky (*vyoma*).
O Dear One, this Māyā, which is the creator of the universe, consists of the fourth state (turya) and begins with the letter *i*.
From the letter *e* arises the Vaiṣṇavī power, intent upon the protection of the universe;
from the letter *ra* arises the Vaiṣṇavī power, which is not intent upon protecting the universe. || 5 ||
O You who are endowed with the splendor of the syllable *ra*, O You whose essential nature is the supreme light! || 6 ||
From the letter *ka* comes the one whose form is the desire for liberation (*kāmadā*), who is the radiance of the imperishable.
But in the half-moon, O Goddess of gods, she is proclaimed as Viśvayoni. || 8 ||
By means of the Bindu, which is the form of Śiva and the form of the Void, she is the Witness.
O Goddess of the gods, by this [power] which is coextensive with it and whose nature is immobility, even the Śrīcakra is, without doubt, of the form of Meru. 10.
O Bhuvaneśānī, Kāmeśī is the supreme seed-mantra (bīja) of all;
by means of this, I shall specifically declare the entire Vidyā.

O blue-eyed one, this six-syllabled Kāmarāja mantra, beginning with Mādana (Ka), enriched by Śiva (Ha) and the Moon (Sa), and ending with Śivā (Ā), is entirely enchanting, O blessed lady.
O Varārohā, the seed-syllable Śakti, preceded by the Moon (Ca), is the all-enchanting one;
it consists of four syllables, while the Night (Rātri) consists of three syllables, being both ancient and supreme.

Alternatively, he states the mantra for the consecration of the child.

[One should visualize the deity] clad in white garments, white in color, and anointed with white perfumes.
