she should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and likewise perform oblations with five or six types of materials.
Then, having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites, the mantra becomes effective;
one should inscribe the seed-syllable upon the tongue of a newborn infant.
By writing with honey on a golden pen, one becomes a poet at eight years of age;
and whoever performs the *puraścaryā* rite at the Vāgmatī or the Gaṅgā [attains the same].
For the second [initiation], he should be without a fixed abode, subsisting on alms, or else observing silence;
he should be a celibate student, sleeping on the ground, wearing white garments, and pure.
One obtains success in speech and becomes a master; who, indeed, is the giver and the enjoyer with you?
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Śrī Kaularahasya, the Essence of All Āgamas. || 25 ||
Now, he states the number of mantras for the ten vidyās.
In the Kali age, the Kālī-vidyā remains divided into ten million varieties;
through ten previous [ages], it was established on earth as the Sundarī-vidyā consisting of seven million.
Three hundred billion, four hundred million, and eighty-five thousand five hundred thousand [miles] is the extent of the severed portion of the sky.
O Sarasvatī, listen to the great lore of Vagalā, the glory of the world; Vagalā, who is the objective of the ultimate reality, has manifested in nine hundred thousand forms.
Dhūmāvatī is the Great Vidyā, while Bhairavī is indeed the Sixteenth.
Mātaṅgī has one hundred thousand eyes, and Kamalā has five hundred thousand;
these Sṛṅkhalikā yogas have emerged from the *prastāras*.
Now follows the result of the distinction of the Kaumārī birth.
O Goddess of the gods, for the complete accomplishment of all desired goals, a Brahmin woman should go to Yaśas, a Kṣatriya woman to Prayāga,
and a Vaiśya woman to Koṭisiddhipradāyaka.

A *svairiṇī* (a woman of loose character) is prescribed for purposes such as fulfilling desires; a *kuṭṭinī* (a procuress) for all rites; a *hartī* for the rite of affection (*prīti*); and a *kumārī* (a maiden) is proclaimed for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*).
The Vṛṣalī is the deity perfected by the Siddhas; she is the Kirātinī through the perfection of the body. She is Pārvatī, the essence of all actions and desires, the very Kalā herself.
The Cāṇḍālinī is born from a weaver for the sake of success in the kingdom;
the Rājasutā is born from a king’s daughter for the sake of success in knowledge; thus they are proclaimed in sequence.
Śrīvālasundarī has been proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing all desires.
Nor is she Kaumārī.
The first is known as Aśuddhā, the second as Vāsikā, and the third is remembered as Lalitā;
the fourth is called Māli, and the fifth is Vasundharā.
Sarasvatī, Ramā, Gaurī, and Durgā shall be the ninth.
Of the person.
That which is the twelfth year among the five and nine years is called the *paṃcādhyāvaṭuka*; it is not a year of the Lord of the Gaṇas (*gaṇeśvara*).
Now, having introduced the topic, he describes various expiations (*prāyaścitta*).
Practitioners who desire accomplishment must never perform ritual applications;
from such applications, one attains hell, and nothing else exists beyond that.
The practitioner who performs the rite incurs sin; however, the seeker (sādhaka) must perform expiation.
To pacify the defects of the ritual performance, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
For killing, driving away, and hatred, it becomes pure after one hundred thousand recitations;
likewise, for subjugation and the like, one should first recite one hundred and ten thousand times.
The Lord said:
179a) Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim for you the rule for expiation:
a disciple who abandons his guru must certainly perform penance.
Having recited one hundred thousand times while taking refuge in Udraka, one is purified from that [sin].
O Dear One, he who does not abandon the mantra should avoid association with such a person.
Pure through burnt offerings and libations, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times when Śaṅkara has been invoked for the sake of all sins whatsoever.

One should know that the atonement for the daily rites and other sequential fire-offerings consists of reciting the mantra ten thousand times; for the sake of pacification, one should recite the Vidyā a hundred times.
Regarding the *naimittika* [occasional rite]: if by chance one obtains the Vidyā from a person of noble family during the slaughter of an animal, one should recite this mantra a thousand times.
Having approached a twice-born Kaulika, one should again receive the Vidyā;
[for otherwise], it would be fragmentary, devoid of seed-syllables, doubtful, and likewise censured.
If the mantras do not succeed and the guru becomes a slayer of Brahmins,
then, having suddenly recognized him as such, one should abandon that mantra-deity and the guru.
One should recite the *līlī* mantra three hundred thousand times, or one may recite it one hundred thousand times;
one should then perform fire oblations (*homa*) with the end of the *dhīpa* mantra, after which one will certainly behold [the deity].
If Vīrīmaheśvara should drink the substance from the same vessel [as another], his drink would become the leavings of a dog; that Kaulika must perform an expiation.
Having thoroughly purified his mind through a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī and three days of fasting, he should offer gold to his preceptor and the deity.
If one has received the mantra from a mother or from a teacher by force, or even with a wrong accent,
one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times and then perform the fire sacrifice with rice husks.
By engaging in sexual union with the daughter of a mantra-practitioner, one’s own daughter, a sister, or a woman of noble family,
a Kaulika becomes purified through a hundred thousand recitations.
Having committed the killing of a hero, the drinking of intoxicants in the presence of a guru,
or having dallied with a mantra-bearing wife of a hero, one should recite the *Rakṣaso* mantra.
Having killed a bone-bearing creature, one goes to the Vanaraka hell;
having killed birds, horses, or a woman, one should recite the Ekādaśa [mantra] eleven times.
Having killed a snake, a cat, a mongoose, a camel, a donkey,
a horse, an elephant, or any wild animals, one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times.

If the killing of small creatures occurs, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra eight thousand times; without offering a *bali* sacrifice, he must never cause animals to fall [in death]. Otherwise, the sages have prescribed a penance for such an act that is pleasing to the Smṛtis.
By ten hundred thousand recitations, one is liberated from the hell called Niraya;
by twelve hundred thousand, a practitioner of mantras is released after having killed a bull.
By killing a guru through negligence, one becomes pure after five hundred thousand [recitations];
by killing a woman, a practitioner of mantra is liberated after ten million.
If a Brahmin falls due to negligence, he becomes pure by twenty lakhs [of recitations];
Kṣatriyas and others are freed from this sin according to what has been stated.
For the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, a hundred thousand [is prescribed]; for a Kṣatriya, twice that is recorded;
for a Vaiśya, three times is ordained; and for a Śūdra, four times.
For killing two animals, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] twenty-four thousand times;
for killing a goat, a sheep, or a pig, five thousand times.
A practitioner of mantras is purified by two thousand [recitations] for killing a mouse;
for killing a snake, a cat, or a fish, one thousand Vedic verses [are required].

For offending a deity or offending a guru, one should recite the mantra thirty million times; likewise, having consumed the property of a deity or the property of a guru, one should recite that same mantra for that long.
O Śiva, for one who reviles the commitments (samaya), the yoginīs and vīras, the scriptures, the mantra-practitioners, or women, one should perform a thousand-fold recitation of the mantra.

Or, at the conclusion of the southern *siddhi*, a practitioner of mantra who observes the *śaiva* vow and belongs to the lineage of Hari becomes purified of sin by reciting [the mantra] forty million times.
The practitioner of mantras is purified from the disparagement of the *arghya* and other offerings by performing ten circumambulations;
first, he should drink the nectar of the *arghya*, and thereafter, he should raise the Goddess.
He shall become a drinker of the flesh of cattle; that merit of his shall be destroyed.
But if he eats without having offered [the food], he shall constantly undergo eight hundred penances.
The wife of a hero is in vain.
The practitioner of mantras should perform atonement through the worship of the divine heroes and other rites,
in the event of the extinguishing of the lamp, the breaking of the vessel, or the spilling of the vessel's contents.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
if done unknowingly, that is considered "leftover" (impure), but if done knowingly, it becomes double [that amount].
O beloved, listen to the means for when a machine is burnt, shattered, or even carried off by a deer; or when it is split, rubbed, or [damaged] in the sky.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire offerings and libations;
having satisfied [the deity] with true devotion, one should also feed the brahmins.
Then the wise one should perform the worship of Śakti and offer the eight groups of eight.
Or even the *Pañcapañcaka*; in essence, Kālī and Tārā may at times have their marks effaced, or their ornaments shattered.
If his hand is broken or lost, death will certainly come to that mortal;
therefore, he [should bathe] at the king of holy places (Tīrtharāja) or in the Ganges and other supreme rivers.
Or one may cast it into the ocean, O Goddess; otherwise, one would incur suffering.
This rite is to be performed for the sake of the vidyā alone; now listen with respect to the specific details.
If two arrows from the Narmadā river are used together, it becomes defective;
however, if the shafts of the Bhadina variety are broken, the liṅga is not then rendered defective.

If a fracture occurs even to the extent of a *śālagrāma*-dust particle, death will occur; if there is a blow to the foot, it results in a quarter of a life-span, and if it is on the head, O Śivā, it results in nearness [to death].
O Pārvatī, when the heart has become tranquil and everything has vanished,
O Goddess, one should dissolve that form and then perform the ritual of assuming a new form.
O Goddess, listen with reverence to the special rule regarding the ritual of Mahāvidyā:
one should abandon that specific region or place where the deity has gone.
Then, having performed the expiation, the practitioner attains happiness;
[he should consume] the Bālāmanīyakaumārī, well-chewed and beautifully prepared.
Having placed [the deity] upon a bed of flowers, one should worship her along with her limbs and her retinue;
O Goddess of gods, the very nature of the Goddess is the nature of that [bed].
Having meditated thus, O Goddess, one should mutter the mantra according to the tradition;
thereafter, one should observe a fast for this specific day with great devotion.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, distinguishing between the recitation and the libation;
having worshipped the Virgin alone, one should perform each of those acts with a lamp.
In the *Triśakti*, *Paravidyā*, and other [tantras], one should practice the King of Lamps (*dīparāja*).
By reciting the *Dīpinī* at the tip of the lamp, one likewise becomes free from faults.
Then, having drawn the yantra with vermilion and encircled it with the root mantra,
one should write the *kullukā* in its corner and perform the lamp ritual there.
O Goddess of gods, by means of the eight fragrances, or even by any other fragrance, or by adyasnṛṇa, or by that which possesses divine color, one shall become Siddhīśvara.
The lamp should face west; the vessel should measure three palas and be made of gold, silver, copper, clay, or any other metal.
Having carefully prepared a lamp with twenty-one threads,
one should fashion a wick one span long using three threads and nine rudra-threads.
One should prepare a vessel from eight palas of dried palāśa wood;
its height should be four aṅgulas, and its excellence is measured at a height of five aṅgulas.

O Śivā, one should offer the armor (*kavaca*) seven times as prescribed for the leather thong and the blue [thread]; O Auspicious One, having worshipped the Goddess together with her limbs (*sāṅga*) and her retinue (*sāvaraṇā*), using a lamp.
In this manner, O Goddess of gods, the practitioner gradually attains perfection;
thereafter, he should perform the offering of oblations (bali) according to the distinctions of *sāttvika* and the other types.
By reciting the *Āpad-ūrdhāraka*, a person becomes free from faults;
for this is indeed considered the perpetual lamp for those who have consumed the poison of the three powers (*triśakti*).
O Supreme Goddess, this has been proclaimed in connection with the topic of expiation;
thus freed from defects, one should again take up the yantra.
Having approached a qualified teacher according to the path taught by one's own guru,
listen to what is declared regarding the ritual of Mahāvidyā for both Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas.
Having observed a fast for one night and recited the Aghora mantra ten thousand times (one hundred thousand),
and having performed the fire-oblation (homa) rite with a tenth part of that number, one then becomes free from defects.
One should mutter this mantra, O Śivā.
Having recited [the mantra] over the sacred turmeric (haridrā) for the Gāṇapatas, one shall become a master of supernatural powers (siddhiśvara).
However, he who acts otherwise will become a sinner.
O Pārvatī, those belonging to the divine current desire three times ten thousand here.
A Kaulika who approaches a bound soul (paśu) may forcibly enjoy the supreme Śakti;
however, in the midst of a gathering, he should not intentionally cause physical contact with her.
He who acts as a teacher while lacking discrimination enters a hundred million wombs and goes to the Raurava hell.
If one abandons the form of the Mother and instead takes up the form of a weapon or a Śakti,
he goes to a terrible hell for hundreds of millions of births.
Having recited the Ajapā mantra three hundred thousand times,
and likewise one hundred thousand times the seed-syllable of the Fourth State (turyā-bīja) characterized by five [elements], one should thereafter perform purification.
Now, he states the expiation for the temple of Mālā and other such sites.
If the rosary is broken through negligence, one should perform an expiation;
however, if the secret rosary is broken, a person should offer a goat as a sacrifice.
If the *lakṣa* is burnt by fire, lost, or dropped from the hand,
one should recite six thousand times; if it falls [into water], one should recite three hundred times.

If, while making a sound with the fingertips during the recitation, one drops the rosary from the hand, one should perform a preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) consisting of a hundred recitations for each [error], as well as a hundred oblations.
Having recited the expiation one hundred times, one should increase it by a tenth part;
then, one should abandon a tenth part of the effort according to the sequence of the expiation.
Some maintain that there should be a preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) here again;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred times as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should then perform the *puraścaraṇa*.
If it breaks at the base of Mount Meru, one should assign that [fault] to women;
if the garland itself breaks, one should perform an expiation.
One should perform a thousand recitations and fire-oblations for Gajāntaka;
then, having performed the re-knotting [of the thread], preceded by the rite of establishing the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Then the garland [of mantras] shall grant success; otherwise it will not, such is the word of Śaṅkara.
(184b) Now he states the mantra of the Grahāmātṛkā.
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the ritual for the propitiation of the Mothers of the Planets (Grahamātṛs);
when the Mothers of the Planets are satisfied, what misfortunes caused by the planets could possibly remain?
When the Mother of the Planets is satisfied, what need is there for auspicious planets?
Maṅgarā, Piṅgalā, Āḍhā, Bhrāmalī, and likewise Bhadrikā—[these are the Mothers].
Ulkāsiddhā, Asaṃkaṭā, Vikaṭā, Garbhapālikā,
and Raudranakṣatrā— these eight are the presiding deities of birth, and their periods (daśās) follow in sequence.
The fruit should be commensurate with the single accumulation of the year;
Piṅgalā is born of the Sun and is the cause of great disease.
When pleased, she bestows a multitude of umbrellas; when enraged, she brings ruin upon the practitioner.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *piṅgale vairivāriṇi*, [one should perform the rite].
Having uttered "Be gracious, O Fruitful One," one should assign the three syllables of the Śakti-mantra to the three eyes;
then, with the first seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels, one performs the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using "Namaḥ" and "Vaṣaṭ."
I worship her who is tawny in complexion, with tawny hair and tawny eyes, whose bow is the rainbow, and who holds a pair of lotuses in her hands.
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship common to all [deities]:
japā flowers are recommended, as is incense produced from *turuṣka*.
Food offerings such as milk-rice and the like, sweetened and illuminated with ghee;
likewise, red ornaments and garments, and sandalwood.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with golden ornaments and abundant fivefold oceanic riches, reciting the respective mantras a thousand times.
Having fashioned a beautiful golden plate, one cubit in length and free of blemishes,
one should worship the Yoginī there upon the yantra as prescribed.
Having recited that respective mantra a thousand times for the sake of pacifying obstacles,
one becomes a remover of the three kinds of misfortunes within seven days.
Then, having constructed a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules,
or else upon a pure altar-ground (sthaṇḍila) well-smeared with cow dung;
Having established the yoginīs and performed the preliminary rites starting from the east, the yogi, with a steady mind, should perform the recitation within a space measuring four cubits.
For other [deities], ten times; for a hostile one, a thousand times;
with bilva leaves, its fruits, and *kamallarāgakeśana* flowers.
One should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) and likewise worship with abundant offerings;
one may perform a thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand repetitions according to one's desire.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain: one should worship the Goddess in the center;
one should worship the powers of Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā) in the three corners.
This indeed is the method of worship and the fire-oblation for all [mantras];
however, there is a specific distinction here regarding the eradication of enemies and the performance of malevolent rites.
One should meditate on Vainasigrahakālikā, who holds the sword and shield mudrā, possesses six arms,
and is seated upon a Garuḍa.
Having first recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should indeed perform the fire-sacrifice (tapana) for one hundred thousand times;
thus there shall be the destruction of all enemies, and one shall encounter no suffering anywhere.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra of Candramātā for the practitioner:
beginning with *māyā* (the seed-syllable of Māyā) and ending with *vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire, *svāhā*), it is auspicious, O abode of auspiciousness.
The eleven-syllable mantra is proclaimed as beginning with Maṅgalā;
having performed the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and so forth by means of the individual [syllables], one should likewise perform the worship of the six limbs using the long vowels.
Meditate, O Goddess, upon the three-eyed one who resembles the rising sun,
whose face slightly smiles, who belongs to the Bhoja lineage, and whose lips are stained with vermilion.
Holding two lotuses, a bow, and arrows with her sprout-like arms,
she is resplendent with a lower garment adorned by a girdle-string and anklets that serve as its bowstring.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, one should perform the worship as before;
then, having recited the obtained mantra-body preceded by the *tāra* and *māyā*, [one should proceed].
The Yoginī, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and Gaṇādhipa should receive the bali offering;
at the conclusion of the worship, all will be established and Maṅgalā herself shall be pleased.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the purpose of pacifying the afflictions of a Yoginī; for the sake of the lineage of two Yoginīs, one should recite it ten million times.
For those who have attained the fruit of auspiciousness connected to what has been seen by the seers,
let there be a daily recitation of a thousand [mantras] while performing the jāpa.
The Yoginī, however, should be drawn up to one hundred syllables;
for the sake of creation, she consists of ten syllables, and one should consecrate the patient with fire.
If another mantra possessing an equal number of syllables should exist for her, then by the utterance of that [mantra],
her suffering shall cease within those very days.
O you who are equal to the gods, the evening rite is not to be understood as [inferior];
it yields fruits equal to those of the Yoginīs through both the Left Path and the Right.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Bhrāmarī, the mother of the earth.
Having uttered the word "bhrāmaya" after "kṣīṃ," [saying] "O Sovereign Goddess, may you be victorious for me," followed by "bhrāmaya klīṃ"— this is proclaimed as your sixteen-syllable mantra.
Having consecrated ten pieces of sugar with the Piṅgalā-mantra,
one should cast them upon the path and in the ten directions.
At dawn, one should set out on the road, for everyone who stands upon the path [is safe];
indeed, all tigers, serpents, and thieves fall into a state of delusion.
One should always perform a single auspicious rite for the earth that is free from defects;
or one may go after having written the person's name upon the sole of a sandal.
One should recite the mantra for one *yojana* and cause the earth to tremble.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Bhadrikā, the mother of the wise.
One should first utter the seed-syllable *vlūṃ*, which is abundant with water, followed by the roar of a thundercloud.
One should say the words "bhaktike" and "mama bhadraṃ dehi," and then again say "parabhadrāṇi"; thereafter, one destroys the pair.
This mantra of Bhadrikā is considered to consist of the syllables "Oṃ jinavarṇa svāhā";
the procedure for the six limbs is declared to be performed with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.

Maṅgalā is the best among those that yield auspicious results, while Dhyānā is said to grant evil fruits like Piṅgalā; the recitation and other rites for these are to be performed according to the prescribed method.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the one named Dhanyā, the mother of the Guru;
having first uttered "Śrīdhvajade," the eight-syllable mantra is "Dhanyā Svāhā."
The ritual for the six limbs is performed here with the seed-syllables beginning with the six long vowels;
there is no other [practice] in this world equal to this in bestowing its fruits.
Having performed the threefold preliminary rite (puraścaryā), with sins previously wiped away, may she—
who bestows auspiciousness upon those who possess the lineage— grant auspiciousness to the practitioner.
To the west of Vṛhaspatīśvara, one should behold Kāśvādhanyā;
by performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) there, one is born into a lineage that purifies its descendants.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mother of Siddhyāśukra:
Hrīṃ Siddhamat-sarvamānasa-muktā; one should accomplish this pair.
The mantra syllables ending with "hṛdayāntā" are declared as the mantra of Siddhā;
one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable alone, and carry out the recitation (japa) and other rites as previously described.
The accomplishment of karma for practitioners is not established anywhere;
for those who do not arise through the lineage of the accomplished practitioners, it does not come to pass.
Indeed, for those who follow that tradition,
everything pertaining to the ripening of their state is accomplished through the sixfold action, even without the propitiation of a personal deity.
188b) Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mother of Cūḍāmaṇḍa:
Oṃ, for the destruction of my disease, to Bhañjakā, the ten-syllable [mantra].
The mantras that remove all diseases [are effective] through sprinkling seven times;
for one whose *ulkā-mantra* is perfected, no disease exists in his home.
In Śītā, Mahāmāyā released a buffalo endowed with auspicious marks for the sake of pleasing Ulkā, and then paraded it again through the city.
Surrounded by various musical instruments and adorned with garments and other ornaments, one should release the ascetic at midnight; thus, calamity shall be pacified.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of Saṃkaṭā, the mother of Rāhu: Hrīṃ! O Saṃkaṭā, destroy my two supreme calamities.
This sixteen-syllable mantra dispels all suffering;
when recited within the house of Kālā, liberation from bondage arises.
189a) To the north of Vīreśvara is Kāśī, where Saṃkaṭā is established;
having recited [the mantra] sixteen hundred thousand times there, the fire-oblation (homa) is indeed difficult to accomplish.
The mantra becomes effective for her if it issues forth from her own mouth;
indeed, whatever suffering of such-and-such a person is to come, that very suffering goes to him.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare Vikaṭā, Ketu, and Mātala:
Tārau, homage to the Blessed One, Vikaṭā, the protector of heroes!
The mantra *prasīda-yugalam* is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
To the west of Vīreśvara in Kāśī, Vikaṭā is situated;
having recited this mantra there, those grains of sand [are empowered] against the seizing spirits (*graha*).
He also saw those with distended bellies, those who were barren, those with deformed heads,
those abandoned by their parents due to poverty and other such reasons, and those who were motherless.
When questioned by a practitioner, those who are healthy and long-lived [should speak].
189b) Now, he states the means to liberation:
The Goddess said:
In some places it is Dakṣa, in some Vāma, and in some the Śāmbhava-śauca;
in some places the Urdhvāmnāya is Dakṣa, and in some places the supreme Paraśvima.
Then there are also the Āmnāyaka, the Gāṇāpatya, and the Vaiṣuva;
the Pārasīka, the Dhaureya, the Pāṣaṇḍa, and the Kaucika in various places.
If, in certain contexts, one praises the laws of the island, the laws of the region, the laws of the family, the laws of time,
or the laws of the wandering mendicant, and in other contexts censures them—
then this Tantra is the supreme among them, provided that even a liquor-drinker is serene therein.
"Then, O Sunīti, tell me the truth without any doubt.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Alas, O Kāla! In various places you have asked me about this and that again and again; since that [inquiry] has increased, I, being such as I am, shall speak of that Time."
I shall endure this virtuous course of action for the sake of the welfare of all, even at the cost of my own life; therefore, I shall speak that truth to you individually.
190a) Just as it is in the Veda, so it is in the world; according to its form, it is produced.
Just as this cosmic egg-sphere is depicted here in the center.
And in that regard, what difference is there between the truth praised in the Veda and that which is found in other scriptures?
Likewise, by a man, [the goal] is attained through time by means of the Veda and not from another scripture.
O Goddess of gods, observe the interval; hear the truth along with the Mother:
how the unstruck sound proceeds within a person after having been dissolved.
Even though it is eternal, it may fall as a particle at some time; it may fall as a particle for a moment, but never for one who is about to die.
The sound of the Vedas is likewise remembered as belonging to the time of the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa);
it lasts for ten thousand years when such a period of the Kali age has elapsed.
The Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself; when it is not heard by living beings due to the divisions of time, then one should know that the [dissolution] time has arrived.
The speech-born [mantras] beginning with the words *vajra* and *jambha*, as well as the sounds arising from the vowels,
the weapons that consume the Vedas, and likewise the deities— one should know them thus.
As long as this scripture exists in this world, there shall be happiness for those who follow the path of truth; indeed, the Vedic path remains unimpeded.
Those who lead her along that path are the disciples who bestow her mantra;
they lead her upon that path so that there may be happiness for her as long as it lasts.
Just as the knowledge of a king is fully realized through the six senses,
so too does certain knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas arise through the six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Likewise, the five organs of action of men are established;
similarly, at that time, the five Āmnāyas of Maheśa were proclaimed by me.
That vocal ritual is declared to belong to the Urdhvāmnāya;
in that regard, the Vedas are the authority, as are their branches and the Sūtras.
The limbs are the Purāṇas, while the deities are Gāyatrī and the others;
likewise, the seed is Brahman, the field is the sacred site, and the purificatory rites originate from Brahman.
One becomes a Brāhmaṇa through the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa and by means of Vedic knowledge.
In whose [speech] we shall speak, or in whose speech it runs in the midst—
when even a single characteristic is deficient, the meaning of the word runs away.
O Goddess, one who lacks two characteristics becomes a self-controlled Brahmin;
he who is devoid of three characteristics attains perfection through the path of Tantra.
For those devoid of the four characteristics, there may be paths such as the Kaulika and others;
yet by one who is distinct from these characteristics, [the path follows] just as the body [follows] its own family.
The gathering of the Dharma should be performed according to one's birth and the appropriate time;
false speech and deception are censured on all paths.
Whatever action may be performed in this life— whether it be recitation, austerity, or ritual act—
the one liberated while living is a speaker of truth, for he is established in universal truth.

Non-violence and freedom from attachment to the doctrines of others— when these are firm through the actions of speech and body, one who possesses them is like a liberated one, regardless of their conduct or birth.
He in whose mind there is no attachment even toward his own body—that Puṣkala too, know him to be liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
For those possessing knowledge of the six senses and their objects, creation arises from sexual union;
he by whom that [desire] has been abandoned through the mind is indeed a liberated soul while living.
The Vedas desire worship, and likewise the elders desire gifts;
tell me, O liberated-in-life one, how one who accepts gifts like a parrot can be liberated while living.
For one who constantly practices purification, the notion of "I" regarding the feces, the intellect, and the body falls away; he alone is indeed liberated while living.
One who is content with whatever is obtained according to his desire does not praise [others], nor does he find fault;
he is not scorched by the heat of the mouth, and through the destruction of karma, he is liberated from suffering.
He who, having abandoned the pleasures of the sense-objects, practices austerity in solitude and desires no fruit whatsoever— he alone is truly liberated while living.
As long as the maintenance of the body lasts, one should cast off a portion [of worldly activity];
for everything is transcended by the Veda, and through that, one attains liberation.
"Who is the agent? What is seen? Whose is this mind, and where does it go?"—contemplating thus constantly, one attains dissolution into Mahākāla.
In this Kali age, which is filled with evil, there is neither equanimity nor yoga;
O Goddess, even if there were yoga, no fruit would arise from it.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should completely abandon the causal yoga of mantras;
these are merely worldly means, and the mind will not become steady through them.
She who devours the mouths of Mahākāla is difficult to discern and impossible to restrain; she deludes with great illusion those tormented by the enemies of desire and anger.
If she is pleased by the propitiation of her own part, she releases it; then,
like a mother who is extended [in love] toward wise and beloved sons, she expands [her grace].
In this way, she is deceived; when the individual soul (jīva) is liberated, he is born [again].
By her, food, drink, and sexual intercourse have been performed for a futile purpose.
If these [practices] do not lead to growth, then one would be liberated by oneself;
therefore, [liberation does not come] from Vāmikas, Ekolikās, or those ignorant ones who are devoid of a Guru.
This [bond] is bound by all forms of knowledge, and not by others;
it is barren regarding its own bonds while simultaneously tearing those bonds asunder.
One should meditate upon Mahākāla, and then one becomes liberated while living;
the methods for liberation from bondage are considered therein to be threefold.
Those who, through the path of the Guru, increase that knowledge which is otherwise difficult to cross, shall become men of merit; and being wise, they shall attain liberation.
Out of eighty-four hundred thousand [births] of embodied beings,
true knowledge is not obtained elsewhere except in the human state.
In this regard, O Pārvatī, even after thousands upon thousands of births, [this is not attained].
Sometimes a living being attains human birth through the accumulation of merit;
having obtained this human state, which is difficult to find and serves as a staircase to liberation.
He who does not deliver himself is the most wretched of men;
for such a person, having attained a supreme birth and having acquired the excellence of the senses, [remains lost].
Even one who has killed a Brahmin may not attain greatness;
for no one’s human goal (puruṣārtha) exists apart from the body.
Therefore, one should employ one's body, wealth, and kingdom for meritorious deeds;
one should always regard honor as the vessel of everything.
One should practice steadfastness in protection; one who lives thus beholds auspicious things:
again a village, again a field, again wealth, and again a home.
Furthermore, virtuous karma does not repeatedly produce a body; rather,
it is for the sake of protecting the body that people constantly perform such actions.
As long as this embodied being remains, so long should one practice that reality;
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are the deities born from the elements.
They pursue only destruction; therefore, one should practice the truth as long as suffering has not been conquered and as long as calamities have not arrived.
"One should practice the reality as long as no deficiency of the senses occurs;
thus everything has been declared before you, O Pārvatī."
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīkaularahasya*, the essence of all Āgamas. || 26 ||
Now, the offering of the bali-oblation.
Now, the offering of the *bali* is being described here;
according to the words of the Tantras, the *bali* is to be known as threefold.
And [the ritual] is Vedic; among these, first, the Tantric is said to be eightfold:
the daily offering to the *paśus*, the daily [offering], and the occasional worship.
Therefore, the animal sacrifice is mandatory in the occasional rite;
animals arrive with distinction, and the act of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is likewise differentiated.
O Dear One, she too will be mentioned at the conclusion of the worship during the moment of offering the *bali*;
buffaloes, goats, and so forth are designated as the *bali* offerings.
There were also water-born creatures, as well as those born in villages and those born in the wilderness—
beasts, birds, insects, and even those of animal wombs.
These have been ordained by the Creator as the offerings for the dwellers of heaven;
the deities are not so pleased with other materials for the sacrificial oblation.
Just as [the offering] of animals and likewise of grains is made with oblations,
for that very reason, O Goddess of gods, it is prescribed at the beginning of sacrifices and other rites.
The term "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priya*) is said to be a synonym for "animal" (*paśu*);
having understood this established conclusion (*siddhānta*) for the sake of pleasing the Goddess.
O beloved, one should offer an animal as a sacrificial oblation; even those [animals] covered in the middle [should be offered].
In the sacrifice named Gomadha, one should immolate a white bull.
In the Naramedha [sacrifice], he offered a man; in the Gajakrānta, likewise an elephant;
in the Aśvamedha, Śaṅkhacūḍa; and in the Kṣepahastina, an elephant.
Even where only one [deity] is present, there too the *cāṇā* is required;
therefore, O beloved, the offering (*bali*) is essential in the rite of the occasional worship (*naimittikārcā*).
It should be offered especially for the sake of pleasing the Goddess;
indeed, without an offering (bali), the Goddess does not accept worship at all.
In that regard, both the buffalo and the goat are praised;
what need is there for other gods or for deliberations concerning sacrificial offerings?
I shall now describe that investigation by which Kālī is satisfied:
[it concerns] those born from wild, domestic, aquatic, or terrestrial sources. 195a)
I shall now first declare those very same species of birds as well.
Fish, deer, boars, tortoises, and likewise buffaloes;
crocodiles, iguanas, and grāhas from the Gaṇḍakī; śārkalas and monkeys as well.
O beloved, there are also nakulas, śalabhas, gavayas, and likewise galas; even among them are humans and birds, as well as their eggs.
The Creator fashioned these as offerings (bali) for the sake of the Blessed Lady;
by the offering of these, one should accomplish all undertakings.
Now, the fruit of the offering.
Through wrinkles the body grows old; through wrinkles diseases are pacified;
through wrinkles one conquers enemies; through wrinkles wealth is obtained.
By means of the folds [of the skin], one may go to the third heaven.
That which is to be attained even by those free from desire when the power [of the winds] arises, and that which is liberation—
this shall now be explained briefly according to the distinctions of birth for the sake of the supreme goal.
There are eighteen kinds of fish and twenty-four kinds of deer.
Boars are said to be of five kinds, tortoises of three varieties, crocodiles likewise of two types, and rhinoceroses are of four kinds.
The crocodile has three varieties, and the shark likewise has two;
both the tiger and the lion are of three kinds, and the mongoose is of two types as well.
O fair-faced one, there is but a single species of locusts and no distinction among them;
the gavaya is said to be of three kinds, and the goat is considered to be of six varieties.
There are four kinds of humans and thirty-six species of birds;
O beloved, I shall declare their names to you in order.
Now follows the characteristics of sacrificial animals.
O Goddess, in that great sacred seat during the Kali age, the human offering is supreme; in the great sacred seat, the human is the oblation.
The best of practitioners should ensure that [the image] is free from disease and beautiful.
196a) Dhātuvardha, Kṛṣṇakūrca, Ukṣarādi, and Anulomaja;
Mūlyodgrīhīta, Pāpiṣṭha, and Devataiḥ-svayamāgata.
One who has practiced according to his desire for a year or six months shall be fit for the *vali* offering; no one else, such as one seized by thieves and the like, is eligible.
The buffalo, born in the forest, measures five cubits above and ten below;
even the village buffalo is very fierce, with a color like that of a ripe *nīra* fruit or a *kusāṇḍa*.
One with reddish eyes, an upturned neck, a long tail, and a fleshy body is fit for carrying loads;
one who is fearful is not suitable for the yoke, while another is fit for it.
One who dwells in the forest, whose youthful complexion is well-preserved, who is a great hero and possesses abundant flesh, is said to be a fit boar.
After three years and before seven, one who has abandoned the sacred fires is considered a month-old [impurity];
he is of a single color, possessing the form and color of the deity, yet devoid of sound.
A bull with testicles, one that sheds blood from its penis, and one that smells like a goat, [are unfit] due to [the application of] medicinal herbs and the like.
O Goddess, having removed the odor from the sacrificial ring, I shall describe in detail the characteristics of the goat that is most excellent for sacrifice.

One with upward-pointing joints, upward-growing hair, hanging ears, and a thick body; one who is self-possessed, well-nourished, free from wrinkles and grey hair, with long ears and a pure black complexion— such is the praiseworthy characteristic of a sacrificial animal.
White, black, red, tawny, variegated, and pale.
A goat with white feet is declared to be the sacrificial offering (bali) for householders;
those that are white, yellow, and black are the best, while those with variegated and pale-red markings are middling.
Lohita and Kapila are proclaimed by Kaviṣṭha as occurring for three months and continuing until two years have passed.
This is declared to be the *ūrta* type of *vali*; those with less than that are considered *dhama*.
When a *vali* is black in color and has a white tail-tip, it is [of this latter kind].
A wise man should avoid such a gateway as that of a goat.
Thus, a wise man should always avoid one that is white with a black tail;
however, if it is black in color, he may accept it provided its backbone is white.
One should recognize that as praiseworthy, but one should avoid the opposite;
a white buffalo five years old is proclaimed to be praiseworthy.
That very buffalo is proclaimed as white and praiseworthy;
that same buffalo, if black, is the lowest offering for the Pāṇḍavas.
Birds of all colors that are auspicious and very beautiful are recommended;
however, one should avoid them for three fortnights and on the day itself.
For all the social classes (varṇas) as well as for the deities, time is exceedingly dear; yet sacrifice alone is distinguished as the supreme.
That ram, though possessing horns, sometimes moves like a hornless goat; yet, when protected at home, it may go forth to rain upon half the land, acting as a powerful ruler.
In the Udāna,
it is said that a crane (*sārasa*) is superior to one who carries a burden of flesh;
he has the luster of a peacock (*nīlakaṇṭha*) upon his neck, and his throat is well-nourished and robust.
One that has been reared at home for more than a year is said to be suitable for the purpose of strength;
it is the one that cries out in many tones in the morning before all others.
But among those of a single color, the one that is fleshy and has copper-colored crests is distinguished as superior.
Now, the prohibited [actions] are set forth.
I shall describe some of the animals that are prohibited even when offerings are prescribed,
as well as those among domestic and wild beasts and birds.
A practitioner should never consume the sacrificial offering (bali) from a woman;
having offered the bali with prior knowledge [of its nature], he falls into hell.
One departs from the path through ignorance and incurs some sin;
one should not employ an animal born of a union with a woman other than one's own wife.
Furthermore, one should never offer to the Goddess a lotus that has fallen into decay,
nor one with a broken stalk, a broken petal, a broken stamen, or one whose stem is severed.
One who is one-eyed, deformed, diseased, or likewise struck by a spike,
as well as one who is wicked, whose body hair has fallen out, or who drinks milk while his two eyes are flowing— [these are to be avoided].
For in that very way, I beheld the animal and likewise the horse.
With its beak severed, its wings clipped, drooping and deprived of food,
unable to fly, it lay thus upon its mother’s lap in the *kāśa* grass.
O best of those who have been instructed, one should not give animals or birds to those who are ignorant.

One with broken limbs, one who is deficient in a limb, a child, or an elderly person is not recommended [as a sacrificer]. A woman should not give the flesh of an animal for offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), especially so.
Now follows the secondary procedure (anukalpa).
O Lord of Gods, quickly tell me the procedure for the secondary ritual (anukalpa),
whether one is a forest-dweller, a student, a householder, or any other [ascetic].
One who is sattvic, established in Brahman, and who avoids violence—
even when performing a substitute rite— should offer the animal oblation by means of that [substitute].
O fair-faced one, for the attainment of the fruits of the various stages,
[one should offer] ghee, wheat, molasses, and so forth, as well as fried grains and younger siblings.
Having prepared each respective animal, they should offer it and thereby obtain that specific fruit.
(198b) The *kuṣmāṇḍa*, the jackfruit (*panasa*), the *sava* (?), the cucumber (*karkaṭī*), the *vīlva*, and the pomegranate (*ḍāḍima*).
Grapes, dates, lakucas, rasālas, āmalakas, and jambūs.
Nālikela, ikṣudaṇḍa, mocā, āmrātaka, and tīrkarā; nālikela, ikṣudaṇḍa, mocā, āmrātaka, and tīrkarā.
The bījapūra, āragvadha, tāla, and the fruit of the lāṅgalī—

One becomes a *kuṣmāṇḍa* through [eating] buffalo meat, a *karkatī* through goat meat,

One who eats fish becomes a wild elephant; one who eats *kulasthaka* becomes a cat; one who eats *paṭola* becomes a pig; and likewise, one who eats sugar-cane or *vālluka* [becomes a pig].
O Great Goddess, when my essence is in the form of a sword, it is the plantain fruit; when in the form of a face, it is the radish; and when in the form of the marrow, it is the kaliñjaka.

With milk-rice, cakes, heated snacks, *snuḍḍraka*, and *kaśara* as the final course;

This offering (bali) is proclaimed as consisting of fried cakes, garlic, parched grain, *kalija*, and *bījahodara*, prepared through various means and endowed with the six flavors.
O Goddess, in the ritual of fierce vidyās,
one should fashion an effigy (piṇḍa) of the sacrificial victim (paśu) made either of barley flour or of grain.
O Goddess, one should cause an image made of ground black gram (māṣa) to be prepared for every ritual;
likewise, half a portion of jaggery, curd and jaggery, salt, and jaggery alone [are used].
Having wrapped a *kuṣmāṇḍa*, a coconut, a *śrīphala*, or even a *cakṣu* fruit in cloth, one should cut it with a sharp blade or similar instrument.
This offering (bali) has been declared according to the Smṛtis and inferred from the Dharmaśāstras;
here too, each preceding one is said to be superior, as is the group of eight deities.
The deity is pleased by whichever person has devotion toward whichever [deity].
One should offer the Vedic bali, consisting of cooked rice prepared with ghee,
along with red ointment and honey, for the sake of the fierce deities.
By means of the practice of the secondary rule (*anukalpa*), this Yoginī Maheśvarī,
having attained the prescribed method, shall obtain the prescribed fruit.
Now follows the sprinkling.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
"O Goddess, how many methods are there for the sprinkling of flowers, O All-pervading Lord?

The consideration of what may be given and what may not be given has been described to this extent, as well as the place, the recipient, the qualified authority, the desired object, the time of giving, and the sequence.
Now listen to the sprinkling of all [the goddesses] in a single form:
Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, and Sarasvatī.
O Maheśānī, the Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Bhairavī,
and Sāgarā rivers should establish their presence here at Ajasraṇa.
Sprinkle the root [mantra] three times with the pure water from the arghya vessel for the destruction of the fettered beings and for him who resides on Mount Hemakūṭa.
One should perform the sprinkling with these bilva leaves and water for Parā, Parameṣṭhinī, Hūṃkāra, and Mūrti, facing the east.

O Goddess, wherever there is an abundance of cattle according to the requirements of the rite, it is precisely there that [the site] endowed with all auspicious characteristics should first be sought.
One should release a vigorous, handsome, and strong animal;
thereafter, one should proceed in due order, and there is no deliberation required in that matter.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra and covered it with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should recite the Mūla-mantra and consecrate it by performing the Dhenu-mudrā.
One should properly worship with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and the various ritual offerings.
Having worshipped the sacrificial thread according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth,
one should contemplate that this triple seed-syllable, the Kāmadākinīs, abides as the vital consciousness.
Speech and feet are Phat; the anus is Para; then the eyes;
the ears; and from all the limbs, the mind is said to remain at the end.
May Sarasvatī, the Earth, Mitra, and Water,
as well as Fire, Space, the Quarters, Kālī, and the locus of action, be dissolved.
The heart-mantra, the base-mantra, and finally the eight head-mantras are clearly considered [the primary parts].
Then follow the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, and so forth, as well as fragrance, flowers, and the sacrificial oblation (bali).
One should worship the deity with the intellect and likewise bow down to them with the mind.
Now, the *paśu-gāyatrī* is as follows:
One should also whisper the Paśu-gāyatrī into the ear of the sacrificial animal;
listen now to the supreme mantra for that, as well as the combined mantra for both.
We know the form of the offering (bali), ending with the seed-syllable of the Yoginī and followed by the word *ṅenta*; O beloved Goddess, we meditate upon that which follows the word *pūrvā*.
Having uttered "tannaḥ paśu," one should then recite "vadeḥ" and "pracodayāt."
Now follows the characteristic of the sword, according to the method of the *Lakṣaṇatantra*,
by means of which the practitioner may attain accomplishment even through its mere cutting.
The sword Candrahāsa, which brings happiness, is the foremost of all;
it should be made fifty finger-breadths long, or else three spans (tāla) in length.
Is it shaped like a *karavīra* petal, or perhaps like a lotus petal?
Or else, one should pierce [the vein] with a curved sword (*kubjakhadga*) or a straight sword (*daṇḍakhadga*).
Among all those possessing great strength, the sickle is proclaimed here as the most effective;
one may cut with a knife, a razor, or even a small dagger, but not with a sword.
One should never cut or pierce with tools resembling axes or spades;
however, at the tip, middle, and hilt of a sword, one should recite the mantra three times for each pair [of syllables].
Accompanied by Vāgīśī, Brahmā; likewise Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
and Umā and Maheśvara—then he should perform the invocation.
O beloved, by means of that [mantra], which is like Kālī, the Destroyer himself, Bali is to be cut down.
Māyā, Kūrca, and Śākinī: come, come, O Bhagavatī! And you, Cāmuṇḍā, grant your presence, presided over by the Couple.
With the root mantra of the sword, one should worship the sword, whose head consists of the pair "phaṭ" devoid of the two syllables "bhava," and whose base is the mantra.
It is said that [this mantra] consists of the *tāra*, the noose (*pāśa*), the trident (*traya*), the *kūrca*, and the *śākinīs*.
One should meditate while holding flowers, and first [offer] a sword to the one with the powerful face (*valānanā*).
He has a black body, holds a *piṇāka* bow in his hand, and possesses eyes as dark as the night;
he is fierce, with a red face and eyes, and is adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Wearing red garments, with a noose in his hand and a frowning face,
he was drinking blood and devouring a mass of raw flesh.
Agitating the entire world through tremors and other such expansions,
he is encircled on his left and right sides by Death and Time.
Indeed, each one is consecrated by reciting the mantra beginning with "pūrva" and so forth.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, incense, lamps, water for the feet, and other offerings.
Then, gazing at the sword-blade, the wise one should join his palms in reverence and recite the mantra.
O you who adorn the world of the gods, the tongue belongs to Caṇḍikā;
the blood and the flesh-eating [portion] belong to that sacrificial animal.
Cut asunder this enemy of mine and bestow blessings upon me;
O you who are intoxicated with the blood of Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, salutations to you!
Having consecrated the sword with this [mantra] while reciting its eight names,
one should seize the sharpened blade, by means of which the killing becomes true.
The sword named Aśiviṃśa has a sharp edge and is difficult to approach;
likewise are Śrīgarbha and Vijaya, while Dharmapāla is indeed worthy of your salutation.
One should recite "tārakāṃ yugaṃ yajña śārilohapadam" followed by "daṇḍāyai namaḥ"; this mantra consists of sixteen syllables.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, the practitioner then rises;
this same procedure is prescribed for each of the watches of the night as well.
One should not employ a woman, a pregnant woman, a blind person, nor even a hunchback,
nor one belonging to the side of an enemy, in the work of covering the roof.
Facing north and likewise looking toward the east of the *vali*,
the practitioner should then recite this mantra:
"You are a sacrificial animal who has appeared before me by my good fortune in the form of an offering;
therefore, I bow to you, who possess all forms and who appear as the sacrificial victim."
Salutations to you, Caṇḍikā, who grants joy through the gift that destroys the misfortunes of the donor;
salutations to you, Cāmuṇḍā, who take the form of the sacrificial offering for those who bow to you.
"Rings were created by the Self-born One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I shall have her killed today, for thus the killing of a sacrifice is not a killing."
This body has been fashioned by Śiva; you, having attained the state of Śiva, are considered to have reached Śiva-hood.
Awakened from sleep, you are the auspiciousness of the non-evil; for you are indeed Śivā.

Having meditated upon the wind as having the form of a *valimat* (one with wrinkles), by means of the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Mi," one should place a flower [therein] while holding the breath (*kumbhaka*) and closing the mouth.
O beloved, having immediately slaughtered the animal with this [weapon],
one should then take its blood, hot and frothing, into vessels made of gold or other materials.
The vessels are as follows.
Now I shall describe the vessels and other items upon which the blood is to be placed;
it should be taken in a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, and the kings [to be sacrificed] must be red.
It may be made by members of the entire mandala out of copper or bronze;
even by poor householders, it may be made of bell-metal or wood.
Or else, one should never [use] a vessel made of bamboo, wood, or iron.
203b) Whether it be from the *nāraṅga*, the *sakeva*, or the rind of the coconut fruit— among all vessels for the *kaula* [practitioners], no other than the skull-cup (*kapāla*) is desired.
O beloved, whatever degree of satisfaction is said to arise for the Goddess from the flesh of those animals, that same degree of satisfaction arises even from their blood.
Whether in the case of a regular or occasional rite, or at the birth of Kātyāyanī,
one should never offer raw meat or blood without the *kali* verse.
Whether it be of an animal, a bird, or especially of a human—
now follows the result of the head-fall.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation to the Goddess according to the prescribed procedure for offering the bali,
one should discern the auspicious or inauspicious results for both the planet and the king.
This applies if [the omen occurs] in the western quarter, or in the south-west, or even in the south.
If it falls upon the head, one should declare that Hari is present here;
now hear the results for the remaining directions and intermediate points.
If the head falls in every direction,
this knowledge bestows all prosperity; one should predict the kingdom of a king.
When the head, having whirled around, falls upon the right ear, then success is attained;
at the end of a month, it will likewise occur on the left ear.
If the head falls in the northeast or in the center, there will be prosperity for kings and auspiciousness for householders.
Then, in a very short time, all success will certainly be attained,
provided that a head with its mouth open is seen fallen.
One should know his sovereign power; one should designate him as a king of kings. In a single day, he shall attain accomplishments (siddhis), and he is liberated from sin.
One should know that for householders and kings on earth,
when tears are seen here, one should then predict loss.
Whenever the sound of teeth grinding is heard anywhere, one should predict death or the loss of half one's lifespan in every such case.
The mantra-practitioner himself should place the head of the sacrificial offering in the south-eastern direction.
One should not join the inverted red vessel to the south of the *tard*;
having turned it toward the deity, one should fashion the severed portion.
At that very moment, one should know it to be auspicious; if the opposite occurs, it is middling. This is the identification of the folds (valīs), and one should place the head in front.
At the end of the ritual of the *kīlaka*, whatever else may arise should be dealt with so that no agitation occurs;
one should offer a lamp burning above the head, along with sandalwood and unbroken rice (*akṣata*).
By means of ghee, one may become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, yet he does not attain [supreme] perfection.
One should place the head facing forward, with a lamp provided without a vessel.
And that [offering] should consist of ghee, or else be sprinkled with sesame oil;
it should be offered with mustard oil, and not produced from any other fruit.
205a) One who is consecrated with the head-abhiseka by means of oil from the *vahusiddha* plant attains many siddhis; however,
one born under other asterisms encounters disease, grief, and death.
Just as hair is burned when it is placed in a fire, so too [is it for] men;
one should offer a wick made of thread, for a wick made of cloth does not shine.
The measurement of the thumb and its length should be six finger-breadths;
one should provide twenty-one threads made from *kārtala* fibers.
One should make it fragrant with substances such as camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood,
especially for the planets, tortoises, and the iguana.
One should not cause a lamp to be placed even on the head of those birds;
for as long as the lamp remains burning over the head, [the merit is lost].
One shall dwell in heaven for that length of time; therefore, one should diligently cause [the offering] to be given.
By smelling the fragrance arising from the burnt oblation (*homa*), the Goddess becomes pleased.
Therefore, one should nourish the lamp; therefore, one should avoid extinguishing it.
For while the lamp is being given, one attains death in Nirvana.
Then, having first prepared the vessel for the Goddess, adorned with sacrificial animals,
one should offer sugar, durvā grass, and the three great clarified butters.
The practitioner, aiming for the fulfillment of desires, should cause rock salt, śṛṅgavera, and plantain fruit to fall among sweet things.
The wise one should divide [the vessel] into eight parts, placing a single blade of *kuśa* grass and other materials in the center;
having offered a small amount of clarified butter there, he should perform the ritual with the *tarpaṇa-mudrā*.
The libation for the goddesses who partake in the portions should indeed be performed twice each;
[this applies] from the first and last Tālāhāras, including the middle and the beginning, up to Manonipi.
One should offer libations with the formula joined as "I satisfy [the name] also by food," and the second form should be in the dative case,
as uttered in the second word.
In the center is the one called Nityoditā; the ritual action (kriyā) is like a vessel for the sacred seat (pīṭha).
In the eastern direction is Diṣṭi, and in the southern direction is Cāmuṇḍā, who is the Yoginī.
Ḍākinī is in the west, Bhairavī in the northwest,
Vidāginī in the southeast, and Pāparākṣasī in the southwest.
Pūtanā is in the northwest, and likewise Kālikā is in the northeast;
then one should perform a hymn of praise with palms joined in reverence before her.
Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World! Victory to you, who removes the flood of sins!
Victory to you, who have acted as a forest fire to the grass of birth, old age, and disease!
Victory to you, O destroyer of all adversity! Victory to you, O goddess worshipped by the thirty deities! Victory to you, whose form is eternal bliss! Victory to you, the bestower of protection!
Obeisance to you who destroy the disease of worldly existence with the hand of the arrow of wisdom;
O Victorious Bhīmā, O Victorious Ghorā, O Savior from the perils of the world!
Her body is full and her form is not languid, having tasted the nectar of victory;
she has three eyes, and her face is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She who brings about the destruction of all asuras, who wields the elephant-goad, the sword, and the khaṭvāṅga staff;
she who is most terrible with a great roar, the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas.
O Goddess Kālarātri, accept this animal offering;
O Great Caṇḍī, be pleased and protect me who has come to you for refuge.
O Goddess, grant me long life, wealth, fortune, and fame;
grant me a wife, sons, and all my desires.
O fierce one, O Caṇḍā, you are Pracaṇḍā, O you who possess a most formidable Karavāla sword;
O Goddess of the Universe, whose great arms are fierce and terrible, salutations be to you!
O Protector, for me who has come to you for refuge with my mind offered at your feet,
remove my sin, O Red One, remove my sorrow, and remove my unhappiness.
O Beloved, remove my fever, remove my agitation, and remove the demon;
having recited this hymn in this manner, prostrate yourself on the ground like a staff.
O Guhyakālī, Mother of the World, Inner Ruler of all, Sovereign Goddess,
accept this animal offering and grant the fruits as described!
Neither by body, nor mind, nor speech is my way other than truth;
you move within all beings as the blazing Supreme Goddess.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīkaularahasyasarvāgamasāra*.

207a) Now, because they are all equally applicable, he explains the meditation and so forth for each of the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the determination of the fifty phonemes,
by which, O Goddess, the entire three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, are pervaded.
For each individual letter, however, there are meditations, dhāraṇīs, forms, weapons, vehicles, assemblies, and mudrās; their ritual functions are distinct for each.
Listen to all this in brief as I tell it to you; for although there are many varieties of mantra-essences, they all possess that same essential flavor.
The animals are said to begin with Satpāda and end with Īśāna, with Sumadhyama and Iḍa in between;
the ignorant man should offer these to Brahmā and the others for the sake of liberation from the cycle of birth.
These are the fifty syllables and likewise the five kalās;
these are the five elements born from the earth, each distinct from the other.
The entire universe of fourteen worlds is pervaded on all sides by Brahman;
