Adorned with three eyes as beautiful as blooming blue lotuses,
her two feet are marked by red lotuses that blossom at the sound of her tinkling anklets.
O Goddess, your waist is exceedingly beautiful, adorned with three folds that shine forth, while the girdle upon it is rendered charming by its contact with the lovely curves of your rounded hips.
Her navel was deep and spiraling, adorned with a circle like a pool;
she was smeared with *yakṣa*-ointment, and her full, elevated breasts were firm.
Adorned with pearl necklaces produced from the jars of the Kumbhīkumbha ocean,
wearing upper garments of fine linen, and decorated with garlands of flowers.
His arms shone with armlets set with rubies, gold, and lapis lazuli;
his ears were adorned with earrings fashioned from radiant gold and rubies; and his fingers were decorated with various glittering jewel rings.
One should meditate upon her who has a neck like a conch-shell, whose hands resound with the sound of bracelets,
who is adorned with various ornaments, and who is utterly amazed by the song of the sage.
Adorned with jeweled earrings as radiant as the light of the rising sun,
her ears were graced by golden ear-ornaments that shone like the crescent moon.
Her lower lip is beautiful with the luster of shimmering coral, and she is adorned by a row of teeth that shine charmingly as they emerge from her youthful smile.
Her beautiful face has the form of a plucked autumn śaradākā bird;
her eyebrows playfully arch like a bow with five arrows.
She bears a nose that is elevated, well-nourished, and blazingly uplifted,
adorned with rays of light resembling the full orb of the cool-rayed moon.
Endowed with the intense fragrance of musk,
his hair becomes especially smooth, glossy, dark blue, and beautiful.
Carrying the fragrance of the flowers of the *pārijāta* tree, with hair standing on end,
they were like a mass of molten gold, a flood of various jewels, the ultimate limit of the earth of beauty, and the birthplace of splendors.
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, the abode of the splendor of grace,
holding a lotus in her left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā) with her right hand.
O Great Goddess, you who bestow long life, I bow to you as you rest upon the palms of your lotus hands,
seated upon a pedestal fashioned from Dharma and the other virtues, and adorned with the four gates.
One should worship this [deity] in the pericarp of a lotus enriched with eight petals, filaments, and spokes.
222a) Now, the Mātaṅgīs:
One should draw a six-cornered [figure] and an eight-petalled lotus, and write the beautiful mantra upon it;
within this, one should worship the nine Śaktis in their proper sequence from the beginning.
His meditation is as follows.

She is dark-complexioned, possessing the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, and has three eyes; she sits upon a throne of excellent jewels, adorned with ornaments of refined gems, and has a slender waist.
One should meditate upon her with full, rounded breasts and a smiling face,
holding in succession in her hands a goad, a sword-blade, a noose, and likewise a khaṭaka.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, [one should worship] the Bhuvaneśvarīs with captivating perfumes and flowers.
Outside, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with sixteen surrounding petals;
in the center of the pericarp, one should draw a beautiful six-cornered hexagon.
His meditation is as follows.
I worship Bhuvaneśvarī, whose crown possesses the splendor of the rising moon, who has breasts like bees, who is endowed with three eyes,
whose face is smiling, who bestows boons, and whose hands hold a lotus stalk.
222b) Now follows the sequence of Dhūmāvatī.
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā on the previously mentioned pedestal for the removal of enemies;
the six limbs are in the filaments, and the eight Śaktis reside in the petals.
His meditation is as follows.
Pale, unsteady, dark and tall, wearing soiled garments,
her earrings fallen off and her teeth sparse— such is the widow.
Mounted upon chariots with crow-emblems, their breasts were hanging down; with heads in hand and eyes extremely harsh, they were filled with haste as they shook their hands.
Their body hair was greatly increased, their matted locks were disheveled, and their eyes were distorted;
they were constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and were always intent on quarreling.
One should always meditate in this manner and then perform the ritual action. Now, [the mantra of] Vagalāmukhī:
Having drawn [the central design] in the middle, one should draw a six-spoked wheel outside of that;
outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that, a sixteen-petaled one.
Outside, there are three squares, adorned with four gates;
this is its visualization.
She was deep and intoxicated with passion, resembling molten gold;
she had four arms, three eyes, and was seated upon a lotus throne.
Mudgala is on the right side, while Jihvā and Vajraka are on the left;
she wears yellow garments and possesses dense, round, and full breasts.
Adorned with golden earrings, wearing a yellow crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
and decorated with yellow ornaments, she is seated upon a golden throne.
Having meditated thus, O Goddess of the gods, upon her who effects the paralysis of enemies.
Now, the meaning of the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī.

Having abandoned and having taken up [the previous and subsequent forms], this very word and its form are said to be uttered as a single, fused [utterance] when joined with the suffixes *mu* and *kṛt*. (1)
O Maheśānī, Mount Kailāsa is established within the seed-syllable of space (vyoma);
and from the seed-syllable of fire (vahni), gold and other precious materials are produced in many ways, O beloved.
Therefore, that which proceeds in the world situated upon the circle of the earth is sustained by the sound of musical instruments in the netherworld (pātāla) through the form of Śeṣa. || 3 ||
She is the mistress even of that great terrestrial circle and of Pātāla;
for this very reason, O beloved Maheśānī, she is the sovereign of the worlds.

In the syllable *ha* is the ether (*vyoma*), by the fourth vowel is the origin of wind (*anila*), and in *vā* with the *i* and the *tila* (anusvāra) is foam (*phena*); these are the very forms of Brahman itself.
The potency of fire (ra) is known by the Vasus; its earth-element (la) is Udraka.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, the letters Ra and La are considered identical.
Flooding the three worlds with the nectar-form of the Bindu, she becomes liquid;
therefore, they flow forth by means of pure consciousness alone.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, she is called Bhuvaneśī.
Now he describes the Yoni-mudrā.
The Goddess said:
The *yonimudrā* has been described with effort by the one who shines as Brahma;
I now desire to hear about it, as well as the characteristics of the *mudrās*.
What is the name of the yoni-mudrā, and what is its fruit, O Lord?
"O Lord of the World, tell me its arrangement and its essential nature.
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, you who are the embodiment of the knowledge of mudrās;
having known this, all practitioners [become] oceans of the nectar of wisdom.
Through the yoga of excessive proximity, they wipe away [their sins] along with their kinsmen once;
the body of Śaśa consists of ninety-six *tulās*, being composed of both.
O Dear One, at the end of the guḍadhvaja is a central point, [measuring] one ḍaccha less than a tulam;
it is twice as wide as that and adorned in the form of a circle.
The primary channel has not arisen there;
rather, the *iḍā* channel is situated on the left and the *piṅgalā* is situated on the right.
The three channels situated in the middle extend to the back of the head;
they reach both big toes at birth, and then to the crest and the head.
She is the abode of Brahman, appearing in the form of a blazing fire.
The channel situated in the middle of that [lotus], called Citrā, is dear to the yogin;
it is the Dharmanī, variegated in the center, located at the region of the vajra-penis.
They know the Brahma-randhra to be located there, appearing like the filament of a lotus;
the Moon moves through the Iḍā, and the Sun through the Piṅgalā.
Listen, O Suṣumnā and Tura, according to all the rules:
situated in the center of the Ādhāra-kanda is a most beautiful triangle.
O Goddess of the gods, in the center of the triangle is the unsurpassed Kāma-bīja;
there, arising from that Kāma-bīja, is the supreme Svayambhū-liṅga.
There, the supreme goddess Kuṇḍarī, dark-complexioned Mahālakṣmī, is in the form of three concentric circles and is encircled by a self-manifested liṅga.
The self-existent Liṅga shines forth to all;
there, the supreme goddess Kuṇḍalī exists in the form of the triple dissolution.
Dark-complexioned and exceedingly subtle, she encircles the self-manifested linga;
the soul of all beings shines forth, appearing like one who is asleep.
225a) She who dwells upon the *haṃsa* bears her own form as one adorned with earrings;
she is eternally supported by the *haṃsa*-prāṇa and rests within the channel of the vital breaths (*prāṇanāḍī*).
Just as the wind rises from the base for all embodied beings,
having reached the body, it moves outward through its own channels.
Therefore, impelled by the vital breath (prāṇa) to a measure of twelve finger-breadths,
one should recite [the mantra] upon a pure seat made of deerskin or kusha grass, which is pleasant to the taste.
By practicing this for one month, the yogi shall become supreme on the path of yoga;
he should draw the external breath through the *iḍā* by means of that very *mudrā*.
One should retain the filled air by means of both [nostrils] through kumbhaka,
and then exhale it very slowly through the piṅgalā nāḍī.
One should practice this repeatedly and gradually through constant repetition;
thus, for a person who has died, the emergence of his own body [from the corpse] is the lowest [of the signs].
The middling [practitioner], being disciplined, should then practice the relinquishing of the ground;
in this sequence, the wise one should effect the purification of the *ḍākinīs*.
Then, one should place the left side of the foot upon the secret place;
the Great Goddess should cause her right foot to rest upon that.
With the body straight and the head and neck aligned, one should not fill the abdomen with air at an improper time by means of the mouth like a crow's beak.
Having firmly bound the sense organs with the fingers, being composed,
one should cover both ears with the two thumbs and both eyes with the two index fingers.
When there is intense pain in the nostrils and the two tendons of the neck (manyā),
one should remember that the vital breath (prāṇa) has become one with the mind.
One should properly retain the vital air (māruta); this is yoga, beloved by yogis.
Afterwards, when it has entered the heart-center, it becomes equal to the sound of a drum, gradually and subtly.

Resembling the roar of intoxicated elephants, deer, and birds, the sound of the drums was vast; another [sound] was like the resonance of bamboo flutes filled with the neighing of horses and other [animals].
After that, it is like the sound of a bell, then like a thick cloud, and finally, it is like one's own voice.
Then, one should contemplate the supreme deity Kuṇḍalinī, who resembles a sevenfold [coil],
encircling the mouth of the Suṣumnā.
The supreme practitioner should meditate upon the form of Kāmaśiva, red in color, revolving within the womb situated in his beloved.
Then, one should meditate upon the Unstruck (anāhata) within the heart, the digit of consciousness (citkalā) resting upon the swan (haṃsa),
having the form of a lamp-flame and possessing the nature of Kuṇḍalinī.
With the mantra *haṃsa*, the wise practitioner should lead the goddess Kuṇḍalinī— who is of the nature of light and pervades the universe— to the lotus of Brahman.
Likewise, through the path of the junctions of the six cakras,
one should lead the supreme Kuṇḍalinī, together with the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa), upward into the Suṣumnā.
Supported by the stationary wind, one should lead the *brahman* very gradually;
by that very wind, those lotuses are turned upward.
The yogi, being well-disciplined, should cultivate [this] with a mind following the path of knowledge.
In the *ādhāra*, one should contemplate a very beautiful lotus with four petals;
in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, at the base of the *liṅga*, one should contemplate a six-petaled lotus.
In Manipūra at the base of the navel, one should meditate on the goddess Surasundarī with ten petals;
in Anāhata at the heart, one should meditate on her possessing twelve shoulders.
In the great wheel called Viśuddha, there is the sixteen-petalled lotus of the moon;
likewise, in the great wheel called Ājñā, in the center of the earth, there is the lotus of ambrosia.
O Goddess, having pierced the cakras beginning with the Ādhāra, you who are of the nature of light lead Kuṇḍalinī,
the supreme deity, to the lotus of Brahman.
Ḍākinī, Lākinī, Lākini, Sākinī,
Kākini, and Hākini— these six are the deities of the cakras.
O Maheśvarī, having joined these [elements] with the nature of Brahman within the six cakras,
one should establish Kuṇḍalī as the consort in the Sahasrāra, the abode of Brahmā.
And there, within that very lotus of Brahman, resides the Lord Paramātman;
Kuṇḍarī is his form as Śakti, while he himself is the head of Paramātman.
Indeed, by means of the necklace of the equality of action, one should perceive the unity of those two;
one should dissolve the principles beginning with earth into the state of the living soul (jīva).
She is that very Supreme Sovereign, the delight of the Moon-headed One,
the supreme state beyond death, an ocean of the nectar of knowledge.
Therefore, one should contemplate the stream emerging from that [lotus] as entering the six petals;
and from the contact with that, one should contemplate the wheels and the forms of light.
One should place the nectar within the thousand-petaled great lotus;
by means of that nectar, one attains Kuṇḍalī, the supreme deity.
By that very armor, O Goddess, he should lead [the deity] back again to its own place;
for that best of practitioners should meditate upon knowledge as his eternal self.
One should contemplate the deities of the six cakras as having become liquefied by the nectar,
and then settle them each in their own respective locations within the great lotus.
O fair-faced one, for the Vaiṣṇava, the Śākta, and the Śaureya,
the union with the power of Śiva leads to the attainment of great knowledge.
Then, one should visualize the rosary within the Citriṇī channel;
it consists of fifty jewels and is Mātṛkā, Sarasvatī herself.
The rosary is proclaimed to consist of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*;
the letter *kṣa* is the form of Mount Meru, and by means of it, the colors [of the beads] are never lost.
O Supreme Goddess, the arrangement of the sequence of letters, starting with 'a' and ending with 'la', proceeds in order both forward and backward through the garland of phonemes.
One should mentally recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
by reciting the mantra with the mind, one will certainly attain the perfection of the mantra.
At the beginning of the recitation of one hundred and eight [mantras], one should first perform the purification of the lineage;
having performed the mantra-recitation eight times, one should again abandon the neuter [syllable].
The wise one should recite [the mantra] eight times for the liberation of the groups.
Having thus recollected the letter ending with the bindu from the eight groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *śa*, one should thereafter recollect the mantra.
Thus, O Goddess, the supreme characteristics of the mudrās have been told to you;
by means of this mudrā, O Goddess, [one attains] satisfaction from sleep and so forth, up to the end.
One should recite the mantra for one month, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with senses subdued;
O Maheśvarī, there is no [obstacle] there regarding the form of the womb.
In that regard, O Dear One, the gods do not accept whatever worship, fire-oblations, and so forth are offered by a guru who is devoid of power; how then can a disciple [attain] power?
When the root of the tree is cut, O Goddess, whence can there be flowers, fruits, and the like?
O Pārvatī, the mind is in one place, Śiva is in another, and Śakti is in yet another.
O fair-faced one, they do not attain success even in ten million eons by those who are deceitful;
therefore, the wise person should diligently understand the Yonimudrā and the Mahāmudrā.
O Goddess, without knowing Śakara, one is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood;
this mudrā has been kept secret by me even in the Tantras and the Yāmala.
"Now it has been told, O Goddess; listen, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Thus ends the description of the Yonimudrā in the *Śrīmantramuktāvalī*, in the dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrīkaularahasya*, the essence of all Āgamas. || 29 ||
Now he speaks the armor (kavaca) of the ten great vidyās.
Therein, first, [the mantra] of Śyāmā:
Bhairavī said:
O Lord, O Anātha, I have heard about ritual action, worship, and the three kinds of dispositions;
now I wish to hear the armor (kavaca) previously mentioned.
"O Lord, you alone are my refuge; deliver me from this distress and calamity.
Bhairava said:
Listen to the secret, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life;
I shall speak the armor named Śrījaganmaṅgala, which is the very embodiment of mantra.
By reciting or retaining this, one may delude the three worlds in an instant;
even Nārāyaṇa, having assumed the form of a woman, [deluded] Maheśvara.
In Yoga, having maintained the state of non-distraction through the practice of *śam*, the bearer of wisdom (*dhudvaha*) [attains stability].
The night-stalker Rāvaṇa, arrogant because of his boon, indeed slew [the gods] beginning with Indra;
yet by whose negligence even the Lord who conquered the three worlds was slain.
Even Kuvera, the lord of wealth, is the lord of the gods and the master of those who roam the earth;
indeed, all these are but portions of the Goddess, the beloved mistress of all accomplishments.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca) of Śrī Pagu Maṅgala is Śiva;
the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity (devatā) is Kā Dakṣiṇeti.
The application of the *Duṣṭavijaya* mantra, which deludes the worlds and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is proclaimed as the means for attracting women.
May the supreme one-syllabled mantra *kālikāpatukīṃ* protect my head;
*krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, may Kālikā, the bearer of the sword, protect my forehead.
HŪṂ HŪṂ may protect my pair of eyes; HRĪṂ HRĪṂ may protect my two ears. May Kālīkā protect [me] on the right, and Maheśvarī protect my pair of nostrils.
*Krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, may she protect the tongue; *hūṃ hūṃ*, may she protect the cheeks;
*hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, O you whose form is the essence of sound (*svarūpiṇī*), may she protect the entire face!
The twenty-two-syllable *skandha* is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) that bestows happiness;
may Kālī, who bears a sword and a severed head, protect me from all directions according to all the scriptures.
May Krīṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Kṣarī protect my heart; may Cāmuṇḍā protect it. Aiṃ Hūṃ Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā protects the pair of breasts and the region of the nape of the neck.
May the Great Vidyā of eight syllables, together with the hand-attributes, protect my two arms;
may the six-syllabled mantra—krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ—protect my two hands.
Hrīṃ protects the middle of the nose, and Caḥ, like Kālikā, protects the south;
Hrīṃ Svāhā protects the back—she is the ten-syllabled Kālikā.
HŪM HŪM, O Dakṣiṇakālikā, HŪM HŪM! May she protect both hips.
The ten-syllable mantra of Kālī is "Svāhā," which protects the pair of thighs at their ends.
Oṃ jrīṃ hrīṃ me svāhā! May Kālikā always protect my knees.
This Vidyā, named Kālī-hṛdaya, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
May Krīṃ Hūṃ Krīṃ, who is like Kālikā at the right ankle, protect me;
may the fourteen-syllable mantra Hrīṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā protect my [other] limbs.
May she who holds a sword and a mace protect [us], and may she who bestows the boons of granting wishes and fearlessness protect us;
and may he who is beneficial to all scriptures protect us with all the sciences.
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kulyā, Kulukulyā, Virodhinī,
Viprācittā, Ugrā, Prabhā, Īsā, and others such as Anviṣā.
And Nīlāṣanāvalākā, who partakes of the measure-seal (mātrāmudrā);
all these carry swords and are adorned with garlands of severed heads.
But in the cardinal and intermediate directions, let Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Maheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā protect me for a hundred thousand leagues.
Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī, adorned with all [their ornaments], [are present];
and a hundred thousand weapons are likewise situated in the various directions.
Thus has this divine armor, most wonderful, been recounted to you.
The great armor known as Śrījaganmaṅgala,
which is the armor of the three worlds and the armor of Brahman, has been uttered from my own mouth.
One should perform the armor-rite (kavaca) either three times, once, or even five times.
By reciting this one hundred times for the Mothers, one shall become victorious throughout the three worlds;
by his grace alone, one shall agitate the three worlds.

By reciting this [hymn] with a handful of flowers before Kālikā, one becomes a great poet and shall become a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*). Whoever performs this, he has accomplished his purpose.
One shall obtain the fruit of worship for a hundred thousand years if one writes [this] on birch bark and wears it,
or if one holds it placed within gold.
If one should wear it on the crest-lock, on the right arm, or on the neck, it will,
through its wrath, delude the three worlds; it will delude the three worlds in an instant.
One shall possess sons, wealth, and splendor, and become a treasury of various sciences.
Furthermore, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others meet their destruction simply by touching his body;
and any woman who is barren, or whose children have died, [is likewise purified].

Whether on the throat or on the left [hand], with the syllables *hau* and *hau*, she who performs the protection (*kavaca*) will have many children and her offspring will live; this is certain regarding the sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
It must not be given to the disciple of another;
[it should be given] to disciples endowed with devotion, and not otherwise, lest one meet death.
Having cast aside rivalry, O Goddess of Speech,
you reside with certainty upon this pedestal in my mouth, remaining steadfast until the end of my descendants.
If one should practice the Akṣakālikā mantra without knowing its secret speech (*vaca*),
then even if it has been recited a hundred million times, that vidyā will not be accomplished for him.
He meets with the destruction of his mantras and shall soon meet death;
therefore, with every effort, one should place this destroyer at the forefront.
When recited with proper repetition, Kālī will certainly grant success to the practitioner.
Thus ends the Śyāmākavaca, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, from the Śrībhairava [Tantra]. || 1 ||
Now he speaks the armor (kavaca) of Tārā.
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, Tālā questioned Śaṅkara;
speak with respect regarding that which you have kept hidden.
By what means, O beloved knower of mantras, would the body become firm and very strong, or how might there be incomparable accomplishment for you?
The illustrious Tārā said:
For this is most secret, having issued from the lotus of my mouth;
O Lord, I declare this supreme mystery unto you.
Having heard this armor from my own mouth with focused attention,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha were told by the Lotus-born One [Brahmā] regarding their heads.
O Lord of Gods, by its power, one does not go to non-existence, nor to Viṣṇu;
O Bhava, you do not remember that which was previously well-spoken regarding the rosary.
This armor, extracted from the essence of the *Yoginīmata*,
must not be spoken of to anyone, nor should it be revealed in any way whatsoever.
O Goddess, if you have affection for me,
then listen with focused attention to this armor that provides complete protection.
Truth, truth, again and again!
O Lord, I am certain that if anyone worships me for even a moment without the armor-mantra, the Yoginīs will immediately seize him like a fierce crocodile.

One should diligently protect the seed-syllable of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, which is the root consisting of one hundred thousand [repetitions]; above that is the seed-syllable of Śakti, which is the Liṅga.
May the seed-syllable *Vadhu* always protect Maṇipūra, especially;
may the seed-syllable *Varma* protect Anāhata for me from every side and in every way.
May the weapons always protect the pure [deity] adorned at the throat;
may Śeṣa, however, eternally protect my station of command, the two-leaved [seat].
May the star Śīrṣamyā protect the matted locks of his head; may Nīlasarasvatī always protect his face, for she is indeed the deity of the seed-syllable *va*.
May the two breasts, which destroy the obstacles of Kurca and Vighna, always protect [me];
may the eternal Goddess Lakṣmī always protect my tongue.
May Sarasvatī always protect the tip of the tongue with effort;
may Rati always protect the seed, and Prīti always protect the mouth during the ritual act.
May Fame always protect fame; may Peace always protect peace;
may Nourishment protect my nourishment, and may Contentment always protect contentment.
May Vairocana protect the conch, and likewise may Śaṅkha protect the eastern direction;
may Loma always protect the cheek, and may Sarvaga protect it eternally.
May Padmanābha always protect the navel and the leaf-like membrane of the abdomen; may Asitābha protect the genitals, and Nāmaka protect the four eyes.
May Māmaka protect my hands; may Pāṇḍara protect my neck;
may Tarakva protect my heart; and may Padmāntaka protect my back.
May Mayāntaka protect my flanks always; may Narāntaka protect my face;
and may Vighnāntaka, whose body is eternal, protect my feet forever.
May Tārā, the Supreme Goddess, constantly protect my eight limbs;
O God, this armor (kavaca), which has issued from my mouth, has thus been told.
O Lord of Gods, if through negligence it is revealed anywhere whatsoever,
I shall slay those [who reveal it], and I myself shall perform the piercing.
One should bestow [the teaching] upon a disciple who is peaceful, endowed with the tantra and mantra, and possessed of devotion to the guru; then, unsurpassed accomplishment will arise.
The entire secret has been told, which bestows infinite fruit;
O Lord, it must be guarded by you and never revealed at any time.
Thus ends the Eka-jaṭā-kavaca as declared in the Śrī-yoginī-tantra. || 2 ||
Now, the Chinnamastā-kavaca.
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
O Lord of my life, those mantras of Chinnamastā which were spoken by you, the Protector, and kept well concealed, have now been heard by me and recounted by me.
Now I desire to hear of the armor previously mentioned;
O Lord, please tell me out of compassion that which is named Trailokyavijaya.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, who are saluted by all the deities; I shall declare the armor known as Trailokyavijaya, which infatuates even Śiva.
Consisting of all vidyās, it directly bestows victory upon gods and asuras;
by its retention, the powerful one becomes victorious over the three worlds through the winds and other weapons.
O Goddess of the Gods, because he sustains Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and because he is the source of the five elements and so forth,
he is the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds.
It should not be given even to those of other sects, and especially not to those who lack devotion.
This was given by Śikhī to his devotee, who is dearer to him than life itself;
it is the armor (kavaca) of the goddess Chinnamastā, [revealed] by Bhairava.
The seer is Saṃprāvirāta, the meter is Devatācchinna-mastakā,
and the application is proclaimed as being for the sake of victory over the three worlds.
May Huṃkāra protect my head; may Chinnamastā, with the luster of fire, protect [my face].
May Hrīṃ Hūṃ Aiṃ, the six-syllabled one clad in red garments, protect my forehead.
Śrīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Aiṃ Dṛpāṇo Tu Muṇḍeka Tridharāpi Sā;
may that Vidyā, beginning and ending with the Praṇava and consisting of two pure syllables, protect me always.
Vajravairocanī huṃ huṃ phaṭ | Svāhā, beginning with the eternal [syllable].
May Cinnamastā, who bears her own severed head in three ways, protect my life-force!
O Śrīmāyā, O Vajravairocanī, [endowed with] the seed-syllables *kūrca* and *vāk*, *hūṃ*!
Huṃ phaṭ svāhā! This is the sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā, whose form is that of Brahmā;
she joyfully stretches out her own garland of rays from the two buds on her sides.
May Chinnamastā, who is intent upon protecting [her devotees] at all times,
who holds the gesture of protection (abhaya-mudrā) and the skull-cup (kapāla), and who is crimson in hue, grant the desires of the practitioner.
May that Varṇinī Ḍākinī, who is joined with Chinnamastā and Śaktikā, also protect me from all sides.
May Ramā and the others protect the tongue; may Larjā protect the palate and the throat;
may Kūrca and the others protect the heart; and may Vāk and the others protect the pair of breasts.
May the Goddess of the Suras, encased by *ramā*, protect the two eyes;
may the sky-clad goddess (*digambarī*), encased by *māyā*, protect the region of the navel.
May the Goddess, encapsulated by the *kūrca* mantra, always protect [me] from behind; and may He, together with Śakti, protect my middle, encapsulated by the *vāgbīja*.
The syllable *īśvarī*, the *kurca* seed-syllable, the *vāgbīja*, and *vajravairocanīya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—
this great vidyā possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Chinnamastā, who always possesses the two thighs of the fallen and the Śakti;
Hrāṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ is the letter-form; Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ is the Ḍākinī at the knees and feet.
May she who abides in all vidyās and is eternal protect all my limbs forever;
O Yoginī of the single liṅga, protect me from the south-eastern quarter.
May Dākinī protect [me] in the south; may Śrī-Śrī-Mahābhairavī protect [me] in the west; may Bhairavī protect [me] in the northwest;
may Indrākṣī protect [me] in the north; and may Sitā protect me in the northeast.
May the Withdrawer (Saṃhāriṇī) always protect [me] in the northeast corner;
may Śivā with her trident protect [me] in the eight directions and intermediate points along with her trident.

*Krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, may she protect me in the east; *hūṃ hūṃ*, may she protect me in the southeast. *Hrīṃ hrīṃ*, may Kālikā protect me in the south; *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, and indeed [may she protect me] in the southwest. *Huṃ huṃ*, may she protect me in the west; *hrīṃ hrīṃ*, may she protect me in the northwest. *Svāhā*, may she always protect me in the north.
Mahākālī, with a sword in her hand, is in the northeast; this great mantra consists of *sadā*, *vartāro*, *māyāvadhu*, *kūrca*, and *phaṭ*.
May she who holds a sword and a trident protect the upper regions;
and may Nīlasarasvatī, with the syllables Hrīṃ, Strīṃ, and Hūṃ, protect the netherworld.
Thus has been told to you the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess, whose very form is mantra;
by wearing which Bhīma became the Lord known as Krodhabhairava from the Wind-god.
He himself becomes the creator and destroyer of the gods, asuras, and sages;
she whose first [manifestation] is Madhumatī comes into the presence of the practitioner.
The Yakṣiṇīs beginning with Bhūtinī, and the Cāraṇas beginning with the Ḍākinīs, carry out his commands; this is due to the grace of the Goddess, by whom their [power] has been severed.
O Goddess, this very supreme Brahman is the armor (kavaca) uttered from his mouth;
having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings, one should recite it thus once at the root mantra.
One shall obtain the fruit of a worship performed for a full year;
this [mantra] written on the arm or placed within a golden pill [yields the same result].
If, by good fortune, one should wear it on the right side,
having become endowed with all sovereignty, he shall bring the three worlds under his control.
Lakṣmī shall dwell in his home, and Vāṇī in the lotus of his mouth;
the Brahmāstras and other scriptures shall meet with defeat against his body.
If one should recite the Chinnamastā mantra without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca),
he too will swiftly meet death by the stroke of a weapon.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Armor of Tārā for Conquering the Three Worlds," within the *Chinnamastākalpa* from the *Śrī Bhairavatestra*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Now, he [the author] states the armor (kavaca) of Mahātripurasundarī.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, O Goddess of the gods, you who bestow grace upon the worlds;
by your favor, O Mahādeva, many mantras have been heard by me in various ways.

O Lord, I have heard from you about the various means of accomplishment (sādhana), as well as the upward-holding of Devakī and Kīra, and the binding and subduing by means of nooses and other instruments.
O Sovereign of the Queens of Kings, you have taught me the mantras and the armor;
O Lord, I desire to hear the truth regarding that—please speak it to me.
The illustrious Īśvara said:
"O Great Queen, you have been restrained again and again for hundreds of thousands of years; yet, O beloved, you ask me about the nature of women."
O Goddess of the gods, listen as I tell you for your own benefit this secret inner armor, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
The venerable Śrīṣoḍaśī Vidyā is recorded as the Ṛṣi of this armor (kavaca); Mahādeva is the Prastāra, and the Pakti meter is declared.
O Goddess, Queen of the Kings of Kings, you are proclaimed as the supreme deity;
O Goddess who accomplishes all aims, the methods of practice have been fully described.
May Bhairavī protect me in the east; may Trāsinī protect me in the south; and may she who is even more terrifying than Trāsinī protect me in the north.
May Mahādevī Mahātripurasundarī protect [me] above;
may the Goddess of the gods, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla, protect [me] below.
May Vāgbhava protect me in the foundation, may Kāmarāja likewise protect me in the heart,
and may Bhārama, the granter of all desires, protect me eternally in the head.
O Supreme Goddess, may the Blessed Mahāvidyā protect me always at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), in all the limbs, and in every location of the subtle channels.
May Aiṃ Klīṃ protect me on the forehead; may Hrīṃ Klīṃ Vlūṃ, together with Śaśvat, protect the two eyes.
One should place *drāṃ* and *draṃ* on the nose and the two eyes, and likewise *drīṃ* on the chin.
May *sauḥ* protect the throat and the heart; may *manu saḥ krīṃ* protect the navel and the secret place.
KALA HRĪṂ KLĪṂ STRĪṂ may protect my secret place; SA HRĪṂ may protect my feet; SA HRĪṂ MĀṂ may protect me everywhere; MA KLĪṂ may protect my joints.
May she who is swift, along with Hrīṃ and Krīṃ, protect me in water, on land, in Kāśī, in the palace of the King of Directions, and in the sky— she who is born of the mind.
And may Haṃśa protect you, O Great Goddess, as well as the supreme, stainless deities:
Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Utā, Kalyāṇī, and Bhagamālinī.
"May Jñānā and Mālinī, the auspicious Vidyā, protect me at all times.
Thus, O Goddess, is this armor, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Out of affection for you, I have related this which must be guarded with great effort; O beloved, this is the supreme secret, more hidden than the hidden.
For one who possesses this pair of mantras, it is auspicious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it destroys evil dreams and brings men, kings, and others under one's control.
O Goddess, O Śivā, O Queen of the Queens of Kings, this armor brings about attraction and the immobilization of the enemy's weapons; without knowing this, [one cannot attain success].
One should worship her with hosts of yoginīs; there is no doubt that she will consume [the offerings].
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, his mantras shall never attain success;
moreover, in this world, he shall suffer from disease, misery, and fear.
Having gone to hell in the next world, one may enter the womb of an animal;
therefore, through constant practice of this, one shall thereafter become qualified.
This most meritorious armor and the procedure for worship have issued from my mouth; by placing them before oneself according to the prescribed method,
one enjoys good fortune, pleasures, delights, and auspicious things, and at the time of death, one attains the state of the Goddess.
Thus ends the complete armor (kavaca) of the sixteen-fold Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, from the Kulāntasaṃhitā.
Now, [the hymn] to Tripurabhairavī.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, expert in all scriptures!
Have mercy, O Lord of the world; you are the knower of dharma, O high-minded one.
O Bhairavī of Tripura, tell me truly that divine armor (kavaca) belonging to that beautiful Vidyā who was previously described.
Having heard those words of hers, the Sovereign of the Universe spoke.
The wondrous armor of the goddess Sundarī was [assumed] by Virūpākṣa and others.
Śrī Īśvara said:
I shall speak the armor of the Great Vidyā, which is difficult to obtain in all circumstances;
listen to it according to the prescribed rite, for once heard, it must be guarded more carefully than even water.
By whose grace I sustain the three worlds in their entirety;
from whom everything has arisen, and in whom it still abides even today.
She is the mother and father honored by the world, whose very nature is the protection of the universe;
she is the bestower of perfection (siddhi) and is perfected (siddha) toward those who are perfected, yet remains unaccomplished (asiddha) toward wicked beings.
May the Goddess Kakāra, who brings benefit to all beings, who is the very nature of all beings, who is full of desire and bestows all desires, protect me.
May the goddess Aiṃ Kālī, whose nature is the root-center (mūlādhāra), protect me;
may the goddess Ikālī, who bestows all splendor and light, protect me.
May Lakārī, the goddess most beloved by Indra, protect me;
may Hrīṃ Kālī, the beautiful goddess, protect me everywhere and grant me peace.
O Śāmbhavī, O Mahāmohā, with these very colors, protect my head on the earth; O Goddess, wife of Hara, protect me in the skull, O Sarvāṇī.
May the Goddess, the destroyer of all sins, protect me at the letter *ma*;
may the Goddess, who assumes forms at will, protect me then at the letter *ka*.
May the goddess Lakālī, the beloved of Śambarāri, always protect me at all times;
may the goddess Lakālī, who assumes the form of the supporter of the earth, protect me.
Hrīṃ! May the goddess Kālī, whose body is half that of Śiva, protect me;
may Mahāmāyā, who is the very embodiment of power, protect me with these syllables.
May Vāgbhava protect the head; may Kāmarājikā protect the face;
and may Śakti, whose form is the syllable *svā*, protect the heart, bestowing the accomplishment of the mantra.
May Sunyarī protect me always; may Sundarī guard me well. May Raktavarṇā protect me always, and may Sundarī grant all my desires.
May Sundarī, adorned with various ornaments, protect [us] forever;
may she who is beautiful in every limb protect [us] forever.
May Sarvāgasundarī, who bestows auspiciousness everywhere,
who generates joy for the world, and whose form is that of Śambhu, protect me always.
May she who consists of all mantras protect [us], the bestower of all prosperity;
the Goddess who embodies all Lakṣmī, the giver of supreme bliss.
May the auspicious Goddess Nānāśaṅkhanidhi protect me at all times;
thereafter, O Goddess, may Padmanidhi, the bestower of everything, protect me always.
May Dakṣiṇāmūrti protect me everywhere; may the Ṛṣi protect the head, and the Sureśvarī, whose form is the meter (Chandas), protect the face;
may Śāntarī, who consists of the eight fragrances (Gandhāṣṭaka), always protect the heart.
May Sarvasanmohinī protect; may Saṃkṣobhiṇī always guard [me].
May she who causes all to flee protect me; may she who effects the attraction of all protect me;
may she who brings joy through the attraction of all protect me; and may she who eternally agitates all protect me.
May she who bestows all accomplishments protect me; may she who effects the attraction of all things, the agitator, and the one who brings all under control, always guard me.
May Ākarṣiṇī always protect me; may Saṃmohinī ever guard me;
may the goddess Rati always protect me; may Bhagā protect me at all times.
May Maheśvarī protect me always; may Kaumārī protect me at all times; may Sarvāhlādanakālī protect me; and may Sarvavaśaṅkarī protect me.
May Kṣemaṅkarī, who is beautiful in every limb, always protect me;
may she who is a youth in every limb and the bestower of all good fortune protect me.
May Vāgdevī protect me always; may Vāṇinī protect me at all times;
may Vaśinī protect me always, she who forever bestows the great siddhis.
May Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me; may Gaṇanātha always protect me;
may Goddess Durgā always protect me; may Vaṭuka protect me at all times.
May Kṣetrapāla always protect, and may Ādhāraśakti protect; may Ananta protect at all times, and may Vārāha protect at all times.
May the Earth protect me at all times, as well as the golden lion-throne; may she likewise protect me from every moment with her red clay.
May Sudhārṇiva always protect; may Kalpakṛkṣi always protect;
may Śvetacchatra always protect; may Raktadīpa always protect.
May the Nandana grove protect me constantly for the sake of all accomplishments; likewise, may all the guardians of the directions, Indra and the rest, protect me at all times.
May vehicles always protect; may missiles protect at all times;
may weapons protect forever; and may the Yoginīs protect at all times.
May the Goddess Siddhyā protect me always; may she grant all accomplishments.
May the Goddess, beautiful in every limb, protect me everywhere and at all times.

May the Goddess, whose form is bliss, whose nature is consciousness, and whose essence is consciousness; who is beautiful in every limb, the beautiful one, the source of all beauty—protect me! O Sundarī, be auspicious!
May the beautiful Śivā protect me in a terrible temple, in a narrow pass, on an inaccessible mountain, or even in a desolate wilderness.
O Pārvatī, this has been declared as the armor (kavaca) and the extraction of the mantra;
he who, having become restrained and pure, recites it at the three junctions of the day, shall attain liberation.
For one who has accomplished all aims, whatever resides in the mind shall be attained;
[this is achieved] with *gorocanā*, saffron, or red sandalwood.
With white *svayambhū* flowers, when Mars or Saturn is present,
one should perform [the rite] at a cremation ground, or in the morning, in an empty house, or in a temple of Śiva.
Having worshipped the yantra with devotion through the Guru, the young maiden [should proceed].
Having caused that mantra to be recited and having especially honored the lineage of gurus according to one's ability, and having praised them with a pure mind, O Asura, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the *yantra* with *kumārī* and the rest as directed by the Guru, one should maintain it;
and likewise, having worshipped *tanyaunau* and the lineage of Gurus (*gurupakti*).
Then, having offered an oblation to the Goddess with human beings,
goats, cats, pigs, mongooses, buffaloes, and rams, he worshipped her according to the prescribed ritual.
Having placed it within a vessel of pure gold around one's neck, on the left head, or on the arm,
on an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation at the rising of the sun;
Having worn this armor, a person shall obtain all perfections;
yet the majesty of this armor cannot be fully described even in hundreds of years.
O Great Goddess, I am indeed able to describe its fruit:
for such a person there is no fear of thieves, nor is there any affliction by disease.
There is no fear of famine there, nor is there ever any oppression.
It pacifies all obstacles, destroys all diseases,
is the source of all auspicious marks, and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life upon the Lord of Jambūdvīpa.
One should never speak of it or give it away here or there;
having received the mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise person should worship it constantly.
Even there, I consider it difficult to obtain the armor of divine form; having propitiated my guru, I obtained that which was well-guarded as a secret.
Even there, this divine armor is difficult to obtain within the three worlds;
yet he who, being self-restrained and pure, recites even a single verse of its true meaning, [attains the fruit].
For him, all goals shall be accomplished; this was proclaimed by Śaṅkara:
the Guru is God Hara himself, and his consort is Pārvatī.
"For him who worships without making distinctions, success is not far off.
Thus ends the *Tripurabhairavī Kavaca* in the venerable *Viśvasāra Tantra*.
241b) Now follows the armor of Lakṣmī.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the armor-mantra (kavaca) which grants all desires;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself.
O son of Pārvatī, a person who performs her worship, adoration, and the recitation of her mantra shall be honored by all the scriptures.
This [mantra], which is especially dear to Viṣṇu, should be served by one who seeks the entry into knowledge.

Of this *Śrī-caturakṣarī-viṣṇustuti-kavaca*, the Lord Śrīnivāsa is the *ṛṣi*, the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter, Vāgbhavī is the deity, Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Larjā is the power (*śakti*), and Ramā is the bolt (*kīlaka*).
The armor [mantra] consisting of the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) is employed for the sake of attaining my own poetic skill, scholarship, and the full accomplishment of all siddhis.
This is the viniyoga.

May the syllable *Aiṃ* protect my head; may the seed-syllable *Vāgbhava*, doubled, protect my intellect and speech. May *Hrīṃ* protect the center of my eyes, and may the goddess Śākarī protect the pair of my eyes.
On the tongue and the perimeter of the mouth are Kaṇa and Vāṇa; on the upper and lower lips and the row of teeth is Sita; and furthermore, on the root of the palate is Hala.
May Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, who possesses the color and form of Śrī, protect me—
O Pārvatī— with her five [faces] upon her two ears and two pairs of arms.
One should bind the heart-jewel (hṛdayamaṇi) at the navel, on both sides,
as well as on the region of the back, and likewise in the private parts on the left and the right.
Furthermore, on the two breasts, the hips, the navel, the two shanks, the two knees,
the two feet, the anus, and the root of the thighs.
Svadhā resides in my vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), while the Great Goddess Samunnati, the mistress of the ripening of all limbs, dwells again in the crown of my head at the parting of the hair.
May Mahāmāyā grant nourishment; may Utkṛṣṭi protect me at all times. O Goddess, may Ṛṣi protect me; may she be victorious everywhere.
May Vāgbhavī protect me always; may the consort of Hara protect me;
may the goddess Ramā protect me always; and may Māyā herself protect me.
May Ugratārā protect me always from all sides; may she protect me for a hundred years.
May Kālikā protect me constantly; may Kālarātri protect me forever.
May Navadurgā protect me always; may Kāmākhyā protect me at all times; may the Yoginīs protect me always; and may Mahālakṣmī protect me forever.
May the goddesses and the hosts of Kuṣṭha-yoginīs always maintain their measure in all places,
in all undertakings, and in every action at all times.
"May Lakṣmī, the Queen of the Gods of gods and bestower of all prosperity, protect me.
Thus has this divine armor (kavaca), which grants all perfections, been told to you.
O Maheśvarī, wherever it would not be right to speak if one desires the welfare of others— namely, to the deceitful, the faithless, and the slanderer— [there it must remain unsaid].
One should never show one's own body when it is deficient in limbs, empty, or marked by scars;
for one who displays such [a body] would be a destroyer of Śiva’s divine form.
One should give the image of Kaca to one who is of noble birth, a great lord, devoted to Durgā, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure.
One should write the mantra for one's own disciple who is peaceful, righteous, and likewise wise, using the letters Śa, Na, Ma, Aṅga, La, Ca, Na, and Nda.
One should draw the divine armor (kavaca), endowed with all its mantras, using auspicious, self-arisen flowers.
With white mustard seeds and black mustard seeds endowed with various fragrances,
one should smear the *mūmenara* with *gorocanā* and fresh red sandalwood.
On an auspicious lunar day or in a favorable yoga, on the day of the sun (Sunday) in the asterism Śravaṇā,
or on Tuesday in Aśvinī, Maghā, or Pūrvabhādrapadā, one should perform the sacrifice.
One should write out or recite the hymn in a divine abode during an auspicious conjunction;
one becomes long-lived through the conjunction of *prīti*, and especially so through the conjunction of *brahma*.
In the conjunction of Indra, in an auspicious conjunction, and likewise in the Śukla conjunction;
and in Kaulava, Vālava, and Vanija as well, O best of men.
In an empty house, in a cremation ground, or especially in a temple,
having worshipped Kumārī, one shall conquer the eternal Goddess.
One should worship the supreme deity with fish, meat, vegetables,
and soups, as well as with offerings such as ghee, and especially with incense and lamps.
O Supreme Goddess, having fed the Brahmins, one should worship them;
there, one should perform the narrative of Āṣeṭaka for three days.
Then there shall be great protection; this was spoken by Śaṅkara.
He will undoubtedly obtain powers such as killing and inciting hatred;
he shall become the son of Pārvatī, yet remain excluded from all the scriptures.
The Guru is Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
for him who worships them without making any distinction between them, spiritual perfection is not far off.
The mortal who recites this here with a mind free from pride shall obtain the fruit of this rite as it is prescribed;
he becomes a high station for the attainment of prosperities, bowing at the feet of the Earth, and for a long time he remains marked by the fortune of the lineage of kings.
Thus ends the Lakṣmī-kavaca in the venerable Viśvasāra-tantra.
Now follows the armor-mantra (kavaca) of Mātaṅgī.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious Mātaṅgī-kavaca;
it must be kept secret, O Great Goddess, and one should perform its recitation in silence.
The Goddess said:
Excellent, excellent, Mahādeva! O Maheśvara, please explain that by which, through the correct procedure, victory shall come to practitioners.
Without meditation on the lute, without ritual procedures, without mantras, without fire-offerings, and without oblations—
by the mere remembrance of whom the practitioner becomes a lord of the earth.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The divine armor of Mātaṅgī provides all protection for men;
it bestows poetic talent, wealth, elephants, horses, happiness, a pleasant face, auspiciousness, and the granting of gems and other such things.
O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, Maheśvarī is the primordial source of them all;
a man who should properly recite even half a verse or a single verse [of this hymn], [attains the supreme goal].
In his hand resides the royal fortune along with the goddess Lakṣmī; of this there is no doubt.
Having made his face [the remains of] food offerings, he sits upon a lotus seat.

Having bound the *yoni-mudrā* at the time of the *kalā*, one who is devoted to the meditation on Śakti and whose mind is fixed on the *brahmarandhra* shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds.
The armor that is the essence of the auspiciousness of the three worlds, whose very body is mantra.
O Goddess, this *siddhavidyā* bestows all sovereignty upon me; Śiva himself is the author of this armor (*kavaca*).
The meter is Virāṭ, the deity is Jagaddhātrī Bhuvaneśvarī;
its application is proclaimed for the attainment of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
May *hrīṃ*, my seed-syllable, protect my head; may *aiṃ* Bhuneśī protect my forehead; may *aiṃ* protect my right eye, and may *hrīṃ* protect my left eye.
May Śrīṃ, the three-syllabled Maheśvarī, protect my right ear;
may Aiṃ always protect my left ear, and may she always protect my nose.
Hrīṃ! May the Goddess protect my face; Aiṃ! May she protect my tongue.
May Vāk protect the three syllables of the *tripura* mantra; may Parāmbikā protect my throat.
May *Śrī* protect my two shoulders constantly; may *Hrīṃ* protect my arms at all times.
O *Tripureśānī*, in the *Kali* age, you who traverse the heavens with the three syllables *klīṃ*.
May the three-syllabled Bhuvaneśvarī protect the heart with *āṃ* and the middle region with *hrāṃ*.

May she who possesses all seeds and always brings everything under her control protect [you] from behind.
Hrīṃ: may the Blessed Lady protect the secret place; Māheśvarī always protect the hips and the pair of knees with the seed-syllable Śakti.
May Arṇā Pūrṇā always protect [me], Svāhā protect my two feet;
may the ten-syllabled Sāmā protect me, and Annapūrṇā protect my entire body.
May she who consists of the syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, *ramā*, and *kāma*, followed by the sixteen vowels,
protect me always with joy, stationed upon my head as the *viśasvanā*.
"Tāraṃ Durge yugaṃ rakṣa svāhā"—thus [is the mantra] for the right side.
"Jaye Durgā ghanasyāme pātu sāṃ sarvato bhavet."

May she who begins with the seed-syllable *bīja*, who is the ten vowels (*daśārṇā*), who is situated upon the head, who bestows everything, and who stands joyfully as the nourishment of the universe, protect me forever.
*Tāram* (Om), *Durge*, *Yugam*, *Rakṣa*, *Svāhā*— this ten-syllable mantra,
as well as *Jaya Durgā*, may the dark-hued goddess protect me from all sides with joy.
May Māyā protect my seed-syllable, and may the ten-syllabled one following it protect my head;
may Jayadurgā, shining like molten gold, grant me victory.
The supreme [mantra] consists of eight syllables: *tāraṃ hrīṃ durgāyai namaḥ*.
May she who holds the conch, discus, and mace, the supporter of the earth, protect me from the right;
she is Mahiṣamardanī, Svāhā, and the supreme Vasuvarṇā.
May she who destroys the demon Mahiṣāsura protect [us] always from the southwest;
Māyā Padmāvatī Svāhā is proclaimed as the seven-syllabled mantra.
May Padmāvatī, seated upon a lotus, always protect me in the west; O Supreme Goddess, who is like a snow-mountain, Svāhā to the Mother who holds the noose and the goad!
Victory! She who begins with the ten syllables, mounted upon a horse as if on a face;
O Sarasvatī, five-arrowed one, eternal, O you who are moist, intoxicated, and flowing!
May the eternal Svāhāratyakṣarī, who is beyond the mind, always protect me!
[Recite] Tāra, Māyā, Kavaca, Khecarakṣa, and then Vadhū.
*krū-oṃ kṣa hrīṃ phaṭ*, this twelve-syllable great vidyā, which bestows everything—
may it always protect me from misfortune and other evils, O Śivakāṇa!
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ! May the head of Sātatīvālāmā protect me from the ten directions.
May Bhairavī Vālā, who dwells at the end of the world, protect me always upon the earth.
Thus has been told to you this meritorious and supreme blessing for the three worlds.
By the mere recitation of this, which is the most excellent essence of merit and the destroyer of the flood of great ignorance,
even Kubera himself instantly became the lord of wealth.
By means of this retention and recitation, all the gods beginning with Indra,
having become lords of all accomplishments, shall attain supreme sovereignty.
One should offer eight handfuls of flowers at the root [of the tree] rather than separately;
one shall obtain the fruit of a hundred years of worship.
Having derived joy from other sources, Lakṣmī shall dwell in your home with her children, and Vāṇī shall reside in your mouth; this is the truth, the truth, without a doubt.
He who wears this supreme, meritorious armor named *Laukikamaṅgala*,
which bestows merit upon its wearer, is himself the foremost among the virtuous.
Having become endowed with all sovereign powers, one shall be victorious over the three worlds.
A man [should place it] on the right arm, and likewise a woman on the left arm;
having thus become possessed of many sons, even a barren woman obtains a son.
This is not merely a pacifying mantra for the Brahmāstra and other weapons;
without knowing this armor (kavaca), one cannot know the World-Mistress born from the knees.
"Having fallen into extreme poverty, he shall meet death before long.
Thus ends the *Trailokyamaṅgala*, the armor (*kavaca*) of Bhuvaneśvarī, spoken in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*.
Now, he speaks the Dhūmāvatī-kavaca.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees,
O ocean of compassion, please tell me the armor (kavaca) of Dhūmāvatī.
Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, there exists in this world a most secret armor that subdues enemies and bestows all things; out of affection for you, it is now being revealed.
249a) Having heard which, Rāmacandra slew Rāvaṇa in battle; and having heard which, Bhogaveṇa conquered the entire host of rākṣasas.
I shall speak that very armor; listen with full attention.
O Great Goddess, Pippada is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor.
O Dear One, Chanda, Virāṭ, and the deity Śrīmaddhumavatī—
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the Vinīyoga for the slaying of enemies.
May she who possesses smoke-like [emanations] always protect my head, O crusher of enemies;
may the Great Goddess Caṇḍarūpā always protect my forehead.
May Kṣukṣā protect my eyes; may she protect my ears.
May she who has the crow as her banner protect my nose—she who is the destroyer of all enemies.
May Praṇamvī, adorned with a garland of skulls, always protect my face;
may Vikṛtāsyā, the beauty of her enemies, always protect my throat.
May the seed-syllable *dhūṃ*, which is ever-renowned as the destroyer of misfortune, protect my neck; may Kaṅkāli protect my shoulders.
Thus ends [the section on] the shoulders.
